file: 13 Officials From Tibet on Two-Week U.S. Tour.txt
text:
ï»¿
Amid reports of the worst unrest in Tibet in three decades, officials from the region and its capital city have been on a two- week tour of the United States.
The 13-member delegation arrived in the United States on Oct. 
7.
The delegation, which includes Luo Gar, the Mayor of Lhasa, and Thang Zhengqi, deputy secretary of the Tibetan Autonomous Region, left Boulder today for San Francisco, their final stop.
Boulder was on the group's itinerary because it established a Sister City program with Lhasa two years ago at the behest of local Buddhists. 
But some Buddhists here have denounced the visitors because they are officials of China, which annexed Tibet in 1950.
On Oct. 
1, when 14 people were reported killed in the worst clashes, the Mayor and other members of the delegation were in Chengdu, 750 miles from Lhasa, en route to the United States.
The Mayor played down the anti-Chinese unrest. 
''If it had been really violent,'' he said through an interpreter here, ''we would never have been able to leave the country.''
He said his group had not been in direct contact with colleagues in Lhasa since leaving Shanghai on Oct. 
3.

file: 60 Shout Out Dalai Lama_s Name And Are Seized in Protest in Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 60 people shouting the name of the Dalai Lama, Tibet's former civil and religious leader, marched today to a Government office, where armed Chinese security forces quickly arrested them.
The marchers, believed to be Buddhist monks in street clothes, did not resist arrest. 
About 2,000 bystanders made no attempt to help them or four monks who were arrested at about the same time in the Jokhang Temple square, where pro-independence protests last week left several people dead.
The Chinese Government has reportedly sent 1,000 armed policemen to Lhasa, the Tibetan capital. 
The troops are to guard against further unrest on Wednesday, the 37th anniversary of the day China occupied Tibet.
Â 
Quiet Day Expected
Tibetans and Chinese questioned on the street said they expected the anniversary to be quiet because of fears that the police would fire on protesters.
Western witnesses said the police fired last Thursday on demonstrators who burned a police station and vehicles in the temple square.
Western doctors in Lhasa said eight Tibetans were shot to death and one unidentified Chinese was stoned to death. 
The authorities said six Chinese policemen were killed. 
It was not known if the Chinese was one of the six.
There was a smaller, less violent protest on Sept. 
27 that resulted in about two dozen arrests. 
The march today was the first significant public protest since Thursday.
Â 
Dalai Lama's Name Chanted
About 100 marchers raised their fists and chanted the name of the Dalai Lama, who fled to exile in India after an uprising against Chinese rule in 1959. 
China annexed Tibet in 1950.
The marchers did not wear the saffron robes usually worn by monks, but they came from the direction of the Drepung monastery, one of three leading monasteries whose members led the independence demonstrations last week. 
The monastery is about five miles west of Lhasa.
Western witnesses said a few were arrested quietly on the way and that others left the march. 
About 60 marchers continued to the gate of the Tibetan regional government office. 
About 100 members of the security forces carrying submachine guns and automatic pistols immediately herded them onto trucks.
Â 
'Very Thoroughly Searched'
''I don't think they were resisting,'' said Derek Olson of Oak Park, Ill. 
''They were very thoroughly searched before being put in the truck.''
Another American witness, Cliff Toliver of Cincinnati, said some bystanders surged forward and shouted when policemen and soldiers struck a marcher. 
No clash ensued.
Mr. Olson said the crowd started to scatter twice, apparently in response to threatening moves from the security people. 
''It was definitely a very panicky situation,'' he said.
Amber Kvanli, like Mr. Olson a student from St. Olaf College in Minnesota, said Tibetans fled in panic from the busy market next to the temple when about 30 armed policemen marched up to four monks who were sitting on the ground chanting.
Â 
Children Gathered Up
''Suddenly people started yelling, moms started gathering their kids, and one young Tibetan came up to me and put me in a doorway,'' she said. 
''The monks stopped chanting, got up and went with the police. 
They left behind their song books and the blankets they were sitting on.''
It was not known what happened to those arrested. 
Monks at the Sera and Drepung monasteries said previously that police came and arrested 47 members and that others were missing after the demonstration Thursday.

file: Amid Turmoil, Journalists Leave Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fourteen foreign journalists from six countries left Tibet today after being ordered out of the region by the Chinese authorities.
The expulsions came after 20 days of protests, led by monks and other Tibetans, against Chinese rule. 
Another journalist covered by the expulsion order left Lhasa, the capital, on Thursday.
A Chinese official declared that the journalists, including this correspondent, were in Tibet illegally and that any effort to report anti-Chinese protests was prohibited.
Lhasa and at least one other Tibetan city have been the sites of marches led by monks to demand that the Chinese leave Tibet, which was invaded by Chinese troops and finally annexed in 1951. 
In one demonstration on Oct. 
1, it now appears that at least 9 Tibetans and 4 policemen were killed.
Â 
Reporting Severely Limited
After permitting sporadic reports of the protests from Tibet for several days, the Chinese authorities here severed contact with Lhasa, preventing foreign journalists there from reporting directly on events. 
Some accounts were carried to Chengdu, a city 750 miles east of Lhasa, but most reporting has been severely limited.
According to a foreign manager of Lhasa's main tourist hotel, Chinese officials have ordered all foreigners to leave Tibet unless they are on official business or on official tours. 
The Chinese have denied issuing such an order.
On Tuesday, an anti-Chinese march by as many as 100 monks from Drepung Monastery, just outside Lhasa, turned violent when heavily armed Chinese policemen attacked the protesters, beating them with clubs, rifle butts and belts. 
Ninety monks were arrested as they tried to march on the provincial government offices.
Since Tuesday, Lhasa has been very tense. 
Although most shops and market stalls had reopened by Thursday, they closed much earlier than usual, and streets were empty by early evening.
A Chinese restaurant owner in Lhasa said many of the Chinese who had been sent there as government officials had gone home early because they feared being attacked by Tibetans.
Â 
Monasteries Sealed Off
On Wednesday, all of Lhasa's monasteries, the religious heart of Tibetan Buddhism, were sealed off by blockades of policemen brandishing automatic weapons and pistols. 
All local cars and trucks were stopped and their drivers questioned.
The Chinese police have plastered the walls of monasteries with posters denouncing the Dalai Lama, the leader of Tibetan Buddhism, whom they accused of encouraging separatist activity from his exile in Dharmsala, India.
Other Chinese officials have been seen lecturing young monks on China's version of Tibetan history and have interrogated all senior abbots at the monasteries. 
At the Jokhang Cathedral, the most sacred of Buddhism's shrines in Tibet, the Chinese police have occupied the upper floors, using the temple as an observation post.
At least 600 heavily armed policemen arrived in Lhasa during the week. 
On Wednesday, the 37th anniversary of China's invasion, they staged a major show of force by driving a convoy of 20 trucks, including 13 packed with policemen armed with AK-47 assault rifles, through the old Tibetan quarter.
The police have patrolled rooftops of the Tibetan quarter and have set up roadblocks in various parts of Lhasa.
Â 
A Meeting in Lhasa
Efforts by journalists in Tibet to send out reports on the events of the last few days proved almost impossible and were in fact ruled illegal at a meeting in Lhasa shortly after midnight Thursday between a senior Chinese official and 15 foreign reporters.
Yu Wuzhen, the director of Tibet's foreign affairs office, read a statement ordering the 15 foreign reporters out of Tibet. 
Mr. Yu charged the journalists with failing to provide the provincial authorities with what he said was a required 10-day advance notification of their intention to work in Tibet.
The meeting was also attended by two American diplomats who were in Lhasa, Raymond F. Burghardt, the political counselor at the United States Embassy in Beijing, and Scott D. Bellard, a consular officer from Chengdu.

file: AT TIBET FRONTIER, CHINA AND INDIA SQUARE OFF.txt
text:
ï»¿
As tension along China's easternmost border with India continues, China is pouring tremendous numbers of soldiers and weapons into the sparsely populated mountainous area along the two countries' disputed border.
In the last two weeks, convoys of troops, artillery, rockets and supplies have been winding over the dusty gravel road leading to the border.
One day last week, Chinese Army trucks covered with thick olive-green camouflage netting trundled through the southern town of Zedang toward the border 75 miles away at a rate of one a minute over a period of six hours. 
In one convoy, 14 four-wheel-drive trucks were seen hauling camouflaged artillery pieces that one Westerner said were probably 88-millimeter field guns.
Unusually High Visibility
Both Indian and Chinese officials emphatically deny that there have been any conflicts between the two armies. 
Nonetheless, both Tibetans and Westerners with long experience in Tibet said the level of military activity exceeded even the usual highly visible presence of the Chinese Army here in Tibet, which was annexed by China in 1950 and made into an autonomous region.
Since 1960, China and India have contested their boundaries, drawn vaguely by Britain in 1913 and 1914. 
After the Communist takeover in China in 1949, the new Government rejected that demarcation. 
In 1962, the two countries fought a brief and indecisive war along sections of the 700 miles of mountain ridges running from Bhutan and Burma, which the British Government had declared the official border.
Concern among Western countries over the possibility of armed conflict between the world's two most populous nations is acute, and diplomats and military attaches from various countries have visited Lhasa and nearby towns in recent weeks. 
Two army liaison officers from the United States Consulate in Hong Kong were in Lhasa, as were diplomats from several other countries. 
#2 Journalists Caught Two Western journalists, a reporter for the Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat and a freelance photographer from Canada, were caught last week by Chinese military officials barely five miles from the Indian border, in an area closed to foreigners. 
This week, officials in Lhasa were to question the journalists about their activities in the closed military zone.
In addition to the continuous flow of arms and soldiers south and east toward the border, there are other signs that Chinese military officials are preparing for the possibility of clashes.
In Lhasa, the army hospital near the ancient monastery of Sera was cleared of ill tourists. 
One such tourist said that the hospital, which is considered the best in Lhasa, was empty of patients when he left but that the staff appeared to be preparing for large numbers of new patients.
For two weeks, from May 6 to 20, Tibet's only civilian airport, in Gonggar, 70 miles from Lhasa, was closed to commercial flights on even-numbered days. 
This has not occurred since Tibet was opened to foreign tourists seven years ago, according to Tibetans and Westerners. 
On even-numbered days, large military transports were seen at the airport unloading equipment. 
A Western diplomat said he saw rockets being loaded onto trucks.
Â 
'That's the War'
In the last two weeks, helicopters and jet fighters have frequently roared over this city of 150,000. 
A resident of Lhasa said when a fighter plane streaked overhead, ''Oh, that's the war.''
Lhasa residents say neither helicopters nor jet fighters have ever flown over Lhasa with such regularity.
Around Lhasa, soldiers and armed policemen brandishing AK-47 rifles and submachine guns have set up numerous roadblocks where all vehicles are checked. 
Soldiers carrying automatic weapons and marching in small groups have occasionally appeared on the streets as well.
Chinese and Indian officials have met seven times since 1981 to discuss the demarcation of their border, but both sides say there has been no progress. 
The contested area, about 34,000 square miles of largely inaccessible mountains and valleys, was declared a state, called Arunchal Pradesh, by India last year. 
That enraged the Chinese, who also claim the land.
When first drawn, the boundary, then called the McMahon Line, was to cut across the ridges of the highest peaks between Bhutan and Burma. 
At the time the boundary was drawn, however, there was no certainty about which were the highest mountains.
China and India also dispute more than 14,000 square miles of their westernmost border. 
New Delhi contends the land belongs to Kashmir; Beijing maintains it is Chinese territory.

file: BEIJING IS BACKED BY ADMINISTRATION ON UNREST IN TIBET.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Reagan Administration voiced support today for China's position in the unrest in Tibet, while the Senate voted without dissent to condemn China for its recent crackdown there.
Anti-Chinese demonstrations in Tibet have turned violent in recent days, with more than 14 people reported killed in one clash on Thursday. 
The protests were renewed today as about 60 people marched to a Government office in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, where armed Chinese security forces quickly arrested them. 
[Page A8.] The divergent positions taken by the Administration and Congress on the events in Tibet reflect contrasting interests. 
The Administration is reluctant to take positions that might damage Chinese-American relations. 
But the 98-to-0 vote by the Senate today highlights Congressional concern over reports of human rights violations in Tibet, which China took over in 1950.
State Department Assails Vote
The vote is certain to be protested by China as an example of American interference.
State Department officials today voiced strong opposition to the Senate action. 
The measure, an amendment to the State Department authorization bill, also urged President Reagan to meet with the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled Buddhist leader.
In addition, it would require Mr. Reagan to certify that China is making progress on resolving human rights issues in Tibet before the United Stats proceeds with any new sales of arms or weapons technology to China.
The amendment does not call for economic sanctions against China, and a provision that would have required the United States to ''reassess and review'' arms sales because of China's actions in Tibet was deleted.
Â 
'Almost Certain Damage' to Ties
One State Department official said that any possible benefits of the Senate action for the Tibetan people were ''insufficient to outweigh the almost certain damage to the U.S.-China bilateral relationship.''
The United States has supported China's stated efforts in recent years to make amends in Tibet after two decades of repression. 
In recent days, the State Department has reaffirmed the American position that Tibet is part of China and that the Dalai Lama is a religious leader, not the head of a government in exile.
The United States has recognized China's sovereignty over Tibet since the 1940's, and has held since 1978 that Tibet is a part of China.
The Dalai Lama, who is both the spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhists, fled Tibet in 1959 after Chinese troops crushed an uprising. 
He is now based in Dharmsala, India, although he periodically visits other countries.
His visit to the United States late last month and his testimony before Congressional panels was cited by Beijing as an interference in Chinese affairs.
Although the United States has often protested human rights abuses since the United States and China formally established embassies in each other's capitals in 1979, it has taken great care not to offend Chinese sensibilities.
Â 
Upbeat State Department Report
In a 24-page report to Congress Oct. 
1 on the treatment of minorities in China, written before the recent outbreak of violence, the State Department took a generally upbeat tone on Tibet. 
The report said that, since 1980, the Chinese Government had made a conscious effort to ease tensions and begin economic and other changes.
''Beijing has stressed its commitment to preserve Tibet's unique cultural, linguistic and religious traditions,'' the report concluded, in an effort to ''strengthen social stabilityI.''
Today's Senate action challenges that assertion and calls for the State Department to present an updated human rights report in 60 days.
The amendment accuses Chinese authorities of executing two Tibetans after the Dalai Lama testified before Congress last month. 
It also blames the Chinese police for violent clashes with demonstrators on Sept. 
27 and for killing at least six Tibetans and wounding many others when they opened fire on unarmed demonstrators Thursday.
Â 
Population Transfer Charged
The Senate also charged that China has moved to transfer millions of Chinese into Tibet in an effort to ''make the Tibetan people a minority in their own homeland.''
One State Department official characterized the Senate portrayal of developments in Tibet as ''inaccurate, incomplete and misleading.''
Reiterating a position first articulated after a similar amendment was passed by the House last June, the official faulted the Senate for failing to acknowledge ''significant changes'' in China's policies that, he said, have led to an improvement of human rights conditions in Tibet.
The Senate amendment is expected to be considered by the House after the Senate passes the State Department authorization bill, which then goes to the President for his signature.
Â 
Dalai Lama Peace Plan
The State Department also takes issue with assertions of large Chinese population transfers into Tibet, accepting the Chinese claim that the number of Chinese civilians there has actually declined since 1980.
The Reagan Administration is also unhappy with support on Capitol Hill for a five-point ''peace zone'' proposal made by the Dalai Lama to Congressional leaders during his little-publicized visit to Washington last month. 
The proposal calls for the withdrawal of Chinese troops from Tibet, an end to China's population-transfer policy and negotiations on the future of Tibet.
In a Sept. 
22 letter to Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China, Senator Claiborne Pell, Democrat of Rhode Island, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, and House Democratic and Republican leaders endorsed the proposal of the Dalai Lama as a ''historic step towards resolving the important question of Tibet and alleviating the suffering of the Tibetan people.''
Mr. Pell is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Although the Reagan Administration did not comment on the proposal at the time, one State Department official today characterized it as ''a veiled independence plan.''
He added, ''At this particular time, Congressional support for Tibetan independence sends the wrong signal to more-violent elements and could lead to more bloodshed.''
Â 
Plan Linked to Unrest
News of the Dalai Lama's proposal was widely disseminated in Tibet and is believed to have contributed to the atmosphere of unrest. 
So sensitive was his visit to the United States that Chinese authorities protested to the State Department and the American Embassy in Beijing even before his arrival and again after he announced his proposal.
Although the Dalai Lama did not request a meeting with President Reagan during his visit, State Department officials said that any request for a meeting with officials of the executive branch would have been denied because it might have given China the impression that the United States supported his political claims.

file: China_s Account of Riot in Tibet Is Disputed.txt
text:
ï»¿
The most senior Tibetan religious figure in China has disputed official assertions that Chinese policemen did not shoot at demonstrating monks during a riot in Lhasa last October.
China's Foreign Ministry, as well as security officials in Tibet and Beijing, have insisted repeatedly that the police never fired their weapons during the protests, in which more than 12 people were killed.
But in a report on Tibetan radio that reached here today, the Panchen Lama, the second-holiest figure in Tibetan Buddhism, said that the police fired warning shots to disperse crowds attacking a police station, and that ricochets killed and wounded several people.

8 and Feb.

file: CHINESE REPLACE LEADER OF TIBET.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has dismissed the Communist Party leader in Tibet and tightened security to prevent monks from staging new anti-Chinese protests, Westerners in the autonomous region said today.
Speaking from Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, the Westerners said that monks and hundreds of pilgrims filled the main square outside the Buddhist shrine Saturday night and chanted the Prayer of Truth.
They said police officers patrolling nearby did not intervene, although the prayer contained lines entreating the ''protectors of Tibet to drive the barbarians of the east from the land of the snows.''
The Westerners said the police began a crackdown on Nov. 
23 during a festival for Lhasa's goddess, the symbol for many Tibetans of their desire for independence from China.
The Communist Party leader, Wu Jinghua, a Chinese, was recalled to Beijing and dismissed for failing to stop a simmering revolt, the Westerners said.
A Communist Party spokeswoman in Beijing confirmed that Tibet had a new party general secretary as of Dec. 
1. She identified him as Hu Jintao, former party leader in Guizhou province. 
And she refused to comment on what had happened to Mr. Wu, who led the party in Tibet since 1985.
Â 
No Longer Separate
The Communist Government in Beijing took over Tibet in 1959 and forcibly incorporated it into China. 
Protests against Beijing's rule over the Himalayan region erupted periodically and notably in October 1987, in perhaps the bloodiest riots since the Dalai Lama, Tibet's Buddhist spiritual leader, to flee across the border to India.
Last March, monks again clashed with the police, and an unknown number were shot or beaten.
Residents in Lhasa said the city is tense with armed police circling the Johkang Temple, questioning people and checking identity papers. 
Foreign tourists had their passports checked and hotel rooms searched, the Westerners said.
The Westerners quoted informed Tibetans as saying more than 100 political prisoners, including at least 30 monks and nuns, had been transferred to other areas of China, perhaps to re-education centers.
Western diplomats were unsure what policy changes the new party leader would bring. 
But they noted that Mr. Hu was relatively young at 46 and had experience in Guizhou and Gansu provinces, both poor areas inhabited by minority people.

file: Communications to Tibet Cut And Foreigners Are Banned.txt
text:
ï»¿
Little new information was available yesterday about the situation in Tibet as telephone and telex communications were interrupted and travel there by foreigners was banned.
A State Department spokeswoman in Washington said ''everything is calm'' in Lhasa, the capital, as Tibetans marked the 37th anniversary of China's takeover of Tibet, but she acknowledged that reports from the area were ''fragmentary.''
The latest communication with an American consular officer visiting Lhasa occurred on Saturday, she said.
A Chinese airline official said a 10-day ban has been imposed on foreigners' travel to Tibet from Chengdu, the principal gateway to Lhasa, The Associated Press reported. 
Western travelers arriving in Chengdu from Lhasa yesterday said the Tibetan capital was quiet.
In Beijing, a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said foreigners were being advised not to go to Tibet at this time ''because Lhasa has a special situation.''
At least 14 people have been reported killed in clashes between Tibetan nationalists and Chinese security forces in Tibet in the last two weeks.
Â 
Lhasa Is Virtually Sealed Off
It could not be confirmed that the communications blackout was ordered by the Chinese Government. 
A spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Wu Zurong, would say only that the way to contact Lhasa was through the telecommunications bureau in Beijing.
The New York Times was unable Tuesday and yesterday to contact its correspondent, Edward A. Gargan, who reported from Lhasa on Monday. 
Mr. Gargan is chief of the Times bureau in Beijing.
A Washington Post correspondent, Daniel Southerland, who left Tibet late Monday to send an article from Chengdu, tried unsucessfully to return to Lhasa Tuesday and yesterday.
The Associated Press said its correspondent had been able to telephone reports from Lhasa on Tuesday but had not been heard from since shortly after midnight yesterday, New York time. 
United Press International received the last 10-minute telex message from its staff correspondent at 4 A.M.
Â 
Second-Hand Reports
The Associated Press and Reuters filed reports yesterday based on interviews with travelers arriving from Lhasa in Chengdu, who . told journalists that security officers visited several hotels in Lhasa around midnight Tuesday night and checked guests' passports. 
They said there were three roadblocks on the way to the airport.
The major American television networks said they did not have crews in the Tibetan capital. 
''They're making things very difficult,'' said Elizabeth Eynon, press representative for the ''CBS Evening News.''
ABC News said a producer and correspondent, Todd Carrel, left Lhasa on Tuesday.

file: Dalai Lama Approves Chinese Role in Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Dalai Lama, the exiled Tibetan Buddhist leader, said today that he recognized China's right to handle Tibet's foreign affairs and maintain troops on Tibetan soil.
The Dalai Lama proposed talks with China to make Tibet ''a self-governing, democratic political entity'' in association with China, which he said ''could remain responsible for Tibet's foreign policy.''
''Until such a peace conference can be convened and demilitarization and neutralization achieved, China could have the right to maintain a restricted number of military installations in Tibet,'' he said.
He made the remarks in a speech to a meeting of members of the European Parliament and reporters here.
The Dalai Lama had previously made little mention of Chinese interests in Tibet. 
He also neither accepted the Chinese military presence in the remote territory nor recognized China's right to handle its foreign affairs.
China regards Tibet as a critical buffer zone between itself and India, a traditional rival. 
Western estimates put the number of Chinese soldiers in Tibet at tens of thousands.

file: Dalai Lama Dismisses China_s Offer to Return.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Dalai Lama, the exiled spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, today dismissed China's offer to allow him to return to Tibet if he abandoned his campaign for independence. 
He said there was nothing new in the offer, which was made Monday, and indicated that he would not accept the restrictions.
''I have had that invitation from the Chinese Government since 1979,'' he said in London.
The Dalai Lama's visit to Britain is his first overseas trip since anti-Chinese rioting broke out in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, last September - there were new riots in March. 
The 52-year-old spiritual leader, who fled to India in 1959 after Chinese troops put down a nationalist rebellion, has long been an outspoken advocate of human rights and independence for the people of Tibet.
In brushing aside China's public offer to return to Tibet, the Dalai Lama stressed, instead, the value of his own campaign from exile for independence for the foreseeable future. 
He expressed a willingness to meet with the Chinese authorities, if there were genuine signs of improved treatment of Tibetans by the Chinese.
The Dalai Lama emphasized the need to solve the Tibetan problem through what he called ''the middle way - some kind of compromise.''
The middle way, according to the pacifist spiritual leader, lies between harsh rule by China and a fierce struggle for independence, the course advocated by some young Tibetan militants.
The Dalai Lama generally struck a conciliatory tone toward the Chinese authorities, saying he would be willing to meet with them in Beijing to discuss the Tibetan issue.

The move follows a speech by the Dalai Lama on June 15 in which, for the first time in 29 years of opposition to Chinese rule over Tibet, he acknowledged China's right to maintain troops there and to control Tibet's foreign affairs. 
Tibet was shaken last fall and in March by anti-Chinese riots. 
A Chinese spokesman here said Beijing was prepared to ''discuss everything except independence'' with the Dalai Lama.

file: Gandhi Heads Off to China for a State Visit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi left India today for a five-day state visit to China, the first by an Indian head of government since 1954.
Mr. Gandhi said the most important topic of his discussions in Beijing would be the two countries' longstanding border dispute, which included a monthlong war in 1962.
China routed Indian troops and then announced a unilateral cease-fire.Diplomatic relations were severed until 1976, with the exchange of ambassadors and visits by Chinese and Indian Foreign Ministers to New Delhi and Beijing respectively.
Indian diplomats said this week that though it would be ''unrealistic'' to expect a solution to major Chinese-Indian problems, they expected a significant improvement in relations.
Mr. Gandhi is to hold extensive talks with Chinese officials, including Prime Minister Li Peng, and the border dispute is said to be central to the negotiations. 
India asserts that China is in illegal possession of 14,000 square miles of territory near Kashmir state, including 2,000 square miles that it captured in the 1962 war.
Cambodia and India's role in seeking an end to the clashes between pro- and anti-Vietnamese forces there are also expected to figure in the discussions.

file: HARD TRAVELING ON THE WAY TO SHANGRI-LA.txt
text:
ï»¿
CLIFFORD D. MAY is the West African correspondent of The New York Times.
Â 
By CLIFFORD D.MAY
W ith travel, there is generally a tradeoff: The more exotic the destination, the more arduous the journey. 
But hard traveling need not be regarded as just the price one pays to get far away. 
On the contrary, those who truly subscribe to the view that it is better to go than to arrive also know that it is when the going gets rough that the excitement really begins.
I understood these rules subliminally at best when, along with seven friends (three other Americans, two Englishmen and two Pakistanis), I recently found myself in Islamabad contemplating a long weekend excursion into Pakistan's remote northern region. 
Within this area, three of the world's great mountain ranges - the Himalayas, the Karakorams and the Hindu Kush - converge, and eight of the world's 10 tallest mountains rise.
Highlights of traveling in Pakistan's remote northern region
The hub of the territory is a city called Gilgit, long ago a far western outpost of Tibetan Buddhism and an important trading center on the ancient Silk Route. 
More recently, Gilgit has been popular with European tourists on the overland route to the Far East; the war in neighboring Afghanistan has virtually put an end to that traffic, however.
Beyond Gilgit lies Hunza, the isolated valley that some say provided the inspiration for Shangri-La in James Hilton's ''Lost Horizon,'' and a place opened to foreigners without special permission only within about the last year. 
Finally, there is the Karakoram Highway, the artery that links these places, two narrow lanes joining Islamic Pakistan with China.
Around 1 o'clock on a Thursday afternoon we boarded a twin-engine Fokker 27 at the airport in Islamabad and settled back for what had been described as the breathtakingly scenic flight to Gilgit, 371 miles to the north. 
A tape recording of a sitar played softly. 
Tea and cakes were served with quiet grace by the hostess.
Through the window we watched the landscape grow rugged. 
On the highest peaks, among smudges of evergreens, the snow shone so brightly that it seemed to be lit from within. 
But the mood that was coming upon us was to be disturbed before we had even drained the tea from our cups. 
The ride suddenly became bumpy and islands of darkening cumulus clouds came into view ahead.
''Ladies and gentlemen,'' said a metallic voice, interrupting the strains of the sitar, ''we are sorry to tell you that due to bad weather we are having to turn back. 
Inshallah, we shall land in Islamabad momentarily. 
Please fasten your seat belts.''
The eight of us moaned. 
The other 40 or so passengers - none of them tourists, judging from the long dark veils draped over the women and the soft, flat-topped felt hats worn by the men - appeared neither surprised nor troubled by the news.
We had two choices: We could return to the hotel and hope for better luck on tomorrow's flight. 
Or we could attempt to reach Gilgit by road. 
Since the weather had already been unseasonably rainy for some days - and since the pilot prudently makes no attempt to maneuver through the tall mountains when it's even cloudy - we decided to go by land.
We hired a minibus and driver and were soon passing through fields carpeted with fresh hail. 
A light rain fell as we continued at a slow but steady clip to Hazara, in the North-West Frontier Province east of the Indus River, an area believed to have been settled by soldiers left behind by either Genghis Khan or Tamerlane.
No signpost marked the point, in the village of Havelian, where the road merges with the Karakoram Highway, constructed by the Pakistanis and the Chinese over a 20-year period. 
It is said that one life was lost for every kilometer of road. 
At the peak of the effort, 15,000 Pakistanis and 1,000 Chinese were working on the KKH, with little in the way of modern machinery.
The rain had just about stopped when we came to the village of Besham in the early evening. 
A queue of trucks lined both sides of the road, an indication of trouble ahead. 
We stopped to inquire at the local musafir khana, a sort of Pakistani truck stop, a squat cinder-block building containing rows of wooden cots, each strung with rope. 
In front of the building, tea brewed on a charcoal fire under a dim gas light.
''I'm afraid it is not possible for you to go any further,'' the man tending the fire told us. 
''The mountain is still moving.''
The leader of our group, Lieut. 
Col. Muhammad Akram Khan - a founding member of the Adventure Foundation (Pakistan), a nonprofit organization modeled on Outward Bound - explained that the recent rains had caused a landslide and the road could not be cleared because mud and rock were continuing to fall. 
''We should be able to get through in the morning,'' the colonel consoled us.
We went to a nearby guest house to pass the night. 
But when we moved out again just after dawn the trucks were still parked along the roadside. 
We pressed on until we could see the road disappear into a thick, smooth slab of mud that began high on the slope above and ended in a gorge several hundred feet below. 
We turned to Colonel Akram in despair. 
''Come now,'' he said. 
''We're not turning back yet.''
We grabbed our hand luggage and followed the colonel on a zigzagging trail down the steep, rocky mountainside. 
A line of men, some carrying boxes or trunks, some herding goats, trekked both ahead and behind us. 
Through the middle of the narrow gorge below ran a shallow stream, a small tributary of the Indus River, which splashed over smoothly rounded boulders. 
Before crossing the gorge, we looked up and listened attentively: Each time the rocks began to roll, people above whistled and yelled out a warning.
We crossed one at a time, as quickly as we could manage without losing our footing on the slick stones. 
Then, relieved that no rocks had made contact with our skulls, we began the long, tiring climb up the other side. 
The slope was so steep that we had to grab bushes for support. 
At one point, a goat just above us stopped, refusing to go farther despite the urgings of its herder and the whacks he was applying with a switch to its rump. 
The exasperated herder finally picked the goat up in his arms like a child and carried it the rest of the way up to the road. 
On the far side of the gorge, too, was a line of trucks that had been waiting since the day before. 
Colonel Akram told us to catch our breaths while he went off among them. 
Within minutes he was back, sitting next to the driver in a small Toyota diesel pickup. 
''Okay, it's arranged,'' the colonel said. 
''This man will take us at least part of the way to Gilgit. 
There will be a phone up ahead. 
I will arrange for other transport to be sent down to meet us.''
We piled ourselves and our luggage into the back and sped off along the serpentine road, high above the Indus River. 
The open cargo bed provided an unobstructed view and an extraordinarily heightened sense of speed. 
The faces of my companions - and probably my own as well - became pale as we swung from side to side, tightly grippling the railing and bouncing painfully on the metal floor.
The steep mountain slopes in which we were cradled were barren and eerily desolate. 
Only occasionally would we catch sight of a tiny plot of cultivated terraces, some no more than a few feet wide. 
Goats browsed among sparse brush nearby. 
And, looking carefully, we would invariably make out one or two small houses, constructed of the same gray stone as the mountains to which they so precipitously clung.
Until the completion of the KKH just four years ago, this area had been almost entirely cut off from the rest of the world. 
The lateral valleys beyond the road are still known as ''Yaghistan,'' which loosely translates as Land of the Unruled. 
In other words, they are tribal territory beyond the control of the Pakistani Government. 
We had been told that the people of Yaghistan could be quite hospitable; they could also draw and quarter you, more or less with impunity.
At a settlement about 50 miles from Besham our driver stopped: He didn't want to be too far away when the road was finally cleared. 
Colonel Akram arranged for us to switch to a small taxi with a canvas-enclosed bed containing two parallel wood benches on which passengers could sit facing one another. 
An assistant to the driver stood on a platform at the rear of the car, scanning the mountaintops for signs of a rockslide.
A little after 1 o'clock the car suddenly jolted and screeched to a halt. 
I had a vision of all the little headlines I had seen in newspapers over the years reporting a ''Bus Plunge'' in places very much like this. 
Luckily, we had not been going fast when the tire blew. 
The spare tire that the driver had brought along did not inspire confidence. 
It was covered in bulging patches, evidence of the many times it had been repaired.
A half hour or so farther down the road we met up with two Toyota jeeps that had set out from Gilgit following the colonel's phone call. 
We packed ourselves into these vehicles and contnued on, riding high above the silty Indus, its bone-colored sand beaches unmarred by human footprints.
At Chilas, a village about 4,000 feet above sea level, we stopped briefly at a small stone hut, another musafir khana, for milky tea, dal maash - a local dish made from yellow lentils and spices - and tandoori roti, flat round bread baked in deep stone ovens.
O n the road once more, the colonel pointed out Nanga Parbat, the Naked Mountain, with its snow-covered 26,660-foot peak. 
Finally, in the early evening, we entered Gilgit, where donkey carts rolled down the narrow streets and where the tiny stone shops in the bazaar were still crowded. 
It is said that long ago the people of Gilgit were fire worshippers. 
Then, beginning in the eighth century, China, Tibet and Arabia conquered the area in turn. 
Today the population of about 25,000 includes people of many ethnic groups: Pathans, Kashgaris, Chitralis, Tshins, Kirghizis and Hunzakuts.
We spent the night at a guest house and rose at 4:40 on Saturday morning to the sound of the muezzins calling the faithful to prayer. 
Because we were now about a day behind schedule, and because the weather looked fairly clear, we decided to set out again immediately, hoping to make it to the Chinese border and back - a round-trip excursion of a little more than 300 miles - by nightfall.
We headed out of town over the 100-year-old British-built suspension bridge that spans the Gilgit River and disappeared into a tunnel roughly carved through a mountain. 
We returned to the KKH, which twisted through bleak, infertile mountains where rare Marco Polo sheep and ibex are said to dwell. 
We neared Rakaposhi, the southernmost peak of the Karakorams, whose 25,550-foot peak was buried in clouds.
Our unofficial but well-informed guide for this part of the journey was the local police superintendent, Ali Ahmad Jan, who happened to be an old college chum of one of our fellow travelers, Syed Husain Mahmud, a freelance photographer. 
Superintendent Ali had blue eyes and a bushy blond moustache. 
His ancestors, he said, were either early Greek or Persian invaders, he wasn't sure which; he could trace only about 900 years of his family's history in this area.
It was fully light by the time we reached the Hunza Valley shortly before 6. 
We came around a turn and there, just ahead of us, three seasons seemed to coexist. 
The mountain summits were white and wintry. 
Just below them was a layer of autumnal red-brown rock. 
And down beside the river, stretched an alluvial plain, lush with pinkblossomed apricot trees, tall, swaying poplars, and neat, Lilliputian green pastures surrounded by sturdy stone fences.
The narrow Hunza Valley is not only fertile, it is also exceptionally rich in semiprecious stones. 
It is said that years ago, when soldiers of the British Empire fought there, the bullets removed from them would often turn out to be garnets coated with lead.
Until as recently as 1974, Hunza was a separate kingdom ruled by the hereditary Mir of Hunza. 
Not long after Hunza's incorporation into Pakistan, the last Mir ''died of heartbreak,'' Superintendent Ali told us. 
I asked him how he knew. 
''Oh well, he was a relation,'' the Superintendent said. 
''It happens that my mother was the Mir's sister and the Mir's wife was my auntie. 
My father and uncle simply exchanged sisters, you see.''
The people of the Hunza Valley -which is surrounded by 21 peaks more than 20,000 feet high - are famous for good health and longevity and a number of books have been written about ''Hunza health secrets.''
One does indeed see many robust old Hunzakut men and women about, but as far as I was able to ascertain there has never been any proof that these people represent a medical marvel.
The villagers of the Hunza Valley are remarkable in other ways, however. 
Hunza is said to be a basically cooperative society with little difference in wealth from family to family. 
Fruit - the apricot in particular - is the staple of the diet. 
Although alcohol is widely prohibited in Pakistan, the Hunzakuts freely - if discreetly -drink a concoction known as ''Hunza water,'' varieties of wine and brandy distilled from mulberries and grapes. 
In contrast to the people farther south, many Hunzakuts have pink-white skin, and green or blue eyes. 
Women do not hide their faces as most Pakistani Moslems do; instead they cover only their hair with a colorful scarf draped over a sort of pillbox cap.
We stopped for a brief breakfast of green tea, sheep liver fried in apricot-pit oil, porridge, potatoes, chicken, phiti - brown bread made from unrefined wheat - and jam, then quickly resumed our journey. 
In places, the shoulders of the road were piled high with snow, cleared after recent avalanches. 
Elsewhere, the mountain slopes were covered in scree, rock pulverized to a fine powder by the force of glaciers over centuries.
One of the largest glaciers in the world outside the polar regions is the 30-mile-long Batura Glacier, which we approached at about 9:30. 
This is normally as far as foreign visitors may go, but we had earlier applied for and received permission to proceed the remaining 60 miles to the border.
T he road followed the course of the clear and shallow Hunza River through a deserted landscape of dry, rocky soil, wild willow and scrub. 
About noon we came to Kara Jilga, the point where the road begins a steep climb to the Khunjerab Pass. 
The countryside was snowcovered; the river was frozen and bluish icicles hung from the rocks. 
Dark, hairy yaks trudged along in the distance, leaving a shadowy trail in the otherwise unbroken whiteness.
Finally, the road flattened out and we drove up to an unimposing wooden sign indicating that China lay beyond. 
The elevation was 15,072 feet, said to be the highest point on any paved road in the world. 
Although I was wearing several layers of clothes, I shivered with cold and my breathing was labored. 
Moving about in the snow to keep warm, I soon became dizzy and light-headed.
''When the Karakoram Highway was completed, the road gang from China and the road gang from Pakistan played volleyball right across the border here,'' Superintendent Ali told me. 
I said I thought I would drop dead if I attempted such exercise at this altitude. 
''As a matter of fact, that's just what did happen to one chap,'' he noted.
We could not spend long in the cold, rarified atmosphere of the pass. 
We climbed back into the jeeps and headed south, stopping for a snack about 5 P.M. and arriving in Gilgit just before 9.
Our plan was to fly out Sunday afternoon. 
No plane had made it to Gilgit in the last few days, but the sky was clear and we were hopeful. 
We attended a polo match after breakfast; Gilgit happens to be the place where the sport originated.
The plane did not arrive, however, and we reluctantly began the long and arduous trip by road back to Rawalpindi. 
By Monday morning we had somehow made it to the airport, more or less on schedule and more or less ready for the long flight back to New York.
Although I don't think any of us would have been prepared to make the trip again right away, we were all pleased to have done it. 
In part, that's because we had learned something about the rules of travel and did not doubt that the destination had been exotic enough to justify the hardships we had endured. 
Equally important was another rule that we were just beginning to recognize: few memories are more savored than those of a risky journey successfully completed.
Â 
Guide for visitors to Gilgit
The Basics The round-trip excursion fare via Pakistani International Airlines from New York to Islamabad is $2,470 in first class, $1,285 economy. 
(For stays of less than a month no visa is required.) The easiest and least expensive way to get to Gilgit is by air. 
P.I.A. has a flight that leaves Islamabad for Gilgit daily if the weather is clear. 
The Government-subsidized fare is very reasonable, about $26 each way. 
A car and driver can be hired in either Rawalpindi or Gilgit for about $10 a day plus five cents a mile. 
The best time of year to go to northern Pakistan is spring or fall. 
Days are warm, but evenings can be quite cool, especially at high altitudes. 
Rain is likely in July and August. 
Exhibition and practice polo matches are held in Gilgit (as well as in many villages in the region) at almost any time of year, but the regular season begins in late spring and ends in the fall. 
In Gilgit, the best known hotels, such as the Rakoposhi Inn and the Hunza Inn, charge about $35 a night for a double occupancy room. 
Less expensive but still quite decent accommodations are also available. 
Making Arrangements Further information can be obtained and arrangements made through the Tourism Division, Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, Government of Pakistan, College Road, Shalimar, 7/2, Islamabad, and the Adventure Foundation (Pakistan), a nonprofit organization modeled on America's Outward Bound. 
The Adventure Foundation's main goal is to introduce indigent youth of Pakistan to sporting activities in wilderness areas of the country, but A.F.P. representatives are also beginning to organize excursions for American groups on a select basis. 
Contact the A.F.P. at No. 1 Gulistan Colony, College Road, Abbottabad, Pakistan. 
C.D.M.

text:

The Chinese Foreign Minister arrives here tomorrow on a fence-mending mission that could pave the way for a new phase of friendship between India and China.
The visit by Foreign Minister Huang Hua is the first by a senior Chinese official since Prime Minister Zhou Enlai came here in 1960. 
Within months of that visit, the relationship deteriorated over Chinese territorial claims.
Chinese Foreign Minister Huang Hua arrives in New Delhi (India) in effort to improve relations between India and China
A border war in 1962 ended in defeat for India and the Chinese seizure of a piece of territory in northeastern Kashmir known as Aksai Chin. 
The border dispute has kept the two countries apart although India took the first step toward reconciliation in 1976 by sending an ambassador to Peking after an absence of 15 years. 
In 1979, the Indian Foreign Minister visited Peking.
Foreign Minister Hua of China was scheduled to come here last year after Prime Minister Indira Gandhi had returned to power, but he canceled the trip when she accorded recognition to the Soviet-backed Cambodian Government.
Â 
Border Dispute No Stumbling Block
In the last few months, friendly signals began coming from Peking and it was announced that Mr. Hua would be making the trip this summer.
Both sides have agreed that the border dispute need not be a stumbling block in the way of better relations. 
The Chinese have indicated that they would accept a boundary along the line of actual control. 
This would leave the Aksai Chin area in Chinese hands, but would confirm Indian sovereignty over the former North-East Frontier Agency, since 1972 constituted as the Indian union territory of Arunachal Pradesh.
India has said that the proposal is unacceptable and wants talks confined to the Aksai Chin area. 
The area is now crossed by a major Chinese highway linking Tibet and Xinjiang.
Indian officials do not expect any dramatic developments to come out of Mr. Hua's visit. 
But they hope to achieve the limited aim of lessening tension along the border and re-establishing trade relations and economic cooperation.

file: IN CHINA, IN MONGOL STEPS, HORDES OF BACKPACKERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
At dawn, when a crescent moon lingers on the horizon, the donkey carts are on the move in this old Islamic town. 
Through an open doorway in a whitewashed wall, the murmurings of young boys reading the Koran filter into an alley. 
Old men in leather boots gather silently on a nearby bench, watching the sun spreading a wash of pink across the distant Pamir peaks.
For more than 2,000 years Kashgar has lived by its own rhythms, absorbing only as much as it has cared to from the alien tides that have flowed through the town.
The Chinese first made their power felt here in the Han dynasty, in the third century B.C. The Russians were a pervasive influence for a century and a half before World War II, and in between the dusty streets were trod by Tibetans, Mongols, Indians and British, among others.
Because the town stands at the furthest fringe of the deserts that cushion China from the west, it has always attracted conquerors, adventurers and traders. 
But none has made more than a passing impact on the Uighurs, a Turkic-speaking people who migrated from the western perimeter of Mongolia and who had been predominant in Kashgar for at least eight centuries when Marco Polo passed through in 1275. 
Today they account for about 90 percent of the town's population of 180,000.
Â 
Geography Has Been Ally
Geography has been the Uighurs' ally. 
It is more than 2,000 miles from here to Peking, most of it desert. 
Travelers from the capital take two days to arrive by plane, longer if flights are canceled because of sandstorms that sweep the Gobi and Taklamakan, the vast seas of dune and scrub that cover much of the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region in which Kashgar is situated.
As if nature's isolation were insufficient, the Communist authorities declared the town closed to foreigners in the 1950's, an edict not lifted until 1983.
Whether approached from the east, across the desert, or from the west, across the 25,000-foot mountains that run like a shield across China's Central Asian frontier, Kashgar has always provided respite to the traveler. 
Now, once more, it is opening doors to strangers, and doing so in the tradition of Uighur friendliness that has impressed virtually every sojourner except Polo, who found the local merchants mean.
A few days here furnish vivid memories of free donkey cart rides, of spontaneous invitations to private weddings, of friendly chatter at dusk in the precincts of the Id Kah mosque, where the muezzin's cry has been heard for 1,000 years.
''Hospitality is a part of our culture,'' said Abdullah Shakir, a carpet salesman encountered in the Hong Kong Bazaar, so named for its profusion of inexpensive goods. 
#20,000 Visitors Expected This year, with the opening to foreigners of the Karakoram highway that crosses the mountains from here to Pakistan, officials expect 20,000 foreign visitors. 
Backpackers, in particular, are arriving in force.
The local foreign affairs director, Abdullahjan Dawud, a Uighur with Chinese subordinates, says the town is the most authentic of all surviving Uighur towns in Xinjiang, whose population of 13.5 million includes a diminishing proportion of Uighurs, now about six million.
''Kashgar,'' said Mr. Dawud with a smile, ''is keeping to its ethnic characteristics.''
This was a polite way of saying that here, unlike the Xinjiang capital of Urumqi, the Uighurs have managed to maintain their culture and religion without major inroads by the Chinese.
The sense of being carried back across the centuries comes most vividly on Sundays, when the citizens of Kashgar and outlying villagers mingle at the weekly market. 
In a clearing off a poplar-lined road that enters the town from the west, as many as 70,000 people crowd together to trade, to eat and to gossip. 
Most travel by donkey, some by horse or camel. 
Whole families ride together.
Officials say the market accounts for 30 percent of the commerce, an underestimate that serves the pretense that Kashgar's economy is predominantly Goverment-controlled.
Every Uighur need is met. 
Whether it is bolts of silk, top boots fashioned from yak hides, or camels - available for as little as $100 for a high-mileage specimen, as much as $450 for an animal that is still breaking in - the Uighur trader retains the shrewdness that sat ill with Marco Polo. 
Hours can be spent haggling over a few dollars.
Â 
Bargaining Can Be Cantankerous
As a customer, the Uighur is no less narrow-eyed. 
Beyond the market's five-cent haircuts and its silk-clad tumblers performing in the open air, traders gather beside a dusty track where draft animals are taken through their paces.
Old men with fierce countenances and jutting beards spend an hour or more testing camels and horses. 
When the animal has been rated the bargaining begins, often in the most cantankerous way.
During Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966, the market was disbanded. 
But the Uighurs revived their trading in a cemetery beyond the town and, in the late 1970's, saw their entrepreneurship embraced and Mao's brand of Communism condemned.
Mao's 40-foot statue still gazes solemnly northward from a plinth on the Chinese side of town, but a local Uighur official says quietly that it is there solely as ''a reminder of our worst times.''
Mao is only one of the alien influences whose course in Kashgar is run. 
Not far from the market is the yellow stucco compound that served as Britain's most remote diplomatic outpost in Asia until it was closed in 1950. 
Once celebrated for its watercress sandwiches, it is now a crumbling relic that serves as a cheap hotel. 
Across town, the Neo-Classical buildings of the old Russian consulate have been transformed into a higher-class guesthouse.
Â 
Past Contacts Recalled
To the Chinese the buildings are redolent of imperialism. 
Uighurs, by contrast, seem pleased to recall past contacts with foreigners. 
A walk in the maze-like alleyways of the old Uighur city is virtually guaranteed to produce invitations into courtyard homes that hide behind high mud walls.
Inside, guests are seated on raised platforms covered with the richly colored carpets for which the region is famous, and, over cups of thick black tea, invited to discourse, among other subjects, on Islam and carpet-making.
A common topic is the matter of relations between Uighurs and Chinese. 
Barely five years ago the town was convulsed with riots that erupted after Chinese youths killed a young Uighur and lost one of their own in revenge.
Uighurs say relations have improved greatly since. 
''After Mao, things were certain to improve,'' said an Uighur doctor who works among Chinese. 
''We still lead our separate lives, but we have learned to co-exist. 
''

text:
ï»¿
A group of Indian pilgrims who for the first time in 22 years were permitted to visit a lake sacred to Hindus in southwestern Tibet have returned with descriptions of monasteries that were destroyed in China's Cultural Revolution.
The 13 worshipers who entered Tibet through the Himalayas traveled 300 miles by horse, mule and truck in a region that has rarely been visited by outsiders since the Chinese conquest of Tibet.
As part of efforts to thaw relations between India and China, Peking permitted pilgrims to travel to the lake, which is known as Manasarowar in India and as Mapam in Tibet. 
The deep blue lake, at an altitude of 14,000 feet, is considered holy by both Hindus and Buddhists. 
Before the Chinese invasion, eight large monasteries housing thousands of monks ringed the slopes around the lake.
Indian pilgrims, permitted for first time in 22 years to visit sacred areas of Tibet, see ruins of temples destroyed in Chinese Cultural Revolution
The travelers had cameras with them but said they were frequently discouraged by their guides from photographing the vandalized sites.
Â 
Buddhist Palace Is Destroyed
The travelers said that the gompas, as they are called, were all empty shells, having been systematically blown up. 
''Our Chinese guides told us that the destruction had all been the work of the Gang of Four,'' one of the travelers said, referring to Mao Zedong's radical associates who have been blamed for the excessses of the Cultural Revolution.
The traveler added that the same guides did not permit the pilgrims to make close inspection of the ruins. 
One gompa, measuring nearly half a mile in length, had been reduced to rubble.
The summer palace of a Buddhist order was also destroyed. 
However, one of the Indian visitors said local residents had apparently salvaged some ancient prayer stones and built ramshackle chapels. 
Above one ruin there flew a solitary prayer flag that had apparently been recently put in place, attesting to the tenacious hold of the religious culture even in the absence of monks.
According to the pilgrims, the group's guides, both Chinese and Tibetans, said several times that they had heard reports that the Chinese Government was preparing to rebuild the religious buildings.
The travelers said that they were kept at a distance from settlers but that they spent some time in the town of Taklakot, now known officially in Tibet as Burang. 
It is a settlement where local herdsmen exchange yak wool for food smuggled in by Nepalese traders, and Tibetans live in huts of stone.
Flags flew from official buildings, the visitors said, but they saw no pictures of Mao or any other revolutionary figures. 
''My impression,'' a young traveler said, ''was that the authorities had given up doing anything for the local people and that the Tibetans were living as hard a life as they had for centuries.''
There was no sign of the kind of rich ceremonial life that dominated the lives of local people. 
There were no communes and no schools, the travelers said, and there were no temples and no monasteries, just high gravel expanses without vegetation and some hardy goats, sheep and people.
In their trek the Indian pilgrims came upon the remains of Shershung, where fairs used to be held on days of the full moon. 
The site is now rubble, the travelers said, marked only by burial mounds of inscribed prayer stones.

file: OF MONKS AND MARTIAL ARTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The vivid frescoes seem startling in a 1,500-year-old Buddhist temple. 
On one wall, monks fight with feet and clenched fists in a cloistered garden. 
On the opposite wall, more monks spar with swords, staves, cudgels and other ancient weapons. 
The stones of an adjacent hall have been stamped down into 48 indentations, a legacy of centuries of practice in the martial arts that have left the floor pitted up to seven inches deep. 
Shaolin Monastery, nestled on the barren slopes of Song Mountain in central China's Henan Province, was the home of Chan Buddhism, a Chinese sect that gave rise of Zen Buddhism in Japan. 
But it is even better known as the cradle of wushu, an ancient fighting skill that has evolved into Chinese kung fu and influenced Japanese karate and Korean taekwondo.
Christopher Wren article on visiting Shoalin Monastery in central China's Henan Province; photos (M)
During the Tang Dynasty 13 centuries ago, the monastery had 500 fighting monks along with 1,000 more prosaic monks who tilled several thousand acres of communal farmland. 
The monastery then fell on hard times. 
It was burned three times, most recently in 1928 during a struggle between rival warlords. 
It was vandalized during the Cultural Revolution, and its remaining monks dispersed to secular labor. 
Several years ago, Shaolin Monastery reopened and now has 20 monks ranging in age from 16 to 76 years. 
The revival of historical interest in Shaolin Monastery is ironically the result of the popularity of China's first kung fu movie, ''Shaolin Temple.''
(Buddhist monasteries in China are usually called temples.) The film followed the formula of revenge and mayhem that has been a staple of the Hong Kong film industry and was shot on location.
The monastery's reputation derives from an incident in 618 A.D., when the Tang Dynasty Emperor Li Shimin, hearing of the martial arts developed at Shaolin Monastery, appealed for help in defeating Prince Zheng in a battle at nearby Luoyang, then the imperial capital. 
Thirteen warrior monks who responded to the Emperor's call helped win the victory, opening the way for the unification of China. 
(With a license that Hollywood might envy, the movie had the monks winning the campaign by themselves.)
The introduction of fighting skills at Shaolin Monastery has been attributed in legend to the Indian monk Bodhidharma, who went to the monastery in 527, three decades after it was founded by Batuo, another Indian monk. 
Bodhidharma allegedly spent nine years in contemplation, facing the wall of a cave on Song Mountain above the monastery. 
For exercise and protection from wild animals, he taught himself self-defense and later passed the skills along to his disciples.
Actually, the ancient martial arts probably originated even earlier as Buddhist monks learned to fend off brigands and other predators. 
Variations of their refined techniques subsequently reached Japan, Okinawa, Korea and other Asian countries that developed their own distinct fighting styles.
Chinese wushu goes well beyond the ''empty-hand'' fighting of the more familiar karate of Japan or taekwondo of Korea because it incorporates 18 ancient weapons, such as nine-sectioned chains, hinged sticks, staves and swords. 
Chinese wushu, like the more contemporary kung fu, has no belt gradings but can take up to 10 years to master. 
It is taught in China for physical exercise and health rather than self-defense. 
The best known of its styles is taijiquan, called tai chi in the West, which has been vastly slowed down to emphasize flexibility and serenity.
Shaolin Monastery has become a tourist attraction, with the government allocating more than $1.6 million for its restoration. 
The monastery, a few miles from the county seat of Dengfeng, is about four hours by car or tour bus from Henan's provincial capital of Zhengzhou, itself an overnight train ride from Peking, 400 miles to the north. 
The monastery can also be reached from Luoyang.
The monastery is entered through its elevated ''mountain gate,'' reached by a flight of 16 broad stone stairs. 
Under the curved tile roof hangs an elegant gold leaf inscription with the three Chinese characters for Shaolin Temple, written in the 18th century by the Qing Dynasty's Kangxi emperor. 
Stately cy press and ginkgo trees planted by the monks centuries ago rise above the reddish walls. 
More than a dozen buildings, including the Heavenly King (Tianhuang) Hall and a library of Buddhist scriptures, were burned down by the warlord Shi Yousan during the civil fighting in 1928. 
It was said that the monastery burned for 45 days.
Fortunately, the last row of buildings inside the monastery was not destroyed. 
The largest is the Hall of a Thousand Buddhas, in traditional red brick with a curved blue-gray tile roof. 
It contains what are regarded as the finest surviving frescoes in China, painted during the Ming Dynasty, covering more than 3,000 feet of wall. 
They show in intricate detail 500 ''arhats,'' or Buddhist saints, worshipping Buddha amid clusters of billowing clouds. 
No two faces or figures look alike.
A martial arts enthusiast may be more intrigued by the green brick floor, with its 48 indentations in four symmetrical rows about one yard apart. 
The depressions were formed over the centuries, when the monks learned to strengthen their fighting stance by pressing their feet down on the bricks. 
Nearby, a rack of weapons displays a vicious-looking collection of spears, halberds and tridents.
To the east is the White Robe (Baiyi) Hall with its equally famous frescoes of the martial arts, only slightly damaged by graffiti and wear. 
Along the southern wall, 34 monks in colorful open jackets, sleeves rolled up, spar in bare-fisted pairs before a small but intense audience of scholars and spectators. 
On the northern wall, other monks show off their skills with the 18 ancient weapons.
Another wall fresco depicts the 13 warrior monks coming to the aid of the Tang emperor. 
There are additional frescoes of a barehanded monk subduing a dragon and a tiger. 
The origin of the art is obscure. 
The robes and pigtails of the onlookers suggest that the frescoes were painted early in the Qing Dynasty, which overthrew the Ming emperor in 1644 and was itself finally toppled in 1911.
Shaolin's monks today go about their duties with shaved heads and coarse gray robes, oblivious to the stream of tourists. 
But they also have tales to tell. 
Fu Yun, now in his 60's, recalled how the monastery had 300 monks when he joined as a child novice in 1930. 
In those days, he said, the monks practiced wushu six hours a day as a respite from meditation. 
''The basic lessons in wushu were to keep us fit,'' said Fu Yun. 
He was forced to go home to work as a farmer in 1949 but returned after the Communist authorities adopted a greater tolerance for religious belief after the repressive Cultural Revolution.
To the disappointment of many visitors, the monks no longer perform wushu. 
''I can still play but not very well,'' Fu Yun confessed. 
''To be good at wushu, you must be obedient and willing to bear suffering and hardship.''
Chuan Qing, a 24-year-old monk from eastern China, said he was not interested in wushu because ''it is very hard to do.''
For the monks, who rise at 3 or 4 A.M. and subsist on vegetables and rice, life is not much more glamorous than that in other Buddhist monasteries in Asia.
Shaolin's traditional martial arts are being preserved at the nearby town of Dengfeng, where a sports school specializing in wushu opened two years ago. 
Its 140 or so pupils practice wushu every afternoon following their academic classes. 
The pupils, some of whom are only 10 or 11 years old, frequently stage fighting displays for foreign tourists on the packed dirt of their outdoor practice field.
Visitors to China do not have to travel all the way to Shaolin Monastery to see wushu. 
In any major Chinese city, simply rise at dawn and head for the local park, where some young people practice before going off to jobs or classes. 
In Shanghai, for example, there is early morning wushu practice along the Bund, or waterfront promenade. 
Just head for the clatter of swords and staves.

text:

This bustling Central Asian city is barely 100 miles from China, yet for 20 years it has had virtually no contact with the other side of the frontier.
Centuries of trading, intrigue and war have given way to silence, broken only by the propaganda broadcasts that each side beams at the other across the towering Tien Shan range. 
On July 1, however, a small beginning was made on restoring some of those ancient ties when the two countries reopened two border points that have been sealed since the ideological and territorial rift between them broke into the open in the 1960's.
The opening of the barriers for local trading, at a mountain pass at Turugart, 130 miles east of here, and another at Korgas, 470 miles to the northeast, will not extend to passenger traffic, and thus will not relieve the forced separation of tens of thousands of families that straddle the border. 
Nor will it mean any major increase in trade, since the major country-to-country traffic, which will more than double this year, passes through rail points thousands of miles farther east.
OSH, U.S.S.R. 
- This bustling Central Asian city is barely 100 miles from China, yet for 20 years it has had virtually no contact with the other side of the frontier.
Nonetheless, it is a symbolic step in the overall effort by Moscow and Peking to improve relations. 
Two rounds of talks since last October, the first in Peking and the second in Moscow in March, have failed to produce any major steps toward resolving their differences, and manifestations of good will have been limited to such things as reopening minor border points, stepping up trade and reviving sports and scientific exchanges.
Â 
Soviet Officials Wary
Local officials here and in Frunze, capital of Soviet Kirghizia, adopt a wary tone when discussing the border reopenings, reflecting the ambivalence that has characterized Government pronouncements in Moscow since the unproductive round of talks in March. 
Sopubek B. Begaliyev, chairman of the Kirghizian state planning committee, mentioned the border points only in passing while reviewing the state of affairs in the republic for visiting reporters, and added cryptically, ''You can say this is some evidence of improved relations.''
A similarly noncommittal view was expressed by Karybek M. Moldobayev, first secretary of the Frunze party committee, who dismissed suggestions that the gradual improvement in ties was of particular importance to Kirghizia, given its proximity to China and the memories of border clashes that have occurred during the years of enmity. 
The clashes, mainly in 1969, never reached the intensity of the fighting on the Amur and Ussuri rivers in the Far East, where the death toll was considerable.
''As part of the Soviet state, Kirghizia will benefit along with other parts of the republic,'' he said. 
Hardly a year ago, when Leonid I. Brezhnev was making little headway with his appeals to China for a turn toward improved ties, visitors here found a more emphatic attitude. 
Then local officials spoke openly of the ''threat'' that they said China's military presence posed to Kirghizia, and they recounted how conditions on the other side of the border caused tens of thousands of refugees to pour across the frontier into Kirghizia at the height of China's Cultural Revolution in the late 1960's.
Today, such matters are approached more discreetly. 
Asanbek Tokombayev, head of the republic's radio and television service, recalled the border skirmishes as ''small-scale matters'' that had long since been forgotten, and described border tensions in general as ''a thing of the past.''
Other officials questioned on the matter said they attached little importance to China's historical claim to Soviet territory on the north side of the Pamir Mountains, part of a much wider Chinese position that places about 580,000 square miles of Soviet territory in the category of land seized from imperial China under ''unequal'' treaties with the Russian czars.
Â 
Slight Interest in China
Mr. Tokombayev said that the border reopenings were not sufficiently interesting to audiences here to warrant sending film crews to monitor the event. 
Indeed, he said, there was little general interest here in what was going on in China, apart perhaps from the people of Uighur, Kazakh or Kirghiz origin who had been residents of China until the 1960's but had taken up residence here and become Soviet citizens.
He said he was ''unsure'' whether China was still broadcasting radio propaganda in the local languages, ''but we do not listen, anyway.''
He denied knowledge of Soviet propaganda transmissions, but Western monitoring services have confirmed that Soviet stations in Alma-Ata, Tashkent and elsewhere in Central Asia continue to vaunt the higher Soviet standard of living in shortwave programs transmitted across the mountains in Uighur and Kazakh.
Almost everywhere, officials questioned on the matter said that the greatest threat these days came not from Peking but from Washington, and President Reagan's program of modernizing United States nuclear arms. 
This is the standard line in Moscow. 
But on the streets of Osh, an industrial city of half a million that sits amid one of the most fertile agricultural areas in Central Asia, ordinary people tended to reverse the view.
''United States?'' a gold-toothed fruit vendor in the Osh bazaar said, as an American reporter sampled one of his melons. 
''Excellent,'' he said, giving a thumbs-up sign.

text:
