China under Deng Xiaoping has patched up ties with the faraway West while remaining at odds with many of its neighbors. 
Last week, it addressed one of those quarrels, welcoming negotiators from India to discuss a Himalayan border dispute that has festered for almost a century and led to a brief, fierce border war in 1962.
Discussion of China's decision last week to attempt to negotiate Himalayan border dispute with India
There was no expectation of early agreement. 
India accuses China of seizing nearly 14,500 square miles of its territory; Peking says India illegally holds about 56,000 square miles that rightly belong to China. 
However, the talks alone represent a comedown from China's previous position that the border dispute was so formidable that the two countries should talk about other aspects of their edgy relationship first.
Diplomatic ties were virtually frozen after the 1962 war until five years ago, when the two countries re-exchanged ambassadors. 
Since then, there has been a slow thaw, interrupted by China's 1979 attack on Vietnam, which India supports, and India's recognition of the Vietnamese-installed Government in Cambodia, which China opposes.
The Peking Government first suggested border talks last year. 
To warm up the atmosphere for negotiations, China has allowed small groups of Indian pilgrims to visit Buddhist holy sites in Tibet. 
Peking has also imported more and more Indian goods, so that trade between the two countries, almost nothing two years ago, amounts to $100 million this year.
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Â 
Barbara Slavin and Milt Freudenheim

file: THE WORLD_With Lasting Doubts, India Fosters Hopes of Better Ties to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
MORE than half a century ago and two decades before he became India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru had a dream. 
Friendship between China and India, he told a conference of anti-colonial parties in 1927, would form the core of a new pan-Asianism, a base on which to build a new order in the East.
But long before the dream died on a snowy Himalayan battlefield in 1962 in a short, sharp border war, Nehru and Mao Zedong had chosen separate roads. 
Nehru and Mohandas K. Gandhi took the difficult democratic path, robbing Indian Communists of their dream of capturing the independence movement, as Ho Chi Minh had done in Vietnam. 
Mao, on the other hand, was crafting a rigid brand of Marxism. 
Led in these separate directions, Asia's two giants strayed apart, and then the 1962 border war ended the era of amity with finality.
This week when Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, Nehru's grandson, makes a trip to China - the first visit by an Indian Prime Minister in 34 years - no one in India expects a revival of Nehru's heady dreams of brotherhood. 
But there are cautious hopes that progress can be made on the still-unresolved border dispute and that cultural ties and improved air links will be initiated. 
More than anything, however, Indian officials and intellectuals want a better atmosphere and more contact to follow Mr. Gandhi's visit to Beijing, Shanghai and Xian.
India is tiptoeing toward East Asia, uncertain what its relationship should be with the world's most rapidly growing economies, or with China in transition. 
In New Delhi - unlike other Asian capitals, Moscow or Washington - there is little fascination with the Pacific Century. 
There is, instead, a continuing preoccupation with the West.
Â 
Appearing Too Friendly
''Despite Nehru's romanticism for Asia, and China in particular, our tradition in political terms has been Western,'' said S. Nihal Singh, an author and columnist. 
Mr. Singh added that Prime Minister Gandhi was making the trip to Beijing against the wishes of some of his advisers, and amid fears in his own party that no Indian leader can yet afford to appear too friendly to the Chinese.
''The feeling is still very strong in this country that we got a beating at the hands of the Chinese in 1962,'' said Nikhil Chakravartty, editor of the left-wing magazine Mainstream. 
He said that the Government has not done enough to educate Indians about the need for give and take in settling the border dispute. 
Instead, Mr. Gandhi is pushed by his own supporters into promising not to give away ''one square mile'' of Indian territory. 
The two border areas in question, in mountain terrain, are nearly impossible to demarcate accurately in any case, Indian scholars say. 
Both countries may have to settle for a rational compromise based on who is in control of what parts of ground.
When the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, was in New Delhi last month, he pointedly remarked on several occasions that there was no problem in Indian-Soviet relations, even though no one had suggested publicly that there was. 
Mr. Gorbachev's comments were interpreted here as an assurance that Moscow's planned rapprochement with China, possibly involving a Sino-Soviet summit next year, would not affect the Moscow-Delhi link. 
But Mr. Gorbachev also made it clear that he would welcome warmer Indian-Chinese ties.
''If Gorbachev makes up to China,'' Mr. Chakravartty said, ''this is an important signal to India not to let itself be left out. 
India could be the only country in this part of the world not to have better relations with the Chinese.''
Â 
Comparing Two Giants
An Indian focus on China invites comparisons between the two Asian giants, the world's most populous nations: China with a billion people and India with 800 million.
In the days of Communist repression and the Cultural Revolution, India could feel more secure in the rightness of its chosen path. 
A free people and a free press have thrived here. 
A mixed economy has opened avenues to development policies of the left and right. 
Poverty and overpopulation were the curse and preoccupation of both nations.
But China has changed and in recent years it can point to many achievements - in agricultural development, rural industry, medical care and, despite criticism of Beijing's methods, population control. 
Now a Chinese citizen is healthier, lives longer and has access to as many or more consumer goods than does the average Indian. 
China is also working hard to integrate itself into the booming East Asian economies.
Lately, India has been close to Vietnam and almost alone outside the Soviet bloc in recognizing the Vietnamese-backed Government in Cambodia - a distinction that has cost it friends in the region but one that has given it a limited interest in Southeast Asian affairs.
Southeast Asia will be discussed on Mr. Gandhi's trip, Indian officials say, especially the problem of Cambodia, and how to get Vietnam's troops to leave. 
But will that whet India's appetite for more contact with the East?
''Not really,'' Mr. Singh said. 
''India has always been ambivalent to Southeast Asia.''
A more active interest in Southeast Asia, many Indians believe, can come only when India feels more comfortable with China - a relationship that will now have to be rebuilt step by step.
Â 
A HISTORY OF CONFRONTATION
In 1962, a dispute over a road built by the Chinese on territory claimed by India and a set of border clashes led Chinese to attack. 
Chinese routed the Indians in Arunachal Pradesh and seized territory in Ladakh. 
After a month of fighting, China declared a unilateral cease-fire.
Fighting broke out between Indian and Chinese troops in 1967 at the Nathu La Pass on the Sikkim-Tibet border. 
Two years later, Indians accused Chinese of firing on patrol in Lip Lekh.
In 1986, India asserted that Chinese troops entered valley of Sumdorong Chu in Arunachal Pradesh, where Indian intelligence post had been set up earlier without Chinese objections. 
Tens of thousands of Chinese and Indian troops confronted each other at height of crisis, which was defused after diplomatic contacts.

text:

Communist officials from Tibet today accused the Dalai lama, its exiled spiritual leader, of fomenting the recent Tibetan rioting.
It was the first time since Tibetan Buddhist monks in Lhasa demonstrated for independence a month ago that officials from China's Government in Tibet talked about the protests to foreign reporters. 
The officials spoke at a news conference held in conjunction with the 13th Communist Party Congress being held in Beijing.
The Tibetans, who are attending the 13th party congress as party delegates also asserted that the Dalai Lama dispatched assassins and saboteurs to Lhasa in 1985 and 1986. 
They offered no evidence to support their charges.
Unrest Blamed on Dalai Lama
''In 1985, the Dalai Lama sent people to conduct explosions,'' said Doje Cering, the Chairman of the Government of the Tibet Autonomous Region. 
''In 1986, the Dalai Lama sent back people to engage in assassinations in Lhasa.''
Mr. Doje blamed the unrest in Lhasa on the Dalai Lama. 
''We have conclusive evidence to show that the Lhasa riot early this month was instigated and engineered by the Dalai Separatistk clique,'' said Mr. Doje. He did not offer proof of his assertion.
Earlier this month, the Dalai Lama said he favored civil disobedience against Chinese rule but not violence and asked his Tibetan supportrs to press their campaign peacefully.
Â 
Violence Is Disavowed
''Violence is not the proper way at all,'' the spiritual leader said at his headquarters near the Indian town of Dharamasala.
The Dalai Lama blamed the rioting on what he termed Chinese repression and Tibetan discontent.
China involved Tibet in 19550 and suppressed an independence rebellion in 1959. 
That year, the Dalai Lama fled to India with thousands of Tibetans and took up residence in Dharamsala. 
Beijing maintains that Tibet is an integral part of China.
Over the last two years, there have been fragmentary reports from Tibetans in India that armed Tibetan exiles had infiltrated back into Tibet for acts of sabotage. 
But there had been no confirmation of these reports and until now the Chinese Government did not comment on them.
In late September and early October, protests led by Buddhist monks turned violent when police attacked the demonstrators. 
A Chinese police station was burned and at least nine Tibetan protestors were killed when armed police fired into the crowd.
Today, the Tibetan officials attending the party congress denied that the police fired on protestors.
Despite reports from travelers that curfews have been imposed in Lhasa and that heavily armed Chinese police patrol the streets, Communist officials in Tibet said that Lhasa had returned to normal.
Â 
Foreign Journalists Expelled
During the disturbances a month ago, 15 foreign jounralists were expelled from tibet. 
Today, Mr. Doje said that Tibet was not closed to froeign reporters but that they had to apply for permission to go there. 
Many journalists based in Beiging have been rebuffed in such efforts.
The Tibetan Communists are among nearly 2,000 delegates to the party congress, which will announce the party's new Central Committee tomorrow. 
It is expected to be smaller and younger than the current Central Committee.
The new Central Committee, to be pared down from 208 to 172 members, will be missing many of the old Communist revolutionaries, including china's senior leader Deng Xiaoping and President Li Xiannian. 
Several Chinese have said that the committee has been reduced in size because it is expected to meet more often and will be less unwieldly.
On Monday, the newly constituted committee will gather to elect the party's ruling Politburo, currently made up of 20 members. 
And the following day, Tuesday, a new Standing Committee of the Politburo, the most powerful organ in the country, will be named.
Only Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, who is expected to be named party head, is thought to retain his seat.

file: TIBETAN PROTEST FOR INDEPENDENCE BECOMES VIOLENT.txt
text:
ï»¿
A march for independence by thousands of Tibetans turned violent Thursday, with demonstrators stoning the police and setting a police station afire, witnesses said today. 
Six people were reported killed.
The official New China News Agency said in addition to the 6 dead, 19 policemen had been seriously hurt. 
It said rioters snatched guns from policemen and shot at the officers, who ''strictly observed the orders of the higher authorities not to open fire.''
China accused the Dalai Lama, the Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader, of instigating the protest.
Â 
Second Protest in a Week
''Yesterday's riot is regarded as a direct outcome of Dalai's activities to split the motherland as an exile engaged in political activities,'' the agency said in a broadcast monitored in Tokyo. 
The Dalai Lama has been visiting the United States, where he appeared before a Congressional panel and called for negotiations on Tibet's status.
The violence Thursday took place in central Lhasa when the police fired into a crowd in the square leading to Jokhang Temple, the holiest place in Tibetan Buddhism, according to tourists arriving today in Chengdu, in central China.
The protest on Thursday, China's National Day, was the second in a week in Lhasa. 
A clash Sunday was the first public report of violent protest by Tibetans against Chinese in more than 10 years.
Â 
Reports of Detained Americans
CBS News said it had received a message in its Hong Kong bureau that two Americans had been detained in Sunday's demonstration, but it could not be determined whether they were still in custody.
The two were identified as John Ackerly, 31 years old, of Cambridge, Mass., and Dr. Blake Kerr, also 31, of East Hampton, L.I. 
[In Washington, a State Department spokeswoman said officials were aware of the reports but had no independent knowledge of whether any Americans had been detained in Tibet. 
''Our embassy in Beijing and consulate in Chengdu have been notified,'' said the spokeswoman, Phyllis Oakley. 
''They're attempting to verify the reports and determine the welfare and whereabouts of the two individuals.''] Reporters from Agence France-Presse and The Associated Press in Chengdu, 750 miles east of Lhasa, interviewed dozens of tourists who left the Tibetan capital today, and their reports were made available here in Beijing.
Â 
Diplomats Caught by Surprise
''I saw one man lying on the ground with a piece of his skull blown off and blood pouring out of his head,'' Lars Pettersson, a Swedish tourist, told reporters in Chengdu, describing the clashes Thursday.
Western diplomats here were caught by surprise over the sudden violence and the scope of the protests. 
Late today, an official at the United States embassy said that it was clear that ''several'' people had been killed in the Lhasa demonstrations Thursday, including at least one Chinese.
An Asian diplomat who returned from Tibet a week ago said the protests in Lhasa were likely to strengthen the hands of more doctrinaire Marxists in the Communist Party who have resisted the country's current policy of increased openness to the outside world. 
The diplomat also said the upheaval would also have a profound effect on an upcoming Communist Party Congress by tempering any impulse within the party to accelerate policies of openness and reform.
Sunday's protest began early in the day when a group of lamas who appeared to be in their 40's arrived from Ganden, a monastery 40 miles east of Lhasa that was dynamited by the Chinese during the Cultural Revolution of the 1960's. 
They began parading through the square outside the Jokhang Temple, tourists on the scene reported.
The lamas were told by the police that they would be arrested if they continued their demonstration, the tourists said. 
Altogether, 27 lamas were eventually arrested, the foreigners said.
On Thursday morning, according to the tourists, who included Americans, Germans, Swedes and Australians, eight lamas began protesting Sunday's arrests in front of the Jokhang Temple. 
The crowd of Tibetans swelled rapidly and then attacked a police station just paces from the square, setting it afire. 
When fire trucks arrived and firefighters tried to extinguish the blaze, they were stoned by the crowd.
The Tibetans chanted slogans in Tibetan, according to the tourists who were there, including, ''Free Tibet!''
''Chinese Out of Tibet!'' and ''Dalai Lama, Come Back to Tibet!''
The red and blue flag of Tibet, emblazoned with two facing lions, a banner that the Chinese have decreed illegal, was unfurled during the protest, some tourists said.
''We heard a great number of rifle shots in the crowd,'' a tourist told Agence France-Presse.
Another tourist said he was told by a Tibetan, ''We are fighting the Chinese.''
The police barricaded the area, according to tourists, but the Tibetan protesters responded with stones they broke from the flagstones on the square.
There were conflicting reports among tourists over the number of foreigners detained during Sunday's and Thursday's protest.
According to a hand-delivered message received by the Hong Kong bureau of CBS News from Lhasa, two Americans were taken into custody Sunday.
At least one tourist in Chengdu said that he saw two Americans being issued expulsion orders, but it was unclear whether he was referring to Mr. Ackerly and Mr. Kerr.
Several foreign tourists said they were detained by police in the during the protest, held in a school nearby for a couple hours and had their film and notebooks confiscated.
Â 
PROTESTS TIED TO EXECUTIONS
WASHINGTON, Oct. 
2 (Special to The New York Times) - A lawyer who advises Tibetan exiles said today that the recent disturbances apparently began after the execution of three Tibetans by the Chinese authorities.
The lawyer, Michael VanWalt, said the executions were reported by the Government radio station in Lhasa on Sept. 
25 and 26.
Mr. VanWalt, the author of ''The Status of Tibet: History, Rights and Prospects in International Law,'' said this week's incidents were not without precedent but seemed to be lasting longer than those in the past. 
''There have probably been 50 revolts since '59, some very small,'' he said. 
''In 1972, 12,000 people were killed. 
The big difference between this one and the others is that this seems to be much more sustained.''

file: TIBET_S BUDDHIST MONKS ENDURE TO REBUILD A PART OF THE PAST.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE brick shells of scores of buildings cling to the steep mountain slopes here, 30 miles east of Lhasa, the Tibetan capital. 
Once the holiest monastery of the Gelukpa sect of Tibetan Buddhism, the temples were dynamited by the Chinese in the 1960's to extirpate religion from Tibet, both in retaliation for an armed uprising in 1959 and as part of the leftist hysteria of the Cultural Revolution. 
Today 300 monks are slowly rebuilding, determined to recreate the grandeur of the 15th-century monastery. 
In doing this, they are also erecting a monument to Tibetan resistance to Chinese rule.
''We are going to rebuild this monastery,'' said a gray-haired monk in a worn maroon robe. 
''We have to find sponsors. 
We have to find donations. 
It will take time, but we will find a way.''
He spoke hesitantly, warily. 
''The Chinese spy on us here,'' he said, leading a visitor into his chamber. 
''The army comes here. 
The Chinese guides spy on us. 
We have to be careful.''
Sweet-smelling yak-butter lamps flickered before a dark photograph of the Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism and symbol of independence, who lives in exile in Dharmsala, India, about 900 miles to the west. 
Officially, Tibet is an autonomous region of China, with special tax benefits and a modicum of self-rule. 
In fact, Beijing maintains tight control.
Before the 1959 revolution, ''there were more than 3,000 monks here,'' the old monk said. 
''When the Dalai Lama came to Ganden, there were often 5,000 monks here. 
After the revolution, the Chinese put the monks in prison. 
Some were sent to villages. 
A lot of monks were killed. 
Others didn't want to be monks any more and got married. 
Even today there are 300 monks still in prison, including 38 from Ganden.
''I ran away when the Chinese came,'' he continued. 
''I was afraid. 
All the statues of Buddha they sent to Beijing. 
They burned all the scriptures. 
All the scriptures we have now are new. 
There is nothing old.''
There were 6,254 monasteries in independent Tibet when China invaded in 1951. 
All but a handful lie in ruins, dynamited, or destroyed by Tibetans who were forced at gunpoint to rip the buildings apart with their hands. 
The Chinese now dismiss the destruction of the 1960's and 1970's as ''leftist excesses.''
But cognizant of Tibetan hostility, they have spent tens of millions of dollars on roads, water systems and electrification. 
A small proportion has gone to rehabilitate some of the more prominent monasteries, not coincidentally the ones most frequently seen by foreign tourists.
Still, Ganden has emerged as a singular example of Tibetan pride and determination. 
This is partly because of the destruction here, far worse than at monasteries in Lhasa, and partly because Ganden is being rebuilt with only scant assistance from Beijing. 
''People come here to make donations,'' the monk said. 
''They also give gold necklaces.''
He led the way through the rubble, reminiscing. 
''When I walked along here, there were so many monks. 
Many, many.''
He pointed to a ragged wall of bricks surrounding a pile of stone and broken rock. 
''There were lots of statues in there. 
Also the monks had their chambers there, six or seven in a group.''
Farther on, he pointed to a spacious square of cement. 
''This was a chanting hall where 5,000 monks could chant. 
We will rebuild this. 
Maybe next year we will begin.''
Most Tibetan monasteries are strictly regulated by the Government's Bureau of Religious Affairs. 
''Before the revolution, before 1959,'' the old monk said, ''anyone who wanted to could come here to become a monk. 
Now it depends on the bureau to allow new students, maybe only 10 or 15 each year. 
The bureau gives permission for the monks to wear these robes,'' he added. 
''The bureau comes here to see if all the monks have permits. 
We ask for more monks but the bureau does not allow it.''
The monastery exerts a lure on Tibetans, drawn by Buddhism and by determination to see Ganden rise from the rubble. 
''My monastery was destroyed, too,'' another monk said. 
''I heard that rebuilding began in 1981, so I came here. 
I was not a monk from Ganden. 
I'm just an old monk from eastern Tibet. 
When I went to Sera monastery and Drepung monastery, I saw there was still something there. 
Here, there was nothing. 
I wept.''
Less than a dozen buildings have been rebuilt, some only partially. 
On a balcony of a new thick-walled, whitewashed building, young monks were painting baked white-clay images of the seated Buddha. 
Watching them, the old monk said there was some hope that the Chinese Government would gradually loosen the controls on Tibetan religious institutions, but only the faintest of hopes that China will ever give Tibet back its lost independence. 
''I don't know if it ever will happen,'' the old monk whispered. 
''Now, we just build.''

By John F. Avedon Today the Dalai Lama is going to New Delhi. 
The journey will take him 250 miles to the southeast, down from the Indian hill town of Dharmsala, where he lives in exile. 
The temporal and religious head of the once-independent nation of Tibet has resided here for 24 years, since shortly after the Chinese annexed his homeland, high in the Himalayas to the east.
An alarm clock rings at 4 A.M. in the Dalai Lama's cottage, part of a compound of buildings crowning a hilltop and surrounded by a high fence. 
He wakes, washes and dresses himself. 
Outside, looming dark against the mountains, is the Central Cathedral, a yellow temple capped by two gold pinnacles. 
It was built by the Tibetans who have followed the Dalai Lama into exile. 
An Indian sentry, rifle by his side, guards the canopied gate of the compound. 
Attendants stir in the staff quarters. 
A kettle is put on the stove for the day's first pot of tea, which will be served the way Tibetans prefer it, with butter added.
In a large, windowless room in the center of the house, the Dalai Lama stands before a golden statue of Avalokiteshvara, the patron saint of Tibet. 
Folding his palms in prayer, he prostrates himself three times and then, sitting on a cushion to the left of the image, prays to the enlightened beings, or Buddhas, to alleviate the suffering of all sentient beings throughout the universe. 
At 6 A.M. sharp, he leans to his left, uncovers a large shortwave radio and tunes in the BBC World Service to catch the international news.
An hour later, the Dalai Lama descends the steep flight of stairs outside his cottage and enters an orange Range Rover. 
The cabinet of the Tibetan government-in-exile is lined up to see him off. 
He is driven past his office complex, through the compound's gate and down the surrounding hills. 
The Range Rover then begins the grueling drive across the state of Punjab to the airport at Amritsar.
In New Delhi, on this January day in 1983, the Dalai Lama is greeted in India's Parliament building by Indira Gandhi. 
She ushers him into a wood- paneled office overlooking the rose gardens and fountains of an interior court. 
Their talk is strictly confidential. 
It is plain, however, that matters of some significance are being discussed. 
Tibetans who know of the meeting surmise that there may have been a development in recent negotiations between the Dalai Lama and the Chinese authorities in Peking, a development critical enough, it would appear, to warrant a meeting with the Indian Prime Minister.
This is heady stuff for the refugees, but when the Dalai Lama leaves, an hour later, nothing is said. 
Not even a rumor slips out. 
The Tibetans in exile will have to wait a further week before learning anything. 
And then, in a sermon preached by the Dalai Lama in a sacred place called Bodh Gaya, with the ruler seated beneath the Bodhi tree, the very fig tree beneath which Siddhartha Gautama, the founder of Buddhism, first attained enlightenment, the Tibetans will hear the quiet announcement that will profoundly affect their lives.
The word ''dalai'' means ''ocean of wisdom.''
A lama is a monk especially noted for his learning. 
The Dalai Lama is the pre-eminent monk of Tibetan Buddhism. 
He is the 14th to bear the title and the 10th to act as both the country's religious and temporal ruler. 
He is the first to rule outside Tibet, a country which, until Communist China invaded it in 1950, had remained virtually hidden behind the Himalayas for more than 2,000 years.
The Dalai Lama did not inherit his office. 
Like his predecessors, he was found - when a vision of his birthplace appeared to the interim ruler of Tibet and after the three state oracles had prophesied where he might be located. 
The process by which he was identified is noteworthy, because, as the Dalai Lama himself has said, the tradition may never be practiced in the same manner again.
He was born in 1935 in the small farming village of Taktser. 
When he was 2 years old, a secret delegation of monks, having been directed by the oracles, arrived and subjected the boy to a battery of tests to determine whether he was a reincarnation of the former Dalai Lama.
The monks offered gifts to the child's family and asked to be left alone with him in the bedroom at the center of the house. 
On a low table, they placed a series of articles which had belonged to the 13th Dalai Lama. 
The objects were a black rosary, a yellow rosary, a walking stick and a small ivory hand drum. 
Alongside these, the monks placed exact duplicates.
Asked to choose one of the black rosaries, the child took the correct one without hesitating and placed it around his neck, a feat he repeated with the yellow rosaries a few moments later. 
Next, the walking sticks were presented. 
At first, the boy pulled gently at the wrong stick, but then let it go and took the correct one, holding it in front of him. 
This was considered particularly significant since the ''wrong'' stick had actually been used briefly by the 13th Dalai Lama before he gave it to a friend. 
The final items were the drums. 
The false drum was beautifully decorated with floral brocade; the genuine one was less inviting. 
Once more, though, the boy took the correct object.
A physical inspection was then undertaken. 
The boy was examined for eight bodily marks which traditionally distinguish the Dalai Lamas from all other men - among them: large ears, long eyes, eyebrows curving up at their ends, streaks like those of a tiger skin on the legs, and a print resembling a conch shell on the palm of one hand. 
Gently drawing back the child's clothing, the examiners found the indications they sought. 
As one of them, a monk named Sonam Wangdu, later recounted, they were overcome with ''deep devotion, joy and gaiety. 
Indeed, we were so moved that tears of happiness filled our eyes,'' he recalled. 
''Scarcely able to breathe, we could neither sit properly on the mat nor speak a word.''
There was no longer any doubt. 
Here, halfway through his third year of life, was the holy one himself, the 14th Dalai Lama of Tibet.
Inside the Potala, the hilltop palace outside the capital city of Lhasa, the Dalai Lama was raised to rule Tibet. 
On Oct. 
7, 1950, however, Communist China invaded Tibet, claiming it, on the basis of past relations with the imperial dynasties, as part of the People's Republic. 
The Dalai Lama assumed temporal power at the age of 15. 
Shortly afterward, he fled the Chinese Army to the town of Yatung on the border of India. 
With him went more than 1,000 pack animals, each secretly laden with 120 pounds of treasure. 
They were bound for neighboring Sikkim. 
The move was taken in case the Dalai Lama should be forced to endure a long stay away from Lhasa. 
Forty mules carried gold, 600 carried silver and the remaining animals had sacks of centuries-old coins. 
For almost a decade, this relatively small share of the Dalai Lama's household treasure remained hidden, guarded by a single unknowing sentry, in an abandoned stable beneath the royal palace in Gangtok, the capital city of Sikkim. 
Only after the treasure was safely deposited in the underground vault of a Calcutta bank did the truth emerge, spawning rampant speculation in India's press over the ''God-King's fabulous fortune.''
After its conversion into currency and subsequent investment, just under million materialized to form His Holiness the Dalai Lama's Charitable Trust. 
This was useful when the Tibetans fled into exile. 
It provided seed money as the refugees began to set up businesses and a government, although it was only a fraction of the resources that were needed.
Although the Dalai Lama's treasure was sent abroad, he himself returned to Lhasa. 
For nine years, he attempted to compromise with the Chinese rulers of Tibet, but then a nationwide revolt sprang up, protesting the Chinese occupation. 
It spread to the capital and Chinese reprisals against the Dalai Lama seemed likely. 
He fled.
While more than 10,000 Tibetans were killed in Lhasa alone in the following days, the Dalai Lama journeyed, guarded by Tibetan guerrillas, down toward India, where he hoped to seek asylum. 
Near the border, he came down with dysentery after spending the night in a badly leaking tent. 
He was moved to a nearby house, where he spent a feverish day in bed and a second sleepless night. 
In the morning, word arrived that Chinese troops were closing in. 
Despite his condition and, as he later described it, in ''a daze of sickness and weariness and unhappiness deeper than I can express,'' the Dalai Lama decided to cross the border immediately.
On the afternoon of March 31, 1959, he entered a large clearing. 
At its far end stood a newly built bamboo welcome gate, beside which waited six Gurkha soldiers in heavy British ammunition boots and floppy jungle hats. 
As the Gurkhas presented arms, their commander stepped forward to offer a white scarf in greeting. 
The Dalai Lama dismounted and slowly walked across the border into India and exile. 
In the months to come, 100,000 refugees managed to escape Tibet and follow him. 
''For the moment, Tibet's sun and moon have suffered an eclipse,'' the Dalai Lama told a gathering of refugees soon afterward. 
''But one day we will regain our country. 
You should not lose heart. 
The great job ahead of us now is to preserve our religion and culture.''
The Dalai Lama's vision of exile society took root in his new headquarters, the abandoned British hill station of Dharmsala, located northwest of New Delhi on the northern margin of the Punjab. 
As a first step, the government had to be reconstituted. 
The members of the cabinet who had arrived in India divided their tasks among six portfolios: home affairs, foreign affairs, religion and culture, education, finance, security. 
A bureau was established in New Delhi to serve as the Tibetan link with the Indian Government and the various international relief agencies that were coming to the refugees' aid. 
The United Nations passed three resolutions condemning violations of human rights by the Chinese in Tibet, and support poured in from all over the world. 
The Dalai Lama, assisted by Indian lawyers, set about drafting a democratic constitution upon which to found the first elected government in Tibet's history.
Rehabilitation, however, was the immediate task at hand. 
''At the beginning of our work,'' related the Dalai Lama, ''two factions existed among the community of our responsible people. 
One thought we Tibetans must concentrate in northern India; the other - including myself - felt that it didn't matter where we lived. 
The important thing was to find a place and settle properly so that we could preserve the Tibetan identity, culture and race.''
The Dalai Lama's view eventually won out. 
Northern India, despite its desirable proximity to Tibet's border, lacked large tracts of unused land. 
India's Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru canvassed the chief ministers of his nation's less populated southern states in a search for vacant countryside. 
The state of Karnataka offered an uninhabited stretch of jungle full of elephants and situated in gently rolling hills 52 miles west of Mysore. 
The wilderness was broken by a single road along which lay a few primitive villages. 
Whatever success the Tibetans managed to wrest from the land would be their own.
At first, a group of 666 refugees left the north to homestead the new settlement. 
Other groups of 500 were sent down at six-month intervals. 
Despite the fertile soil, farming was not easy. 
A crop of lentils, cotton, tobacco and coriander sown on 28 acres in 1961 did not do well. 
A second crop of cotton and tobacco was sown, and also failed dismally. 
The exiles, used to Tibet's unique high-altitude agronomy, were foundering in southern India. 
Hundreds died. 
Just as the Dalai Lama had fallen ill when he came down from the Himalayas, so most of his followers took sick. 
They were unused to the low altitude, and they lacked immunity to many diseases unknown in Tibet's high, dry atmosphere but prevalent in subtropical India. 
Slowly, the survivors began to bring about a small economic miracle. 
An agricultural adviser from a relief organization called Swiss Technical Co- operation arrived in the jungle to offer guidance. 
Conducting soil tests, he determined that maize should be planted, sustained by fertilizer and farmed by tractors rather than the bullock plows the Tibetans were using. 
The new methods and crop worked. 
Maize proved so successful that by 1966, six years after its founding, the settlement was self-supporting. 
Three years after that, with 77,000 fruit trees planted, a dairy and poultry farm and a second crop of ragi (a cereal grass) raised to diversify the harvest, the area was producing a substantial profit.
By then, 38 settlements, harboring almost 60,000 people, had sprung up throughout India, Nepal and Bhutan, all starting out on land too remote or inhospitable for the local people to care about. 
In many places, farming proved so recalcitrant that the settlers had to rely on traditional Tibetan handicrafts, such as carpet weaving, for their income. 
Thousands of refugees began to sell gaudy green, purple, yellow and red sweaters made by machine in Punjabi factories. 
Each winter, these exiles set up shop in bazaars and marketplaces all across India. 
Their success was such that by the latter half of the 1960's a Tibetan sweater fad had swept the subcontinent.
By the early 1980's some 44 settlements, linked by commercial, political and religious ties, looked to Dharmsala as their capital and housed almost all of the 100,000 exiles. 
Given a head start by the outpourings of international economic aid and propelled by their own determination, the survivors of the original refugees thrived.
With economic security, the refugees' cultural reconstruction was assured. 
The Dalai Lama had begun the work of preservation from his first days in India. 
''We divided our culture into two types,'' he explained. 
''In the first category we placed that which needed only to be retained in books as past history. 
The second category included whatever could bring actual benefit in the present. 
These things, we resolved, must be kept alive. 
Many of our old ceremonial traditions I discarded. 
No matter, I decided, let them go. 
However, our performing arts, our literature, science and religion, as well as those crafts from which we could earn a livelihood - painting, metalcraft, architecture, woodworking and carpet making - these we took special pains to safeguard. 
To achieve this, we employed modern methods although they were altogether new to us and posed many difficulties.''
Religion is the wellspring of Tibetan civilization, and it had first priority in the Dalai Lama's plans. 
Buddhism spread from India to many countries in the Orient, but only Tibet received the full panoply of its liturgy and literature, and only Tibet kept all its disciplines alive. 
(Buddhism was almost completely wiped out in India itself by Moslem invasions in the 11th century.) In 1959 there had been nearly 600,000 Buddhist monks in Tibet and 4,000 lamas. 
Only 7,000 monks and 200 or so of the lamas escaped after the the suppression of the nationwide revolt that year. 
Those left behind in Tibet were defrocked by the Chinese.
The monks in exile sought to preserve their heritage by initially organizing sessions of memorization, debate and tutorials with senior scholars. 
They collected as many scriptures as could be found and lithographed more than 200 volumes of major works - only a small fraction, however, of Tibet's 1,200 years of philosophic writing. 
Nevertheless, they gradually built more than 150 new monasteries, filling them with young monks and, in effect, bringing Buddhism back to India, the land where it had begun.
Other institutions were set up to aid the cultural preservation. 
Three months after the Dalai Lama's arrival in Dharmsala, the Tibetan Dance and Drama Society came into being. 
Its 74 members - only 24 of whom had been performing artists in Tibet - managed to conserve in their repertory four abridged operas (the often weeklong spectacles performed in Tibet's larger cities), two historical plays and numerous cham or monastic dances.
Tibet's unique medical science, which had developed indigenously over 2,000 years, was salvaged in a hospital and pharmacy with an astrology department. 
A medical school was set up, and, by the late 1970's, its graduates were serving in all the refugee settlements in India. 
The Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, started in November 1971 at Dharmsala, soon became a magnet for hundreds of Asian and Western scholars who previously had scant access to Tibetan culture. 
In New Delhi, Tibet House, founded in 1965, supplemented much of the library's work, while the Tibetan section of All-India Radio was enlarged and a number of refugee publications appeared.
But the most extensive and important of the cultural projects was the school system. 
Created by the Dalai Lama to preserve the Tibetan identity while introducing the ''exile-generation'' to the modern world, it was looked on by all the refugees as the most fundamental hope for their future. 
The children were the first in Tibet's history to see maps of the world and hear of other nations. 
As one of them, now a young man, remembered, ''When we were first taught geography, it was almost unbelievable. 
The teacher showed us a globe and pictures of different peoples, but until it was thoroughly explained, I found it hard to accept that the world was really so large. 
I just couldn't comprehend it. 
In Tibet, India had always been the end of the earth for us.''
A large foster home, the Tibetan Children's Village, was established in Dharmsala under the direction of the Dalai Lama's younger sister. 
At the close of the 1970's its citylike campus housed more than 1,000 destitute Tibetan children from six months to 18 years of age and was regarded by United Nations agencies and others as a paradigm for the rehabilitation of refugee children.
In 1976, a series of events in China signaled the start of a new era for Tibet. 
Within a nine-month period, three Chinese leaders died - Zhou Enlai, Zhu De and Mao Zedong himself. 
Mao's Cultural Revolution was swept aside. 
Moreover, it soon became apparent that the new leaders in Peking were prepared to rethink Chinese policy on Tibet. 
Early in 1977, Peking realized that it had a powder keg on its hands; Tibet had never ceased to be ridden with revolts, and the area continued, despite a quarter- century of harsh repression, to be the most volatile region in the People's Republic. 
Rather than pursuing a policy of continual mass arrest, as Mao Zedong had done, the new Government sent a secret message to the Dalai Lama. 
It set in motion a process of delicate negotiation which continues to this day. 
Whether the talks will finally result in restored independence for Tibet remains to be seen. 
But it was clear by Jan. 
24, 1983, the day the Dalai Lama met with Indira Gandhi, that a breakthrough was imminent.
Today the Dalai Lama speaks to 30,000 of his followers as he sits beneath the sacred Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, in the eastern state of Bihar. 
The crowd rises as he comes before them, palms pressed together at his chest, smiling broadly. 
The weather is bright and warm, the flowering gardens of Buddhism's holiest shrine are filled with birdsong. 
The Dalai Lama prostrates himself, dons his yellow teaching robe and mounts a throne draped in brocade beneath a red and blue cotton canopy. 
As he places his wristwatch, face upward, on the table to his right, the assembly completes its own prostrations - thousands of heads bobbing up for a final time before settling into a motionless sea as the crowd sits upon the ground. 
The preliminary prayers begin. 
At their conclusion, the Dalai Lama starts to speak. 
As always, he prefaces his teaching with informal remarks on the usefulness of religious practice in daily life. 
Today, however, he delivers a piece of news that - even more than explaining his meeting with Indira Gandhi - amounts to perhaps the most significant statements he has made since coming into exile.
''If conditions permit,'' he says matter-of-factly in the middle of his talk, ''I am thinking of paying a visit to Tibet sometime in 1985. 
I am not likely to fall into any traps,'' he quickly adds to reassure the crowd. 
''I've had 30 years' experience dealing with the Chinese.''
The Dalai Lama's announcement, which he has chosen to deliver on this religious occasion, signals a quantum leap to the Tibetan refugees. 
The Tibetan diaspora may be coming to an end.
Despite the torrent of speculation, however, the Dalai Lama seems almost unconcerned with the nuances of the present political maneuvering between himself and the Peking Government. 
Already, following his return from Bodh Gaya, he is thinking of the future, toward the day when Tibet once more will control its own destiny.
And for the distant future, the Dalai Lama reveals that he has long considered retiring - doing so though, in a manner which would radically alter the nature of his position and, with it, Tibet's government. 
''There are many prophecies which predict that I will be the last Dalai Lama,'' he says. 
''The world is changing so dramatically that there may no longer be a need for the lineage. 
Even if the institution of the Dalai Lama does remain, the method of choosing the new Dalai Lama may not be the old, traditional way. 
I may pick the next Dalai Lama myself. 
Theoretically, this is possible, and for practical reasons it may be more sound. 
Then, once I have chosen him, I can become an extra Dalai Lama. 
Just a simple Buddhist monk,'' he adds, laughing. 
''In any event, the future is very open, very large. 
Anything can happen. 
In general, if we handle our situation carefully and act in accordance with our beliefs, it is quite possible that things will turn out well for Tibet in the end. 
Many of the prophecies concerning Tibet's future make this point, and I myself have always been convinced of it.''

text:

Before Dang Gatasai turned 14 years old, his family in Inner Mongolia, following a tradition that the fourth son become a Buddhist monk, wrote last year to ask if he could enter one of the venerable monasteries on Mount Wutai in neighboring Shanxi Province.
''I thought that he was too young,'' said Da Erji, 54, a senior monk who became a novice himself at age 7. 
''But without getting my permission, his parents sent him here because they believe in Buddhism.''
The boy traveled for 13 days to reach Mount Wutai. 
His name was changed to Sangdanjiacuo, and his head was shaved. 
Now, with three other teen-age novices at Xiantong monastery, he wears the lama's coarse brown robe and yellow sash.
Article on plans by Chinese Government, recognizing potential for tourism, to repair Buddhist temples atop Mount Wutai, carve out roads and build hotels in order to attract tourists; illustration; map (M)
Mount Wutai is really a cluster of five huge summits ranging in altitude up to 10,000 feet that is breached only by a few dirt roads twisting over the windswept passes of northern Shanxi. 
It is the most revered of the four mountains sacred to Chinese Buddhists, more than Mount Emei in Sichuan, Mount Putuo in Zhejiang or Mount Jihua in Anhui.
Â 
Zenith in 17th Century
The first temple on Mount Wutai was founded 19 centuries ago, before Buddhism fully took root in China. 
The site reached its zenith as a center of enlightened piety in the 17th century, when 2,000 monks, lamas and nuns inhabited the mountain's 360 monasteries and temples, and even emperors arrived from afar on pilgrimages.
War, revolution and Communist power shattered the tranquillity. 
During the Cultural Revolution, the monks were abused and dispersed and the monasteries were closed, but the buildings were protected from serious vandalism. 
Today, 360 monks and 20 nuns have reopened 31 of the monasteries.
The beauty of the main valley, tucked a mile high among the peaks, inspires contemplation. 
Groves of poplar and birch grow outside the red-walled monasteries, which have gracefully curved tile roofs. 
Bright wildflowers and reforested clusters of spruce trees enliven the otherwise barren slopes. 
The local peasants live out a more secular existence, growing corn, barley and hemp, raising bees or carving bowls from tree roots.
Until now, the biggest intrusion was a horse-trading fair that attracted thousands of herdsmen every summer. 
But the Government, realizing the exotic area's potential for tourism, plans to open Mount Wutai's monasteries to tourists next year.
Â 
$4 Million in Improvements
Deng Huailiang, a deputy director of the local administration bureau, said the Government and the province would spend more than $4 million by the end of this year, repairing temples, carving out roads and building hotels. 
Despite the hectic construction under way, Mr. Deng, who is not a Buddhist, assured some visiting journalists that religious activities are going smoothly.
By opening up Mount Wutai, the Government says it hopes not only to earn hard currency but also to create a showcase for its professed new tolerance of religious belief. 
The monks seem ready to endure public exposure in view of promises that the persecution of bygone years is over.
Jie Du, an elderly monk who came to Mount Wutai from Sichuan 44 years ago, recalled how he and his fellow monks were paraded in dunce caps through the streets of Taihuai, the local town, and harangued by Red Guards in the late 1960's. 
He survived the ordeal, but his old teacher, Neng Hai, did not.
''My master was persecuted to death during the Cultural Revolution,'' Jie Du said. 
''He was struggled against by the Red Guards. 
At that time, he was 83. 
How could he withstand that?''
Â 
Prayers in the Early Hours
The monks of Mount Wutai, who represent both the Lamaist and Chan sects of Mahayana Buddhism, rise several hours before dawn for long morning prayers in the cool, dark temples. 
As they go about their daily chores, the rhythm of worship is maintained by whirling green metal prayer cylinders with yellow Tibetan scripture. 
Noontime summons forth sutras, a scriptural narrative chanted to the accompaniment of pipes, cymbals and a big drum.
The vegetarian diet is partly subsidized by the Government, which Mr. Deng said paid $6 to $18 a month for each monk.
''We eat rice and wheat flour provided by the state and also some corn,'' said Yi Huan, a 66-year-old gray-robed monk. 
''Our life is better than before. 
The only difficulty is the shortage of vegetables in dry weather, but we do have potatoes.''
In return for the acquiescence of the monks in the looming commercialization of Mount Wutai, local authorities overlook some irregularities. 
Like other Chinese, the monks must live where they are legally registered to qualify for food-ration coupons. 
The abbot of Puhua monastery, Zang Ming, said that only 6 of his 37 monks had registration permits for Mount Wutai and that the rest were supported by the monastery.
Â 
Some Practices Persist
Some young monks at other temples undergo the painful ritual of having their heads tattooed with burning incense during the ordination ceremony, though Chinese law warns that religious activities must not be used to impair the health of citizens. 
Qing Fu, the senior monk at Mount Wutai, said the ritual, although not common, persisted. 
''It shows that a monk can withstand the pain and can sacrifice all he has for the happiness of others,'' he said.
The Communist Government does not like people to be exposed to religion before the age of 18, but some monks at Mount Wutai arrived earlier. 
Hua Ming, a novice at Xiantong monastery, said he was 16, though he looks younger. 
He had come from southern Shanxi with his divorced father, who was now living as a monk at Puhua monastery down the road.
Because many of the monks at Mount Wutai are elderly, the Communist authorities have let some young men join to keep the monasteries going. 
They do not add up to a revival of Buddhism in China; instead, their significance lies in their formal rejection of the official Marxist state ideology.
Â 
'It Is Our Duty'
Yuan Kai, 19, a former auto-repair worker, said he quit the Communist Youth League and became a Buddhist, though his father is an old revolutionary, because ''it is our duty to inherit Buddhism in China.''
The young Mongolian told some visitors to his cell at Bishan monastery that ''in my family, only I believe in Buddhism.''
''The others believe in Marxism,'' he said.
Mr. Yuan, who has impressed older monks with his diligent scholarship, said he believed Buddhists were not in conflict with the Communist regime because the goal of Buddhism is to set an example to be a good human being.
When a visitor reminded him that Marxism dismissed religion as mere superstition, Mr. Yuan agreed that some Buddhist ritual might strike outsiders as superstitious. 
''We can only say it is all part of the spiritual life of a Buddhist,'' he said. 
''If you say it is all superstition, why has it lasted until today?''

file: Troop Buildup Raises China-India Border Tension.txt
text:
ï»¿
American officials reported increasing concern today about rising tension between India and China as a result of a buildup of Indian and Chinese troops in a disputed, mountainous border region near Bhutan. 
The State Department has urged both sides to keep the situation calm, officials said.
The tense atmosphere developed when China began sending additional troops into the area about two weeks ago, a State Department official said. 
Then India followed suit. 
Since last weekend, the situation has become ''more threatening,'' he said, as more soldiers have been moved in, along with logistical support, to make a total of about 30,000 troops on both sides, according to American estimates.
Most of those troops were in secondary lines of defense, one official said, with relatively few facing each other on the ridge line that marks the border.
The region, which was fought over by China and India in 1962, is dominated by mountains 14,000 to 16,000 feet high, which preclude mechanized warfare. 
One specialist said only foot soldiers can fight there, and extensive combat is possible only during short periods of the year because of the weather.
This is one of those periods, shortly after the snow has ended and before the monsoon rains begin. 
A longer period of suitable weather follows the end of the rains, in late summer. 
That is when the 1962 battles were fought.
The United States has made diplomatic approaches to both India and China in an effort to dissuade them from attacking each other, a State Department official said. 
But Washington has little influence on the issue with either country.

text:
ï»¿
Some senior Reagan Administration officials have concluded they may not have reacted strongly enough to China's crackdown on recent unrest in Tibet.
They say they are now trying to determine the most effective way to express the Administration's growing displeasure with China over Tibet.
These officials concede that, in trying to avoid irritating Chinese authorities, the United States did not stand firmly enough behind its policy of promoting human rights worldwide. 
China has accused the United States of interfering in its internal affairs and threatened that continued emphasis on Tibet would damage relations.
Senior State Department officials held what were described as ''serious discussions'' this week on the issue of rights in Tibet.
Â 
Crackdown Reported to Continue
The Chinese, according to some reports, are continuing their crackdown in Tibet against Buddhist monks and Tibetans who are seeking independence for the autonomous province.
The monks have led three major demonstrations since Sept. 
27, in which at least 14 people were killed. 
Foreign journalists have been expelled from Tibet.
In the last few days, tourists have reported dozens of arrests in nighttime raids by policemen carrying automatic weapons as they swept through the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, in trucks in a show of force.
Officials in Washington said they were seeking a way to express dipleasure that would not offend China unnecessarily and would assure it that the United States has no intention of upsetting China's security arrangements on its border.
Â 
Inconclusive Discussions
The discussions this week, which were inconclusive, were prompted in large part by sharp criticism from lawmakers of both parties. 
The lawmakers argued that the United States was slow to promote the cause of Tibetan independence and that official messages deploring the recent violence were ineffective, the officials said.
''We're talking about a lot of ways we can make our views crystal clear on what we believe in and stand for,'' a State Department official said. 
''Maybe our position wasn't understood as well as it should have been.''
Successive Chinese dynasties and governments have claimed Tibet over the centuries, and it was occupied by Communist soldiers in 1950. 
In 1959, Beijing put down a bloody rebellion by the Tibetans. 
It still maintains large garrisons of troops there.
China is universally recognized as having sovereignty over Tibet. 
Since 1978, the United States has taken the position that Tibet is part of China.
Â 
Congress on the Offensive
Because the State Department criticism of China up to now has been muted, one official said, Congress has ''run away'' with American policy, taking actions and making statements that run counter to United States position on Tibet.
To compensate, the State Department has made statements that give the appearance of siding with the Chinese. 
These statements have contributed to a sense in Congress that the State Department needs to aggresively pursue the human rights issue.
Officials said they failed to realize that world attention would be focused on Tibet over the unrest.
Â 
Moves on Fact-Finding Trip
As a first step toward strengthening its position on rights abuses, the State Department is expected to urge China to reverse its decision to prohibit a Congressional fact-finding mission from visiting Tibet.
China's Foreign Ministry said Friday that the trip would not be permitted because ''matters concerning Tibet are the internal affairs of China in which the U.S. 
Congress has not right to meddle.''
The State Department is considering whether to send a message protesting the decision through Winston Lord, the United States Ambassador to China, or a more senior official, officials said.
Officials are hoping to resolve the matter before the coming Communist Party congress in China, on the assumption that the Chinese will want to end the feud soon.
Â 
Administration to Press for Trip
In testimony before two House Foreign Affairs subcommittees on Wednesday, J. Two decades of official animosity between China and the Soviet Union have created some strange situations for the minority peoples divided by the border between the two countries in Central Asia. 
Two frontier points will reopen next month for resumption of local Chinese-Soviet trading. 
But there are no prospects for reviving normal cross-border traffic, sealed off since the 1960's.
A visit among relatives separated by the border is a major operation that requires official permission and epic round-about journeys to distant crossing points. 
For example, the large town closest to Kashgar in China's Xinjiang-Uighur Autonomous Region is Osh in Soviet Kirghizia, less than 200 miles away. 
But Li Dianying, a Xinjiang official, said that a Chinese Uighur wishing to visit a Soviet relative in Osh would have to fly nearly 10,000 miles - first east to Peking, then west to Moscow and back southwest to Tashkent. 
Or he could take an equally inconvenient train to a crossing in Manchuria at the opposite end of the country.
URUMQI, China - Two decades of official animosity between China and the Soviet Union have created some strange situations for the minority peoples divided by the border between the two countries in Central Asia.
A professor at Xinjiang University recently was able to visit a Soviet relative, officials said, and a language specialist in Urumqi had a visit from his mother in the Soviet Union, but such contacts are rare.
After an estimated 30,000 Uighur refugees fled from Xinjiang into Soviet Kazakhstan in the 1960's to escape forced assimilation, China shut the border. 
It was delineated when the weak Qing dynasty ceded a chunk of Central Asia to czarist Russia in the ''unequal'' treaties of 1864 and 1881. 
China has not demanded return of this land, which includes the Soviet city of Alma-Ata, but it does lay claim to territory along Xinjiang's border with Soviet Tadzhikistan.

But no other improvement is visible in Chinese-Soviet relations in Central Asia. 
The former Soviet consulate in Urumqi has been taken over by a song-and-dance ensemble and the consulate in Kashgar is now a guest house for tourists.
The exchange of mail is slightly easier. 
Mr. Li said parcels and letters cross but language is also a barrier. 
The Cyrillic alphabet has been adopted in Soviet Central Asia, while Arabic script is again used in Xinjiang, after nearly two decades of experimentation with Roman letters.

A man in Urumqi said a relative in Alma-Ata had bought a Zhiguli sedan.

Chinese officials stress the advantages on their side - ample markets and relative tolerance for Moslem religious practice.

text:

In his 26 years of unchallenged rule in Burma, U Ne Win, whose name means ''Brilliant as the Sun,'' has preserved the facade of Burmese independence while turning a country with extraordinary economic potential into one of the poorest nations in Asia.
As a young man, Mr. Ne Win was engaged in the political and revolutionary efforts to rid Burma of British colonial rule, a goal finally achieved in 1948 amid the general British retreat from empire after World War II. 
He seized power in a bloodless coup in March 1962.
His justification for ousting a freely elected former colleague, U Nu, as Prime Minister was that Burma's multiparty democracy seemed incapable of coping with a host of ethnic and ideological rebellions that had brought warfare to the edges of Rangoon.
What he put in place was a xenophobic military dictatorship under the rubric of socialism, but marked by such inefficiency, corruption and incompetence that East European diplomats would complain that Burma was giving socialism a bad name.
Not What Marx Had in Mind
Mr. Ne Win's ''socialism,'' in fact, was a borrowed title for a murky and contradictory ideology that had little to do with Marx, whom few in Burma had read, but that served as a barrier to the modernization that continues to transform much of the rest of Southeast Asia.
It was also an excuse for the wholesale expulsion of most of Burma's merchant, commercial and technical classes, who were almost all Indian and Chinese.
The economic nationalization that followed covered almost all aspects of commercial activity and stifled it; private foreign investment ceased as Burma was increasingly isolated from the outside world. 
Last year, the United Nations assigned Burma to the category of one of the world's ''least-developed nations.''
The 38 million Burmese feed and clothe themselves through an intricate black market and a pattern of smuggling that results in much of the country's natural wealth being exported with little or no benefit to the official treasury.
Â 
Widespread Insurgency
Burma's frontiers are controlled by insurgents, and the nation's rich gemstones and hardwoods are smuggled out through Thailand. 
Burma's rubber leaves the country through Penang and is labeled Malaysian, and its art and religious treasures have been lost wholesale to the markets of Bangkok.
It has been a harsh fate for a strategic and attractive corner of Asia, stretching from the tropical waters of the Andaman Sea and the Bay of Bengal to the point in the foothills of the Himalayas where India and China meet. 
Bordering India, China, Bangladesh, Laos and Thailand, Burma was an important battleground in World War II.
Its isolation since Mr. Ne Win's ascension in 1962 has given Burma a romantic quality, especially to Westerners, who can secure a seven-day tourist visa to experience a more ''pure'' Southeast Asia, unencumbered by pollution, traffic jams and advertising slogans.
But for the Burmese, the isolation from the modern world and real political discourse has meant a life of dinginess and poverty, making great spiritual demands on the Buddhist ethos of passivity and concentration on the next life that commands the allegiance of 85 percent of the population.
Â 
Tinkering With the System
Only last year, amid overwhelming evidence of economic and social decay, did Mr. Ne Win concede mistakes and begin to tinker with Burma's stifling, corrupt and contradictory system and its complete domination by a single party, consisting almost entirely of the military. 
In September, without warning, the Government reduced the value of its highest banknotes to nothing in an effort to stop hoarding and to damage the black market. 
The effort destroyed the savings of many.
But even timid efforts at reform, after so long, led to violent protests by students in March and June that spread through Burma's major cities and flared again this month despite significant brutality by the security forces.
Diplomats reported that more than 200 people were killed by the army and police in the first major manifestation of civic unrest since student riots were put down in 1974, three years before a failed coup.
Mr. Ne Win was born Shu Maung on May 24, 1911, in Paungbe, in the Prome district 180 miles northwest of Rangoon. 
He was born into a country that had become a British colony piecemeal, after Anglo-Burmese wars in 1824, 1852 and 1885. 
In 1937, the British had separated Burma from India; in 1941, on the eve of the Japanese invasion, the British evacuated the country.
Â 
Trained by Japanese
The tall, bespectacled Shu Maung studied medicine for two years but failed his examinations and became a Rangoon postal clerk. 
By 1940, he had drifted into an anti-British revolutionary grouping and had taken on a new name. 
He was among 30 young Burmese nationalists, known as the ''30 Comrades,'' who left secretly for Japan that year and were trained to fight, as collaborators, with Japanese troops when they invaded.
When Japan declared Burma independent in 1943, Mr. Ne Win became army commander in chief; in 1945, the nascent Burmese Army, seeing the fortunes of war changing, turned against the Japanese, and had significant influence when the British returned after the war. 
The British reorganized the Burmese Army but maintained Mr. Ne Win and his colleagues in command positions.
Burma was declared independent on Jan. 
4, 1948, but was immediately confronted by widespread insurrections by Communists and Burma's ethnic minorities, the Karens, Shans, Kachins, Mons and others, who demanded autonomy. 
In 1958, Mr. Nu, faced by a potential civil war, gave Mr. Ne Win temporary control of Burma to deal with the emergency.
To the delight of Westerners, Mr. Ne Win then relinquished control, and Mr. Nu returned to power in the 1960 elections. 
Two years later, however, Mr. Ne Win, apparently obsessed by Burma's fragility and the economic domination of foreigners, overthrew Mr. Nu, and began his transformation of Burmese life.
Â 
The 'Burmese Way'
He set up a revolutionary government, removed Buddhism as the state religion and set out the ''Burmese Way to Socialism'' and ''The System of Correlation of Man and His Environment,'' two confusing documents that were taught in schools but never discussed. 
He did, however, extend literacy and basic medical care throughout the country, and maintained a stiffly neutral course between superpower blocs, despite intermittent tension with the Chinese.
An avid womanizer and gambler, Mr. Ne Win banned gambling, closed nightclubs and promoted a strict morality while marrying at least four times; he has at least one son and three daughters.
Said to have a violent temper, he nonetheless persisted in a passion for golf, making it a popular game among Burmese officials. 
Because such officials needed permission to entertain foreigners, the golf course also became an important meeting ground for diplomats and journalists. 
In earlier years, he traveled widely and lavishly in the West; lately he has spent much of his time as a recluse in a lakeside villa, emerging only to hit the heavily guarded fairways.
Mr. Ne Win officially retired from the military in 1972 and became president in 1974 under a new Constitution, a position he relinquished in November 1981, citing old age. 
But until yesterday, he retained control of the Burma Socialist Program Party, the country's one legal mass organization, and is thought to retain the loyalty of the military.

text:

When Thubten Samphel visited a Tibetan monastery near Clifton, N.J., he was surprised to find one of the monks waiting at the bus station in a car to drive him there.
''As the foreigners are fond of saying, the only wheel in Tibet is the prayer wheel,'' said Mr. Samphel, one of four native Tibetans studying in the United States under a new Congressional scholarship program.
Monks with driver's licenses and monasteries with hot and cold running water are the least of the cultural differences that Mr. Samphel, whose parents were servants 30 years ago of the Dalai Lama, the exiled leader of Tibet, has encountered in the last two months.
Recently, Mr. Samphel, who is studying at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, watched a game of touch football in Sakura Park in Morningside Heights and spoke of such differences.
'Getting Your Facts Straight'
''Tibetan culture and American society are so totally different,'' said Mr. Samphel, 32 years old, who followed the Dalai Lama to India after a Tibetan uprising against the Chinese was put down in 1959. 
In India, he attended Western-style schools and learned English.
''Tibetans are considered very spiritual,'' he said. 
''Here everything is material. 
Everyone seems to be working all the time.''
An experienced writer and editor in India - from 1980 until last August he edited the official English organ of the Dalai Lama's Government-in-exile in Dharmsala, India - he nonetheless is now getting his first formal training in journalism.
''The most important thing is getting your facts straight,'' said Mr. Samphel, who for class was recently assigned to cover the Larry Davis trial in the Bronx. 
''In India it's more laid back toward getting the story; you use the first word that comes to your mind. 
In China and Tibet, the Government is the newspaper. 
What the Government decides to inform the public becomes the daily news.''
Â 
Making Adjustments
One of Mr. Samphel's professors, Stephen D. Isaacs, said that Mr. Samphel had asked not to be treated differently from other students because of his language problems or cultural differences.
''You take anyone from out of town, much less out of this world, and send them to the Larry Davis trial - it's going to be difficult,'' Professor Isaacs said. 
Perhaps the most challenging assignment of all has been learning aggressive street reporting.
''We tend to be very polite,'' Mr. Samphel said. 
''Here you have to leave this pretense and get what you want.''
For now he hopes to work for an American newspaper after he graduates, but he can see himself ultimately returning to his old job in India. 
He even holds hope for an independent Tibet someday.
''We Tibetans have not too many choices,'' he said. 
''Emotionally we would like Tibet to be independent, free. 
But you run into these practical problems: How do you proceed to do that without an army, without anything, without the support of one single government?''
''Whether we like it or not, we have to adjust to the modern world,'' he said. 
''We must be absolutely realistic.''
Such feelings are common among young Tibetans, said Tenzin Chhodak, the director of the Office of Tibet, a New York branch of the Dalai Lama's government and a friend of Mr. Samphel for more than a decade. 
Mr. Chhodak, who administers the scholarship program for Congress, hopes to bring 11 more young Tibetans to the United States by next year.
Although Mr. Samphel received both his bachelor's and master's degrees in modern Chinese history, and his one visit to Tibet in almost 30 years was as part of a tour sponsored by the Chinese Government in 1985, like most Tibetans he retains deep hostility toward China.
''My next-door neighbor is from Beijing,'' Mr. Samphel said. 
''We have been very polite to each other.''
