"I know that in Tibet there've been some separatist activities, but it's not like that here," he said. 
"Relations among the nationalities are good here, and we've got religious freedom."
Â 
Chinese Learned in School
Mr. Suonan Dajie and Mr. Wenchangtai, who spoke in the fluent Chinese they learned in school, were interviewed at random along with dozens of other Tibetans, mostly during several days of hiking along the trails of Gonghe County in central Qinghai Province. 
No one else was present for most of the interviews, although the security forces made considerable efforts to trace this reporter's steps and interrogate those Tibetans who were interviewed.
Local officials, who had previously refused to allow a visit to Qinghai, allowed this trip to an international conference in Qinghai. 
They protested vigorously when this reporter slipped away to roam the countryside, and they also assigned "tails" to try to determine who was contacted.
The jitteriness among officials contrasted with the bucolic scenes of yellow wheat and snow-capped mountains, and paradoxically most of the rural Tibetans seemed more content and less politicized or fearful than the urban middle class in cities like Beijing and Shanghai -- or Tibet itself. 
In Lhasa, many Tibetans are enraged by the shootings and torture and repression about them. 
But here in Qinghai there appear to be few detentions and little or no torture to radicalize the Tibetans, although conditions may not be so idyllic as the authorities claim.
"There've been no conflicts, not even one," claimed Suonan Tsering, a Tibetan who is director of the Government's nationality affairs commission in the provincial capital, Xining.
Â 
Confrontations Reported
In fact, however, there have been several confrontations since 1987 in the East Qinghai town of Tongren, and two Tibetan monks there were sentenced last year to prison terms of 12 months and 18 months for unfurling a Tibetan national flag on the street. 
Both presumably have now completed their sentences.
In Xinghai County, two young men were forced to flee to India last year when the police sought to arrest them for distributing 100 pro-independence leaflets, villagers said. 
And in Gonghe County, a young man was detained after he visited associates of the Dalai Lama in India. 
He was released and fled back to India.
Robert Barnett, coordinator of the London-based Tibet information network, an independent monitoring service, cited several past arrests in southern Qinghai, not far from the town of Yushu. 
But he said it was not known if there were now any Tibetan political prisoners in Qinghai.
Villagers in Qinghai said they were unaware of the new Tibetan-language broadcasts by the Voice of America, but they all knew of the shootings of protesters in Lhasa. 
They said the news had spread by word of mouth, rippling across the grasslands from hut to hut, tent to tent.
Â 
'Our Hearts Are Breaking'
"Our hearts were breaking," a middle-aged Tibetan peasant said in the privacy of his home. 
"We don't count as people here. 
We're becoming a minority, and the only way to protect ourselves is independence. 
People don't dare say it, but everybody feels it in their hearts."
That was far from a uniform view among Tibetans interviewed, but even those who opposed independence were deeply distressed by the violence in Lhasa and by restrictions affecting religion. 
While many young Tibetans said they had religious freedom, there are stark limits. 
A half-dozen shopowners said independently that they were not permitted to sell photos of the Dalai Lama.
The photos are enormously important to Tibetans, who revere the Dalai Lama and want to display photos of him in their shops, monasteries and on altars in their homes. 
In the Tibet autonomous region, repression is in many respects greater than in Qinghai, but there photographs of the Dalai Lama are allowed to circulate freely.
"We can display the photos in our homes, but not here at the monastery," said a young monk at Kumbum monastery, also known as Taer Si, in eastern Qinghai. 
As in Tibet, the monasteries function as an alternative university system, and what little resistance has surfaced in Qinghai has come largely from monks.
"That is the space of the picture of the Dalai Lama," said a lean old monk in Kumbum monastery. 
He pointed reverently to a blank space on a wall, as if it were one of the monastery's most precious possessions.
The authorities also place loose restrictions on the numbers of monks who can be inducted into any monastery. 
Kumbum, for instance, had 3,000 monks at the time of the Communist revolution, according to the American-published "China Handbook" of 1950. 
Now it is officially allowed to have 400 monks, although in fact there are about 500.
A common source of antagonism appears to be family planning restrictions in rural areas. 
The rules in Qinghai are similar to those in the rest of China: Han couples are allowed one child each, or sometimes two in the countryside, while Tibetans and other minorities are given special dispensation and are allowed two or three each. 
Fines equivalent to $100 to $200 are now imposed on those who have unauthorized births.
While many peasants all over China complain about family planning rules, here the grumbling sometimes takes on nationalist overtones because those who enforce the unpopular policies tend to be Han Chinese.
"They didn't sterilize anyone around here until recently," said a Tibetan peasant who already has more children than he was supposed to. 
"But now they're trying to sterilize women after they give birth to two babies. 
They keep coming to me and saying that unless my wife agrees to be sterilized, then they'll take our land and smash our house."
He shrugged his shoulders helplessly. 
"So we'll give in," he said. 
"She'll be sterilized."
Still, standards of living for Tibetans in Qinghai are unquestionably rising, as they are in all of China, and that may be one of the most important reasons why there is not more political and religious ferment.
While the villages visited were all accessible only by dirt path, they had electricity, bicycles, often tiny tractors and among young people, the first hints of an interest in fashion. 
A teen-age girl was toiling one evening in the fields, arranging stacks of grain -- a timeless scene, except that she was wearing a bright-red blazer.
"They control religion pretty tightly," said a 29-year-old Tibetan peasant who seemed to fit in the middle of the spectrum of opinion. 
"But life's getting a lot better for us. 
Most folks have televisions, and a few even have a color television. 
So life's getting more comfortable, and a lot of us are reasonably satisfied."

file: INFERNO IN CHINA_ FINALLY THE RAINS CAME.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE GREAT BLACK DRAGON FIRE 1
A Chinese Inferno.
By Harrison E. Salisbury.
Illustrated. 180 pp. 
Boston:
Little, Brown & Company. 
$17.95.
In terms of sheer destruction and ecological damage, the fires that swept the Hinggan forests of Manchuria and Siberia in May 1987 rank as one of the worst environmental disasters of this or any other century. 
The fires were more than 10 times the size of last year's fires in Yellowstone National Park. 
Yet little is known about them outside China and official circles in the Soviet Union. 
Even among experts, there is only sketchy information on possibly the world's largest forest fires in the past 300 years, conflagrations that blackened an area almost the size of New England.
Harrison E. Salisbury, the distinguished former New York Times correspondent and the author of, among other books, ''The Long March: The Untold Story,'' is one of the few foreigners to have visited the remote, devastated region. 
''The Great Black Dragon Fire'' is the sobering story of a catastrophe whose full impact has yet to be measured or understood. 
The Chinese are convinced that the fires affected their climate, and there has been speculation that they may have further damaged the fragile ozone layer.
The Greater Hinggan Forest was the world's largest stand of evergreens, stretching like a green velvet sea, approximately 500 miles long and 300 miles wide. 
It is bisected by the Heilongjiang, or Black Dragon, River (known in the West by its Russian name, the Amur), which forms the border between Chinese Manchuria and Soviet Siberia. 
Before the fires, the Manchurian part of the forest accounted for a third of China's timber reserves.
There had been a prolonged period of dry weather, and the danger of fire was high on both sides of the river in the spring of 1987. 
From Mr. Salisbury's description, it would seem that the Chinese fire prevention and detection methods and firefighting resources were primitive by American and Canadian standards. 
Despite the hazardous condition, people smoked in the forest, built campfires and used unsafe logging practices. 
From natural and accidental causes, a number of fires broke out about the same time in Manchuria and Siberia, quickly consolidating into several large ones.
One known cause was Wang Yufeng, an 18-year-old who was temporarily working as a brush cutter. 
Ironically, brush cutting is done to reduce the danger of fire, but the inexperienced teen-ager violated every safety rule and, as Mr. Salisbury notes, became a modern Chinese version of Mrs. O'Leary's cow. 
He overfilled his machine, spilling gas, which ignited from an engine spark and set the machine and the grass on fire. 
It jumped to the trees and flashed into a raging inferno that destroyed the town of Xilinji. 
(The hapless young man was whisked off to jail even as the alarms were sounding.) Thus began one of the largest Black Dragon fires. 
The monthlong battle was fought by Chinese Army troops, the local inhabitants and what appears to have been a small number of professional firefighters. 
Missing were the battalions of trained forest firefighters who are deployed in the American West and specialized apparatus, effective communications and airplanes that drop fire-retardant chemicals. 
There was no contact between the Chinese and Soviet commands that were fighting fires on each side of the river.
Mr. Salisbury's interviews with the people involved reveal the strength of the human spirit when faced with overwhelming tragedy. 
There were some notable cowards and incompetents, but there were more heroes. 
Most of the inhabitants of the Manchurian timber towns did the best they could as the fiery monster devoured their homes and livelihood and killed their families and neighbors. 
No one really knows how many died, but Mr. Salisbury believes the official Chinese report of only 250 is far below the actual toll.
As the Mayor of Xilinji, Wang Zhaowin took firm command, anticipated the tricks of the wind and saved thousands of lives by evacuating her people from the river - where they would have been trapped - to an open road junction. 
Incredibly, 18,000 people huddled at the crossroads as flames fanned by a 40-mile-an-hour wind engulfed the town. 
(Later, her bitter reward was to be relieved of her job by the provincial government.) The Black Dragon fires burned until it rained in early June. 
When they were over, China had lost more than three million acres of timber. 
The total damage is estimated at more than $4 billion. 
The long-range environmental impact has yet to be calculated, but the outlook is grim. 
It could be several generations before the dominant larch evergreens grow again, and the Hinggan forest may never be the same.
One can only guess at what happened on the other side of the river in Siberia. 
Between 9 million and 15 million acres are believed to have burned there - at least three times larger than the area destroyed in Manchuria. 
Despite glasnost, there has been no report from the Russians. 
What may have been the greatest forest fire in history remains a nonevent in the Soviet Union.
Mr. Salisbury's book penetrates some of that secrecy and provides a fascinating look at a remote pocket of the world. 
It is also a dramatic and compassionate account of the people who live there and the disaster that befell them. 
And ''The Great Black Dragon Fire'' is another warning to everyone who is concerned about what is happening to planet Earth.

file: Lawmakers Cheer Tibetan in Capitol Rotunda.txt
text:
ï»¿
Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, speaking to a receptive gathering of members of Congress today in the Capitol rotunda, appealed to the United States to aid Tibet in its struggle against Chinese Government control.
Setting aside his prepared text to speak in halting English about what he termed the "universal responsibility" Americans should feel for conditions in Tibet, the Dalai Lama was greeted with applause and cheers from several hundred people in attendance.
China filed a formal protest objecting to the Dalai Lama's travels, which included today's address to Congress and a meeting at the White House on Tuesday with President Bush.
The Chinese Government has maintained that the Dalai Lama, a Buddhist monk, is an outcast and troublemaker who is encouraging other countries to meddle in China's affairs.
Until this visit, the White House has maintained its distance from the Dalai Lama in favor of cordial relations with China. 
But this time the Dalai Lama gained entry to the highest levels of Government when President Bush, once an American envoy to China, met with the religious leader at the White House for 30 minutes on Tuesday.
Marlin Fitzwater, the White House spokesman, said the President's meeting with the Dalai Lama had led to a protest, but the White House expressed no regret over the decision.
Mr. Bush's decision to meet with the Tibetan drew praise from ideologically disparate members of the House and Senate who had initially wanted the Dalai Lama to address a joint meeting of Congress. 
House Speaker Thomas S. Foley and the Senate Majority Leader, George J. Mitchell, who shared the stage with the Dalai Lama, turned down that request and gave permission for the rotunda ceremony instead. 
"The joint session is not taking place because of various reasons," Senator John F. Kerry, Democrat of Massachusetts, said in remarks on the floor of the Senate today, "but I think most realistically because we do not want to offend China."
An aide to Mr. Foley said holding the ceremony in the Capitol rotunda was unusual enough to convey heightened respect for the Tibetan leader and sympathy for his cause.
"As His Holiness and the people of Tibet move forward on their own great journey, we stand with them," said the Senate Minority Leader, Bob Dole. 
"We stand with them and we want the People's Republic of China to hear this message. 
We stand with them."
The Tibetan leader, who has lived in exile in India for 32 years, wore the scarlet and yellow robes of a Tibetan Buddhist monk and acknowledged the applause with his palms pressed together and his fingers pointing upward.
"Here I enjoy the freedom of speech, freedom of talk, freedom of movement," the Dalai Lama said. 
"You, this nation, I think very much involved or very much cherish these principles. 
However when I was about 15, I lost that freedom."
Â 
Nobel Prize in 1989
The Dalai Lama, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989, governed Tibet until his flight in 1959, after Chinese forces took control. 
The United States officially recognizes Tibet as a part of China.
A spokesman for the Chinese Embassy said that Beijing was "firmly opposed" to the Dalai Lama's travels on behalf of a Tibetan state and that it had lodged a strong protest with the United States Government. 
"It is unacceptable to the Chinese Government for officals of any country to meet the Dalai Lama or his representatives in any form," he said.
But the Dalai Lama, in his prepared remarks, urged other nations to take a "stronger stand" toward China on the matter of human rights in Tibet.
"Recently, the United States has led the international community in freeing a small country from cruel occupation," the Tibetan leader said. 
"I am happy for the people of Kuwait. 
Sadly, all small nations cannot expect similar support for their rights and freedoms."
A "new world order" without freedom is oppression, he said.
The Dalai Lama won support from his supporters in Congress and the Senate passed a resolution supporting Tibet's right to self-determination.

file: Man in the News_Prophet of the Middle Way.txt
text:
ï»¿
A fundamental tenet of Buddhism is that the path to salvation runs between the extremes of self-denial and self-indulgence. 
Therein lies a hint of the path by which the Dalai Lama, spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhists, eventually hopes to return from exile.
The cause of 54-year-old Tenzin Gyatso, the Dalai Lama, 14th earthly incarnation of Avalokiteshvara, Lord of Compassion, was bolstered yesterday when he was named winner of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize.
Sixteen months ago, when the Chinese, who have occupied Tibet for 39 years, said they would let him return if he renounced independence, the slight, soft-spoken, seemingly ever-smiling Dalai Lama rejected the offer, but left the door open to compromise.
''I am trying to find some other way, a middle way,'' he said. 
''We need more patience.''
Two months later, he recognized China's right to determine Tibet's foreign policy and even to maintain troops on Tibetan soil, but called for creation of a ''self-governing, democratic political entity'' in association with China.
Â 
'A Question of Holiness'
With hard-liners holding the upper hand in Beijing, that middle path seems blocked. 
And so for now - in the humble, detached manner that has irritated militant Tibetans and impressed the Nobel Committee -the Dalai Lama may have to continue preaching nonviolence as the only practical path to Tibetan freedom.
''Nonviolence is not a question of holiness,'' he once said. 
''It is a question of reality.''
There are six million Tibetans and a billion Chinese, he pointed out, and China has tens of thousands of troops in Tibet.
Still, practical detachment is no measure of ardor. 
In an interview in August, the Dalai Lama observed that freedom is a human need, adding, ''It may be even more than human.''
''I have a cat,'' he said. 
''People feed this cat. 
They pet this cat. 
They give the cat everything he needs. 
But every time the window is open just a little, he runs away.''
Â 
The Awaited Sign
The son of peasant parents from the Kokonor region of northeastern Tibet, the future Dalai Lama was born on June 6, 1935 - the day the 13th Dalai Lama died. 
By Mayahana Buddhist tradition, that passing inspires a wide-ranging search by the most venerated monks for the next god-king.
And so, when an array of objects was placed before the 2-year-old and he immediately grabbed one that belonged to the 13th Dalai Lama, it was the awaited sign that the embodiment of Buddha had been reincarnated. 
On Feb. 
22, 1940, in the holy city of Lhasa, he was enthroned and immediately moved into the Potala, a 1,000-room palace overlooking the city.
But there was a prophecy at the time, that the 14th Dalai Lama would one day leave Tibet, to return later, still the Ocean of Wisdom, which is what Dalai Lama literally means.
In 1950, the 12th year of his reign, China invaded and grabbed power from the Dalai Lama. 
Then, after Chinese troops crushed an uprising in 1959, he trekked across the border into India, soon followed by 100,000 other refugees. 
Since then, he has headed a government in exile based in the Himalayan town of Dharmsala.
In exile, the god-king's way of life is ascetic. 
Rising at 2 A.M., he meditates for several hours a day, eats two small meals, putters in his garden, tinkers with machines and studies world issues.
Â 
Of Wide Learning
Although schooled exclusively by the monks in his childhood, the Dalai Lama has shown a prodigious capacity for learning about the more material aspects of life. 
Among his studies have been mathematics, geography, English and the social sciences.
He is the author of several books on Buddhist theology and practice and has written an autobiography. 
In 1987, he won the Albert Schweitzer Humanitarian Award.
The purpose of his exile, the Dalai Lama insists, is to rally world support for the preservation of Tibetan culture until the day independence is restored. 
''The world community has a responsibility to preserve one of its ancient cultures,'' he said in March. 
Tibetans assert that more than 6,000 of their temples have been destroyed by the Chinese since 1959, their treasures often stolen and sold.
But he also sees his role as promoting world harmony, particularly through the Buddhist notion of self-improvement. 
''Without inner peace, it is impossible to have world peace,'' he told 5,000 people on a visit to St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York in 1979.
''Through compassion, through love, it is possible to become a true human family,'' he said. 
''Through love, we can have true happiness, real disarmament.''
Global though his concerns may be, the Dalai Lama never seems to lose his impish sense of delight. 
Asked once what he missed most about Tibet, he said, ''Yaks.''

file: Mongols to Elect New Parliament With China Watching the Results.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mongolians go to the polls Sunday, in some areas by horse or camel, to vote in sharply contested parliamentary elections that are in part a referendum on the pace of the nation's transition to democracy and a market economy.
The campaign is a triumph of pluralism, with a dozen political parties representing the interests of everyone from shepherds to capitalists. 
But many Mongolians say they have lost the enthusiasm that they felt for the first competitive election, held two years ago in the aftermath of the democratic revolution that ended seven decades of Communist rule.
"I was very excited by democracy when it first arrived," Ninj, a 55-year-old housewife, said as she prepared dinner over a fire in her ger, the traditional white felt tent in which many Mongolians still live. 
"I thought everything would get better, but in fact not much has changed. 
I'm very disappointed."
Â 
At Issue: Pace of Change
While each party has a different platform, the main issue facing the new Parliament is the pace of democratic change. 
The governing party, the former Communist Party, is privatizing the economy and freeing the press, and seems committed to continue doing so, but an opposition victory would probably accelerate the process.
Ms. Ninj, who like most Mongolians uses one name, said she would vote for the former Communist Party, formally known as the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party. 
The Party had intended to modernize by dropping the word "Revolutionary" from its name, but in the meantime, a Buddhist monk registered his own party called the Mongolian People's Party and so the former Communists are stuck with their old name.
"I got used to the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party when I was young," said Ms. Ninj as she sat in her ger, which is 20 feet in diameter and has a smoke hole in the top. 
"And so that's who I'm going to vote for."
The generation gap cuts across this ger, as it does all Mongolia. 
Ms. Ninj's 25-year-old daughter, Ulziy, said she would vote for the newly formed Capitalist Party. 
Ms. Ulziy said she thinks the Capitalist Party will lower tariffs and allow the import of the food and clothing that Mongolia lacks.
Ms. Ulziy has another reason to support the new democratic forces: They helped overturn the Communist policy that banned abortion and all forms of artificial birth control. 
The Communists felt that Mongolia needed more than its 2.1 million inhabitants in a country about three times the size of Texas. 
But Ms. Ulziy already has two children and thinks that is plenty.
The voting here in Mongolia could reverberate across the border into the Inner Mongolia region of China, where nationalism has been rising among ethnic Mongols ever since Mongolia's free elections in 1990. 
The Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party won those elections after it renounced Communism, and China clearly hopes that it will win again on Sunday.
Â 
Beijing Aids Party Paper
Last year China even intervened in Mongolian politics, donating 500 tons of newsprint to the newspaper published by the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party. 
China apparently worries that if the former Communists are voted out of power in Mongolia, China's Mongols will be inspired to seek democracy or independence.
The elections will choose the members of a new 76-member Parliament, which will replace the previous, much larger legislature. 
President Punsalmaagiyn Ochirbat, a former Communist who says he has turned a new leaf, is not up for re-election.
The architect of the democratic revolution two years ago, Zorig, is today the chairman of the main opposition coalition. 
Mr. Zorig, who now teaches politics, is 29 years old and reflects the general youthfulness of the campaign. 
Nearly 40 percent of the 300 candidates are 30 years old or under, while only 25 percent are 46 or more.

file: More in China Willingly Rear Just One Child.txt
text:
ï»¿
Gong Daifang, a 36-year-old peasant, has made a decision that her ancestors probably would never have understood: her 10-year-old son is enough, and she will not have another child.
Even when local leaders in this brick-and-mud village in Sichuan province offered to allow her to have a second child, she decided that for practical economic reasons she would have only one, instead of seven like her own mother.
''My husband and I thought it over, but we believe that this way we can save money and lead a better life,'' Miss Gong explained. 
China's population, the world's largest at 1.1 billion, is still increasing. 
But there are indications of a revolution in attitudes, with more and more Chinese couples falling in line with the nation's one-child policy as a matter of choice rather than compulsion. 
In view of the changing attitudes, some experts are predicting that China's population will actually decline after peaking in the early 21st century.
Coercion still underlies the one-child policy, and the rationing of the right to become pregnant remains a source of tension and bitterness in many parts of China. 
Many peasants grumble that the policy is not always carried out fairly, or should not be applied to them until they give birth to a son. 
Even Government officials acknowledge that some women are probably still forced to have abortions, and that many parents would like more children than they are allowed.
But there is little doubt that young people's attitudes are changing and that China's family planning campaign has much broader support than it did.
Interviews over the last year with families in scattered parts of China, including rural areas in Sichuan, Hunan and Gansu provinces as well as in Beijing, suggest that many young people today want only one or two children and that the traditional Chinese enthusiasm for large families is rapidly declining.
Deng Daoyun, a 24-year-old peasant who lives in the picturesque Sichuan hamlet of Sancun, 40 miles north of the city of Chengdu, is proud of her 3-year-old son but said she was happy to stop where she was.
''One child is enough. 
More kids, more nuisance,'' she said, mocking the old saying that goes, ''More sons, more joy.''
Liao Zhenxiu, a housewife in Duanjiaba, pointed at her television set and tape recorder as the reasons for not having a second child. 
''If I had lots of kids, how could I afford these things?'' she asked. 
''If you have lots of kids, you're poor.''
Â 
The Bottom Line Is Money
Two factors underlie the changing preferences. 
The first is the emergence of a quasi-market economy, in which a mother can get a job and earn more money if she has fewer children. 
The second is the institutionalizing of the Chinese Government's system of incentives and penalties that give enormous advantages to those who have just one child.
The incentives vary by region, but often a couple with just one child will get more land, a better house, a reduction in grain taxes and a subsidy amounting to about $15 a year -equivalent to more than a month's income for many poor peasants. 
On the other hand, those who have children without permission must pay fines annually for 10 years, amounting each time to 5 to 10 percent of the parents' income.
The upshot is that there is much less need today to drag women to abortion clinics, because cool calculation of the penalties may well lead them to seek abortions voluntarily.
It is clear that without the system of incentives and penalties, there would be more children. 
In Qinmi in Sichuan, 24-year-old Tan Wenbi cuddled her 20-day-old son and said she would have no other child. 
But asked what would happen if there were no one-child policy, she thought for a moment and then said that if that were the case she would like a girl as well.
In Tongzhi, a village in Hunan, 28-year-old Rong Maozi said she was delighted to have one boy and one girl. 
But if there were no pressure whatever, she said, she would continue to bear children.
''I'd like more kids, boys and girls, but they won't let me,'' she said. 
But her voice held no rancor, suggesting that more than a dozen years of propaganda about family planning have had an effect.
Â 
Acknowledging the Problem
''The lessons really have sunk in,'' said Aprodicio Laquian, a Filipino who recently completed a five-year assignment in China as country director of the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. 
''If you ask a person on the street if China has a population problem, they'll immediately say 'yes.'
''
Despite the new attitude, however, foreign experts and accounts in China's official press say the family-planning program faces severe problems in meeting its short-term targets. 
Chinese officials acknowledge that it will be extremely difficult to meet their goal of holding the population to 1.2 billion by the turn of the century. 
China now has 1.1 billion people, and the number is growing by more than 15 million a year. 
The principal challenges are these:
* China's baby boomers, born after the famine at the beginning of the 1960's, are now in their reproductive years and will produce an echo of the earlier baby boom.
* Many young Chinese are now so prosperous that they can afford the fines for having a second or third child. 
In some areas these fines are called the ''extra baby fee.''
* The Government no longer has such tight control over the country as it used to.
In Sancun, the family planning official, a woman named Zhuang Dazi, keeps record books of the menstrual cycles of all women in the village, and there has not been an unplanned child in a decade. 
But control mechanisms are disintegrating in some other parts of the country. 
Some women now travel away from their hometowns when they become pregnant, and give birth without ever registering their baby. 
And because of the decline in control, it is also possible for women to bribe doctors to remove their intrauterine devices, or IUD's, the most common form of birth control in China.
Â 
Misguided Short-Term Goals
China's population goals are at risk partly because the Government relaxed the Draconian controls it began implementing at the end of the 1970's. 
Some foreign diplomats worry that the authorities could institute a new policy including forced abortions and other harsh measures. 
But officials here, recalling the bad publicity China received around the world for such measures, say that will not happen.
''The situation is rather grave,'' said Shen Guoxiang, a spokesman for the State Family Planning Commission. 
''But that doesn't mean we should tighten control over family planning.''
While China will almost certainly miss its target for the turn of the century, that goal is widely regarded as misguided. 
If China had been more successful in carrying out its one-child policy, experts say, a result would have been a rapid aging of the population and social strains as a relatively small number of workers supports an unusually large proportion of retired people. 
Concern about this problem appears to be one reason why China is not implementing the one-child policy as strictly as it used to.
China's continuing population increase has more to do with demographics - half the population is 25 or younger, and so is still producing children or is yet to produce children - than with family size. 
But after this demographic bulge reaches middle age and retirement, the population is expected to contract. 
Accounts in the official Chinese press even muse that the nation's ''ideal'' population is 700 million, implying that this figure could be a longterm goal.
Â 
A Closer Look at the Statistics
Chinese officials and foreign commentators frequently say that Chinese women still have an average of nearly 2.5 children, despite the one-child policy. 
But this is misleading, Chinese and foreign demographers say. 
While China's total fertility rate is about 2.3, this statistic measures births for all women in their reproductive years, ages 15 to 49. 
Thus the figure includes some women in their 40's who bore three or four children long before family planning controls were introduced.
A more accurate reflection of the present situation is the distribution of births. 
More than half of all births are of first children, and an additional 25 to 30 percent are of second children. 
Only 15 percent of all births are of third children.
The family planning rules that achieved the declines in fertility differ by province, but here in Sichuan, couples can apply to have a second child if the first is sickly or if the parents are disabled and need help. 
In remote areas, couples can normally have two children and occasionally they are allowed three. 
Partly because of this relaxation, there are scarcely any accusations within China these days about forced abortions.
''The Government absolutely doesn't allow forced abortions,'' said Tan Sushun, director of the Sichuan College for Family Planning Professions. 
''When a woman is pregnant outside the plan, we give her education and tell her not to give birth. 
But if she really wants to, she can.''
Miss Tan acknowledged that some village officials do resort to force, against the rules, but villagers interviewed said they did not know of such cases. 
Indeed, force is usually unnecessary, for even the most strong-willed couple will normally wilt and agree to an abortion after months of reprimands and threats from village officials.

file: Nepal_s Economy Is Gasping as India, a Huge Neighbor, Squeezes It Hard.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dispute with India is forcing Nepal, one of the world's poorest and least accessible countries, to fight for its economic survival, a fight that is also testing its political stability.
New Delhi cut most of the landlocked kingdom's vital trade links to the outside world more than two weeks ago, and Nepal was shaken by student demonstrations on April 3 and 4. 
The protests became as anti-Government as they were anti-Indian. 
Universities in the Katmandu area were closed amid conflicting reports of casualties as the police suppressed the riots.
Lines at gas stations are long, straining tempers. 
The streets of Katmandu, the capital, are nearly devoid of cars, and travel around Nepal by air or bus is becoming more difficult. 
Forests are being stripped for cooking fuel.
In an interview Sunday, Nepal's Foreign Minister, Shailendra Kumar Upadhyaya, said Katmandu wanted to end its special relationship with India, which had become one of economic dependence.
''It is in our interest to let interdependence grow,'' he said of ties with India. 
''It is in our interest to see that our dependence on one country does not grow.''
Â 
Border Crossings Closed
Nepal, wedged between China and India, the world's two most populous nations, has only one reliable outlet to the sea, overland through the Indian port of Calcutta, more than 700 miles away.
On March 23, after a dispute over how to renegotiate lapsed trade and transit treaties, New Delhi suddenly closed 19 of 21 border crossings with this Himalayan nation, severing links not only to the port but also to northern Indian cities.
The Indians want a single pact. 
The Nepalese want two, as they have had since 1978, to separate their important transit rights from trade and commercial ties to India. 
The two accords were a concession made by a previous Government in New Delhi under Prime Minister Moraji Desai.
Foreign Minister Upadhyaya said Nepal had in the last few days proposed a new trade treaty that would include no special concessions but only most-favored-nation status, putting economic relations with New Delhi on a more equal footing. 
Indian officials have not responded.
At the end of March, two more agreements expired, covering Nepal's imports of petroleum products and coal through India. 
Almost immediately, there was a sharp drop in supplies of kerosene for cooking and gasoline for the buses and trucks that link remote villages to sources of food, medicine and other necessities.
Â 
Trees Cut for Fuel
Rationing of petroleum products has been introduced. 
Prices of other commodities like sugar, salt and processed foods, many imported from India, have risen.
Even protected trees have been cut to meet fuel shortages. 
Trucks arrive daily, bringing precious logs to be burned in cooking fires.
Chirin S. Thapa, a principal adviser to King Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev, called the damage to forests ''an unfortunate part of this emergency.''
He said the emergency measures could endanger the survival of Nepal's 18 million people.
Deforestation in Nepal, apart from eroding local hillsides, is contributing to flooding in India and Bangladesh as swollen Himalayan rivers rush down to the plains.
Interviews with Nepalese and Indian officials here and in New Delhi, Nepalese businessmen and journalists, and Western diplomats in Katmandu reveal a complex interaction of causes and perceptions that led to what the Nepalese say was a completely unexpected blockade by India.
Â 
Links With China a Factor
It is almost universally believed in Katmandu that the trade dispute was only a pretext for New Delhi to vent its displeasure with Nepal for an accumulation of grievances. 
Growing Nepalese-Chinese cooperation, culminating in Katmandu's purchase in August 1988 of Chinese antiaircraft guns, is a major factor.
The presence of Chinese contractors working on World Bank or Government aid projects in Nepal, especially near the border with India, has led to protests, Nepalese officials say.
Many Chinese consumer goods are on sale in Nepalese bazaars. 
Some, like small appliances and crockery, have displaced Indian products, although Nepalese officials say the trade gap with India continues to widen.
In addition, the fast-developing Nepalese tourist industry - a vital hard-currency earner - has in recent years ceased to be an appendage of Indian tourism. 
With direct air links to Europe, Southeast Asia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Burma and Hong Kong, Nepal is bypassing Indian travel agents, airports and airlines.
Personal relations between King Birendra and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi are reported to be frosty. 
The 43-year-old King, who inherited the throne from King Mahendra in 1972, saw India annex the neighboring kingdom of Sikkim in 1974, and later, in Nepal's view, reduce the King of Bhutan to an Indian vassal.
Â 
A Martial Tradition
Diplomats say that the royal family, which dominates a party-less Government, is sensitive to the fate of Sikkim and Bhutan and concerned about Katmandu's independence. 
Nepal is the oldest nation in South Asia, with its own architecture, language and distinctive forms of Hinduism and Buddhism.
''They are proud of their martial tradition,'' a diplomat said. 
''Beneath this placid, gentle exterior, there is a determination there.''
Indian officials, who acknowledge their annoyance with Katmandu's Chinese arms purchases, say they are also perplexed by what they see as a new and inexplicably uncompromising attitude in Nepal, which has benefited from nearly 40 years of Indian aid and special trade concessions and an open- door policy for millions of Nepalese job seekers.
Indians say Nepal, apart from resisting a combined trade and transit treaty, refuses to reverse decisions that New Delhi regards as violations of a 1950 treaty of friendship between the two capitals that has been the base of their relations ever since. 
These violations include the levying of tariffs on Indian goods and the introduction of work permits for Indian nationals in Nepal. 
Nepalese in India are not required to have them.
A new trade treaty, initialed by Nepal and India last November, was rejected by New Delhi when the Nepalese would not withdraw tariffs, an Indian official said.
Â 
Government Is Criticized
If the economic crisis in Nepal is prolonged, the King and his Government will have to rely on the willingness of the Nepalese to stand behind their decision to defy New Delhi, and to make adjustments to lives that are already borderline for many.
Most Nepalese interviewed said they were strongly opposed to the large Indian presence in Nepal and to any attempts by New Delhi to dictate this country's policies.
But they were also critical of the Government, which they said has failed to develop the country or allow people effective democratic rights. 
Nepalese are limited to voting in party- less elections for local councils. 
Open criticism of the monarchy and the Government is rarely tolerated.

file: POPULATION POLICY IN ASIA IS FAULTED.txt
text:
ï»¿
Serious flaws in family-planning programs in China and India make it unlikely that the world's two most populous nations will be able to stabilize growth until well into the next century, by which time they may have added more than 1.5 billion people to the world's population, according to findings published this week by the independent Population Crisis Committee.
The problem is especially acute in India, the research group says. 
India, with a population of about 882 million that is growing 2.1 percent a year, is likely to overtake China as the most populous country by 2035, the committee says; India's population may reach 2 billion before leveling off.
China, with about 1.165 billion people, is likely to stabilize at about 1.5 billion, the group says.
The world's population is estimated at 5.4 billion.
Â 
Burdens on the Environment
The continued growth in India and China contributes to an intensifying crisis in ecological and human resources in large areas of Asia, where land is being rapidly degraded by overuse, water supplies are under strain and agriculture must struggle to stay ahead of soil and water depletion.
Throughout Asia, there is no longer time to let economic development lead to smaller family size, as happened in industrial nations. 
Some Asian nations, led by South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia, have made significant reductions in population growth through effective family planning.
"For people who are concerned about problems like global warming, ozone-layer depletion or world poverty, we just have to be vitally interested in the success or failure of the Chinese and Indian programs," said Sharon L. Camp, senior vice president of the Population Crisis Committee.
Copies of the reports are available for $5 each, including postage, from the Population Crisis Committee, 1120 19th Street, Washington, D.C. 
20036.
Â 
India 'Most Critical'
The studies of China and India conclude that the success of China's much-publicized population-control efforts have been "exaggerated," and that most couples have not one, but two or three children.
The situation in India is more dire.
"From a demographic perspective, India may be the world's most critical country," the Population Crisis Committee says. 
Nearly half the illiterate people in the world live in India, where a third of the people suffer from malnutrition.
The studies -- "India's Family Planning Challenge: From Rhetoric to Action" and "China's Family Planning Program: Challenging the Myths" -- call for more international assistance to the two countries, and more receptivity in Beijing and New Delhi to outside advice and help.
Â 
U.S. Angry With China
Under the Reagan and Bush Administrations, however, Washington has denied family-planning aid to China because of coercive population-control programs, including forced abortions.
Under the influence of Republican conservatives, Washington also halted its contributions in 1985 to the United Nations Population Fund, citing its involvement in programs like China's. 
Washington supplied 20 percent of the fund's resources, and its withdrawal has hobbled the fund's work in both Asia and Africa.
The United States policy took shape in 1984, just before an international population conference in Mexico City, where Washington took a strong stand against abortion and population control in general. 
Abortions are used frequently in poor nations to regulate child-bearing.
Although Congress has been generous in appropriating money for programs in many other countries, and the United States Agency for International Development is a major contributor to family-planning programs worldwide, the policies on China and contributions to international organizations continue.
The reports on China and India, written by Ms. Camp and Shanti R. Conly, the committee's director of population policy analysis, fault both countries on the limited options available to women seeking contraception.
Â 
Flawed Technology
In India, sterilization (mostly of women) accounts for 70 percent of contraception. 
Because of the near finality of the method and the risks to health from unsterile operations, many women wait until they have had four or more children, Indian experts say.
In China, an outdated and often risky steel-ring intrauterine device is used by 60 million women, the study says. 
About 36 percent of women rely on tubal ligation.
The roots of the problems are different. 
In India the Government has pledged a renewed effort to slow population growth, but many earlier efforts have been undercut by cultural resistance and a lack of political will. 
Conversely, in China, the determination of the Government to cut growth drastically led to Draconian measures that also aroused opposition.
But the Population Crisis Committee study found similarities in the shortcomings of the two nations' programs.
"Local programs in China and India are typically characterized by poorly trained personnel who lack both the interpersonal skills and technical knowledge necessary to adequately counsel clients on the risks and benefits of contraceptive measures," the committee said.

file: Q&A.txt
text:
ï»¿
Jumping Chinese
Q. If all the people in China were to jump up and down all at once, would it affect the Earth's orbit?
A. The Earth's orbit would be unaffected, though a simultaneous hop by the 1,133,687,501 people reported to live in China on July 1, 1990, would release approximately as much energy as the magnitude-4 earthquake in Westchester County, N.Y., six years ago, according to calculations by the seismologists at the Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory of Columbia University.
Using just a round billion people weighing an average of 50 kilograms jumping one meter in the air, they came up with an energy release of 1018 ergs, or 1 followed by 18 zeros, said Nano Seeber, one of the seismologists. 
An erg is the force required to move one gram by one centimeter.
Even a jump by the whole population of the world, about five billion people, would not alter the Earth's orbit, Mr. Seeber said. 
The only things that would do so would be the loss of a large piece of the Earth or the impact of a large outside agent, he said. 
The hop's action and reaction would cancel each other.
Â 
Eliminating Alcohol
Q. How long after a person stops drinking does it take for all alcohol to be removed from the body?
A. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism of the National Institutes of Health estimates that alcohol is cleared at a rate of approximately 100 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per hour, or about half an ounce of pure alcohol every two hours, so that if a person ingested approximately three drinks in a half-hour period, it would take about six hours for that alcohol to leave the body.
Dr. T. K. Li, an alcoholism researcher at the Indiana University School of Medicine, emphasized that the speed could vary widely, as much as threefold, because of the range of individual variation in factors like body weight and blood alcohol levels.
Readers are invited to submit questions about science to Questions, Science Times, The New York Times, 229 West 43d Street, New York, N.Y.

file: Quiet Tibetan Influx_Devout, Exiled but Kept Out by U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Pema Tsering's escape from Tibet began 30 years ago with a nighttime trek through the Himalayan mountains and ended three weeks ago on an Alitalia jet to Kennedy International Airport. 
With hot buttered tea and steamed beef dumplings, New York's entire Tibetan community turned out to help him celebrate, fitting comfortably into a small East Side restaurant.
For the 500 Tibetans in the United States, Mr. Tsering's arrival was a very big deal, the beginning of a wave of Tibetan migration to the United States that will ultimately quadruple their minuscule but passionate exile community. 
It was made possible when Congress authorized 1,000 special visas for Tibetans.
Although Tibetans have been fleeing the Chinese occupation of their homeland for 40 years, the United States has never granted them refugee status. 
Like tens of thousands of other Tibetans in India and Nepal, Mr. Tsering, who is 42 years old, lived for decades in a refugee settlement, stuck in an odd sort of limbo with no country to call his own.
Tibetans register only a blip in the great human drama of international migration, but immigration experts say their story highlights just how political, and how arbitrary, the refugee policy of the United States really is.
Â 
Working With Dalai Lama
The resettlement of the 1,000 Tibetans, scheduled to arrive over the next 3 years, also represents an unusual effort, organized and financed not by a government but by a national network of volunteers -- a small subculture of Tibetans and friends of Tibet working with the Dalai Lama's exile administration in Dharamsala, India.
"I personally see the resettlement project as a fantastic gift from America to Tibetans, which has been very late in coming," said Losang Gyatso, president of the Tibet Association in New York. 
Mr. Gyatso is a senior vice president at Lintas New York, an advertising agency, where he works as a creative director on the Diet Coke account.
Early this month, gazing upward at "enchanting skyscrapers," Mr. Tsering stood on a Manhattan street corner in the Murray Hill neighborhood that could be called Little, or Tiny, Tibet. 
It was far from the jungly Tibetan village where he was born, far from the mountainous Nepalese terrain where he labored on road gangs as a boy and far from the refugee camp in India where, until last month, he worked at a Tibetan school.
As the ever-present sirens of New York wailed, he spoke with calm about his childhood vision of the United States, taking a metaphorical step beyond the typical immigrant's dream of streets paved with gold.
"When I was little, in my village, we believed that America had made a spiral staircase from the Earth reaching to the moon," Mr. Tsering said. 
"And each stair was extremely wide, planted with a wild field of crops. 
And beyond each stair there was another, waiting to be developed."
It was a plain, linoleum-covered staircase that Mr. Tsering climbed that first night to the new apartment in Murray Hill he was to share with Tashi Dorjee, the second of 18 Tibetans to arrive in cities across the country last month. 
The apartment is still largely unadorned, but Mr. Tsering and Mr. Dorjee have constructed a colorful altar to the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetans call His Holiness, on a mud-brown bureau from the Salvation Army.
New York City's Little Tibet, where the new immigrants live, is so petite as to be mostly invisible to others in that part of Manhattan -- the 30's between First and Third Avenues. 
Besides the apartments of individual Tibetans, it consists of two restaurants and a brownstone, which houses the Office of Tibet, Tibet House and a bookstore. 
A sign on the brownstone door typifies the mellow Tibetan style: "While opening the doors, please be gentle with the door handles."
The 120 New York-area Tibetans, the biggest Tibetan community in the United States, are scattered from Murray Hill through Long Island, New Jersey and Connecticut. 
They get together several times a year, particularly for Tibetan National Day on March 10, when they demonstrate for Tibetan independence at the United Nations, and for the Dalai Lama's birthday on July 6, when they retreat to the mountains for an extended picnic, draping their leader's portrait with multicolored scarves.
Â 
Immigrants and Advocates
Unlike other immigrants they are not linked by churchgoing; their practice of Tibetan Buddhism tends to be a very private affair. 
But they are fiercely cohesive in their politics, and they see the new arrivals, first and foremost, as colleagues in advocacy for a free Tibet. 
That is also how the new immigrants see themselves. 
"Our mission here is not to get rich -- well, who doesn't want to get rich?
-- but to speak up and enlighten the American people about the Tibetan situation," Mr. Tsering said.
The Tibetans have been displaced for decades by Chinese rule, which, they say, has resulted in a million dead, 120,000 in settlement camps, and a population in Tibet itself outnumbered by the Chinese, 6 million to 7.5 million. 
But the United States, unlike India, Nepal, Canada and Switzerland, does not allow Tibetans into this country as refugees.
Technically, this is because they are coming through another country -- Nepal or India -- willing to grant them residency. 
Politically, it is because the United States Government has been unwilling to offend the Chinese by acknowledging that Tibetans could have a "well-founded fear of persecution," as refugees must under Federal law. 
China claims historical sovereignty over Tibet predating its military occupation of that country in 1950 and the Tibetan uprising, bloody and failed, in 1959.
Mr. Tsering's group of Tibetans is being allowed into the country not as refugees but as "qualified displaced Tibetans" under a special provision, sponsored by United States Representative Barney Frank, Democrat of Massachusetts, in the 1990 Immigration Act.
Â 
Fans, Gurus and Mormons
"It didn't make any difference to us what they were called, as long as they were provided haven," Mr. Frank said in a recent interview. 
He described their special status as "semantic" politics by the State Department intended to keep China happy.
The Tibetan U.S. 
Resettlement Project, based in New York City, is working to establish 19 "clusters" of Tibetans across the country, in cities including Minneapolis, San Francisco, Salt Lake City, Ithaca, N.Y., Portland, Ore., and Amherst, Mass. 
The project brings together an unusual assortment of volunteers, from Tibetan political enthusiasts to New Age gurus to Mormons.
Some volunteers spoke of the project with political fervor, like the national project coordinator, Tenzin Taklaj, a 26-year-old Tibetan-American in New York. 
"It is up to us here in exile to preserve our culture because it's being destroyed in Tibet right now," he said. 
"The more we are, the stronger we will be."
And others sounded idealistic on a more cosmic level, like a volunteer, Jed Miller in Amherst, Mass., a chiropractor who said he uses Buddhist meditation to reduce his patients' stress. 
He referred to the value of the new immigrants' "highly developed inner technology."
The volunteer network was constructed over the last few years, as the organizers of the project persuaded members of Congress to support their effort. 
Since two earlier intiatives had failed to earn the Tibetans refugee status, the organizers -- Tenzin Tethong, now a minister in the exile Government of the Dalai Lama, and Edward J. Bednar, an American friend of Tibet since discovering the Tibetan Book of the Dead after "a near-death experience" -- decided to go another route. 
They promised to bring Tibetans in at no cost to the U.S. government, which spent about $7,000 a person to resettle Indochinese refugees.
Congress agreed to grant the Tibetans something every immigrant wants: an instant "green card," allowing permanent residence in the United States, and full work authorization. 
The 500 Tibetans already living in this country arrived separately, on student visas or after marrying an American. 
The new immigrants, when joined by their families, will quadruple, at least, the Tibetan-American population.
"The Tibetans' situation has always been a clear illustration of the connection between immigration and foreign policy," said David Reimers, a New York University history professor and immigration expert. 
"But it also shows how immigration policy is made up of a whole series of weird things. 
Someone gets the ear of someone in Congress and these flukes happen, like instant legalization for 100 Burmese students, or, in this case, 1,000 Tibetans."
The State Department authorized the Tibetan Central Administration of the Dalai Lama to choose the immigrants from 47 refugee settlements in India and Nepal. 
Half will be poor refugees, including those who recently left Tibet; the other half will be more educated and considered likely to succeed in the United States.
Â 
'Big Smiles, Open Faces'
Across the country, the Tibetans are sponsored by families with whom they live. 
Volunteers find them jobs before they even arrive in the United States. 
The Minneapolis coordinator, Tara Dadak, an American whose husband is a former Tibetan Buddhist monk, said, "Tibetans come at you with big smiles, open faces and an ultra-American work ethic very pleasing to employers."
After they adapt to life in America, which other Tibetans say won't take long, the new arrivals will face something familiar to all Tibetan-Americans: They will be considered exotics.
"A lot of people project onto Tibetans their own fantasies about Tibet," said Mr. Gyatso. "Older Americans, in particular, who have known Tibet through National Geographic and 'Lost Horizon,' see Tibet as a very special place, like a crack in space or something. 
Which is terrific, in a way. 
But the negative side is that they don't want to confront the reality that the paradise has been shattered. 
They'd rather remember the Shangri-La."

file: REFORM MOVEMENT GROWS IN MONGOLIA.txt
text:
ï»¿
The revolutionary changes in Eastern Europe appear to have swept eastward into Asia, with the Communist leadership in the remote nation of Mongolia preparing for a meeting on Monday that may lead to the ouster of its Politburo.
Wedged between the Soviet Union and China, Mongolia has only two million inhabitants, about half of them herdsmen who roam the nation's vast grasslands. 
It has long been under Soviet domination, but in the last three months an increasingly vocal democracy movement has pressed for more independence from Moscow and for the replacement of many top officials.
Responding to ever larger demonstrations and to hunger strikes by dissidents in the central square of the capital, Ulan Bator, President Zhambyn Batmonh announced on television Friday night that the Communist Party Central Committee would meet on Monday and consider the replacement of the entire Politburo.
Mr. Batmonh indicated that the Central Committee would move up the date of a party congress, which would elect a new leadership and institute policy changes. 
The President also said that leaders might call at the meeting on Monday for a national referendum to measure public confidence in the People's Great Hural, a rubber-stamp legislature.
Â 
Prospects for Change Unclear
A diplomat in Ulan Bator, reached by telephone from Beijing, said it was unclear whether changes in the Politburo would come as early as Monday or be delayed until the party congress. 
Nor is it clear whether the entire Politburo will be replaced or if some members, like President Batmonh, will remain on the new committee.
The diplomat said that Ulan Bator was quiet today, and that the hunger strike had ended Friday night after Mr. Batmonh's speech. 
A general strike proclaimed by the democracy movement also appeared to have been called off, the envoy said.
The democracy movement in Mongolia may have influence beyond its borders, in the Chinese region known as Inner Mongolia. 
The three million ethnic Mongolians living on the Chinese side of the border are said to be aware of the protests in Mongolia, and the authorities in Beijing appear to be nervous that unrest might spread. 
Prime Minister Li Peng already has called for vigilance against separatists among China's ethnic minorities.
A front-page article last month in China's official People's Daily praised officials in Inner Mongolia for spreading socialist ideology, and Beijing announced in January that it would boost investment in Inner Mongolia to create an industrial base.
Â 
Movement Born in December
Mongolia's democracy movement began in December with a few demonstrations of only a few thousand protesters, but it has gained momentum with its demands for greater political change, more prosperity and more assertions of Mongolian nationalism. 
The leadership has reacted with some criticism but primarily with accommodation, even giving live television coverage to a convention last month that brought the birth of Mongolia's first opposition party.
Prime Minister Dumaagiyn Sodnom said last month that he did not rule out the possibility of a multiparty system in Mongolia. 
But it is not clear to what extent the leadership as a whole is willing to give up power. 
Tserendashiyn Namsray, a Politburo member, was quoted on Radio Ulan Bator last month as saying there were differences of opinion within the Politburo on these subjects.
The second-oldest Communist regime in the world, behind the Soviet Union, Mongolia is unlikely to duplicate the changes in Eastern Europe, according to diplomats in Ulan Bator. 
They say that the bitterness in Mongolia is not as deep as it was in Romania or Poland. 
And while Mongolians are resentful of Soviet domination, the diplomats say, they also are wary that they might be vulnerable to pressure from China if they entirely leave Moscow's orbit.

file: Salaxi Journal_For Chinese, an Ancient Scourge Loses Its Terror.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Du Dayi found out that he had leprosy, the short, soft-spoken peasant was as worried about his neighbors as about the disease. 
In those days, more than four decades ago, Chinese villagers sometimes burned leprosy patients alive in an attempt to destroy a disease that they loathed like none other.
"People were afraid of us then and looked down at us," said Mr. Du, who has lost an eye as well as his nose to the disease, the latter affliction apparently distorting his speech. 
"But now it's no problem, and I can go around easily. 
I can even go to the bank!"
A hundred-odd villagers clustered around Mr. Du as he spoke and seemed a testimony to a monumental change in attitudes toward leprosy. 
The peasants in this remote village in south-central China were unconcerned about touching him and were staring wonderingly not at his severely disfigured face but at something they found even more astonishing: the face of an American interviewer.
Leprosy, which for thousands of years has been a scourge mainly of regions with warm climates, still afflicts some 4 million to 10 million people around the world, and hundreds of thousands of new cases are reported each year. 
But the number of victims around the world appears to have declined by more than half over the last decade, and in China and many other countries the progress has been enormous -- in fighting the disease and the fear that surrounds it.
"The struggle is being won; there's no doubt about that," said James A. Gittings, an officer of American Leprosy Missions, which fights leprosy in China and other countries. 
A multidrug treatment regime that became widely used in the 1980's has played a key role in the decline of leprosy, and doctors hope to conquer the disease by the year 2000 so that it is only a relatively minor problem in the third world.
Â 
An Energetic Campaign
In poor parts of China like this one, political issues like freedom of expression seem to many peasants remote and hazy compared with concerns of health and poverty, for villagers are far more likely to have seen a leprosy patient than to have seen a dissident. 
Responding to such concerns, the Chinese Government is campaigning energetically against leprosy and appears to be enjoying great success, for this is the kind of activity that the Communist Government does best.
If it sometimes outrages the West by mobilizing people against dissidents, it is also impressive in its ability to mobilize people against disease and other common threats. 
The authorities force doctors to work in remote areas, and while this may offend Western ideals of freedom it is nonetheless helpful in fighting a disease like leprosy.
"What they've managed to achieve is to reduce leprosy to a level where it's not really a public health problem any more, not a major contagious disease," said Dr. B. P. Kean, the representative in China of the World Health Organization. 
"They've done extremely well, especially in recent years."
China claims to have only 30,000 reported cases of patients now undergoing treatment, down from about 100,000 a decade ago. 
Four decades ago, it says, there were 500,000, although all the figures in China and elsewhere are uncertain and not particularly reliable. 
There are often variations in methods of counting and in estimating the number of people who carry the disease but whose condition has not yet been diagnosed.
The rural-based attack on leprosy is evident here among the rock-littered hills of Guizhou Province, one of the poorest in the country. 
Doctors hike from village to village, explaining the symptoms of leprosy and looking for patients. 
Most victims are now caught in the early stages and are treated, free of charge, before they are disfigured.
"The biggest problem we face is that leprosy victims don't go to the doctor soon enough," said Liu Fangmin, the deputy director of the Salaxi Leprosy Hospital here. 
"We tell them that the faster they come to us, the easier it is to cure. 
But the biggest headache is still finding the leprosy patients."
To overcome this problem, the medical authorities have begun to provide cash incentives, and consequently the easiest way to make a bundle of money in this poor area is simply to turn in a person with leprosy. 
The local government will pay the equivalent of $20 to anybody who reports such a person. 
Sufferers can even turn themselves in and claim the money, or doctors can turn in their patients.
The reward amounts to half a year's income for many peasants, and those who supply names are guaranteed secrecy -- because some villagers might resent it if they discover that a neighbor has fingered them.
Leprosy is an infectious disease that causes changes in skin color and deadens the sensation in various parts of the body. 
Because they do not feel pain, patients often injure themselves and as a consequence in later stages sometimes lose their fingers.
Despite an ancient misconception, leprosy is not easily spread and most healthy people seem to have a natural resistance to it. 
In any case, these days drugs can cure the disease in a period ranging from a few months to many years.
"When they are first diagnosed, the patients are afraid and feel they've been robbed of their dignity," said Wang Yongjuan, the health director for Bijie Prefecture, a poor region that encompasses Salaxi village. 
"But we tell them that they can be cured quietly, that we won't tell anyone about it. 
And they get their self-confidence back."

file: Shanghai Journal_China Slipping Into a More Comfortable Sex Life.txt
text:
ï»¿
The largest population in the world is proof that it must go on, but sex in China is still laced in secrecy more than sensuousness.
Only recently have social scientists shed light on what happens in the Chinese bedroom -- or, given the acute housing shortage, the living rooms, kitchens, closets and fields to which couples must sometimes resort.
The new research suggests that many young Chinese are enjoying their own sexual revolution. 
That tends to be confirmed by the incidence of venereal disease, which by some official accounts is rising by about 70 percent a year.
A mammoth new survey, already described as the Chinese "Kinsey Report," has led the way in charting the changing mores of the post-Mao period. 
The study, which is expected to be published as a book at the end of this year, profiles a society that remains fundamentally prudish, yet one that is becoming more free-wheeling at the youthful and intellectual fringes.
Â 
Interviews With 23,000 People
To be sure, "free-wheeling" in a Chinese context may mean little more than removing one's clothes. 
The new survey, which was based on interviews with 23,000 people of all ages and backgrounds, in 15 provinces, found that 60 percent of those surveyed "often or sometimes" were naked during sex. 
The researchers thought that was surprisingly high.
"This is quite different from how it used to be, suggesting that with the reform and opening policies, people are more liberal about sex," Liu Dalin, a Shanghai sociologist who is the architect of the survey, wrote in a recent unpublished essay.
Foreplay is often rudimentary or nonexistent, the survey found, perhaps because many couples keep as much clothing on as possible. 
Among peasants, 34 percent engaged in less than one minute of foreplay.
Â 
'How to Conceive a Son'
"Older people don't understand the idea of foreplay," Professor Liu, one of China's best-known researchers into the erotic, said in an interview.
Mr. Liu has written some 41 books, including many recent best sellers about sexuality. 
But Chinese publications are very tame by Western standards, and the priority of many peasants seems to be less along the lines of "The Joy of Sex" than something like "How to Conceive a Son."
Partly because of the hasty and purposeful manner with which sex is apparently conducted, more than a third of women reported pain during intercourse. 
The survey did not ask about female orgasm, for fear that many respondents would not understand the concept, but only a third of urban women and a quarter of rural women said they "very often" felt pleasure during intercourse.
"We don't know how to estimate, but we think that female orgasm is very rare," Mr. Liu said. 
"One reason is that traditionally women are very modest and suffer from closed minds and pressure not to feel too much pleasure. 
Another reason is that husbands engage in little foreplay and lack the knowledge and skills to elicit orgasms in their wives."
Shanghai and some other cities now offer "School for Newlyweds": a special class in which new couples are given a basic introduction into sexuality and contraception. 
Giving satisfaction to the woman is among the topics now addressed.
While Mr. Liu's survey is one of the largest conducted anywhere in the world about sexual behavior, he acknowledges that there are flaws in it.
Perhaps the most important is that the sampling often has not been very scientific, and that rural respondents accounted for only one-quarter of the total -- even though they make up about three-quarters of the population. 
In addition, those rural areas chosen for the surveys were somewhat more prosperous and educated than the Chinese countryside as a whole. 
As a result, China as a whole may be even less sensuous in its sex life than the report would suggest.
China has no Judeo-Christian tradition associating illicit sex with sin, and rather seems to regard sex less as a matter of morality than as an issue of propriety and decency. 
In ancient times, China was much more open about sex, and one of the great works of ancient literature, "The Golden Lotus," brims with explicit descriptions of the under-the-covers activities in a wealthy household. 
China recently published the first unexpurgated version of "The Golden Lotus" since the Communist revolution, but only scholars may buy it.
Â 
The Times Are Changing
"We never used to talk about sex, but there has been a dramatic change," said Hu Jinhua, the editor of Shanghai Public Health News, a daily newspaper. 
"In the 1980's sex education was even introduced in the schools, with Shanghai in the lead. 
The change has been very rapid."
The shift in attitudes is most pronounced among young Chinese, especially university students. 
More than 78 percent of the students questioned in Professor Liu's survey approved of premarital sex, and 90 percent of the students said China's sex education policies are too conservative.
Fewer than 11 percent of the students said they had any sexual experience, but this may reflect opportunities more than appetites. 
University students are often housed six or eight to a room, so arranging a rendezvous is difficult, and in any case students risk expulsion if they are caught sleeping together.
"We've been pretty much Westernized," said a woman who graduated recently from one of Shanghai's best universities. 
"Sex was regarded as no big deal, and while the school authorities discouraged us from falling in love, most of us had boyfriends."

A series of earthquakes rattled northern China late Wednesday and early today, killing at least 18 people and flattening about 8,000 houses in a largely rural area, the authorities said.
Officials of the State Seismological Bureau said the quakes were not related to the tremor in Northern California on Tuesday.
The bureau said that five tremors, registering up to 6.0 on the Richter scale, shook an area along the Shanxi-Hebei provincial border and that at least 28 people had been injured.
