file: The Mystique of Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
TIBET is manifest proof of the smallness of human beings. 
The Himalayan landscapes are so vast, so bereft of any inhabitants except the odd nomad, that here it is the land that has shaped the people instead of the other way around. 
When Tibetans die, they do not build tombs; they leave the corpse for the vultures to devour. 
Occasionally the Government makes an effort to tame the plateau, to show who is boss, by carving a road through the emptiness, but nature gets its revenge by bogging down vehicles in snow or mud.
It is from the roof of the Potala Palace, where the Dalai Lama as a boy rigged a telescope to study ordinary people as they strolled among the yaks on the streets below, that Tibet is at its most magnificent. 
As Tibetan pilgrims shuffle by, turning prayer wheels and mumbling chants before disappearing into little chapels to light yak-butter candles, the mysticism and beauty of the land are simply overpowering.
Tibet inspired the notion of Shangri-La, and it retains a remoteness and exotic quality now rare elsewhere in the world. 
The Tibetan pilgrims who prostrate themselves in the dust have nothing but their faith, but they count themselves as very rich indeed -- for they have been able to make the holy journey to Lhasa. 
The pilgrims clutch prayer wheels as they walk clockwise around the Jokhang Temple, according to ritual.
In recent years, to be sure, Tibet has been an unhappy sort of Shangri-La. 
It had links over the centuries with the Chinese empire, and in 1950 the newly installed Communist Chinese Government used those relations to justify sending its army to "liberate" Tibet, which it claimed was part of China. 
These days there is a Tibetan Government in exile, but the United States and other Western governments recognize Chinese sovereignty over Tibet -- while urging Beijing to halt the torture and repression there.
In the mid-1980's there seemed to be some hope for a compromise between the exiled Dalai Lama and the Beijing authorities, but then pro-independence demonstrations erupted in September 1987 and were bloodily suppressed. 
Tensions rose, and the unrest culminated in clashes in March 1989 that left at least a dozen dead and led to the expulsion of all tourists and the imposition of martial law. 
China lifted martial law in May 1990, and since then the region has been largely quiet. 
As a result, the Chinese Government is again encouraging Western tourists -- so long as they come in organized groups and do not encourage Tibetan separatists.
The groups are escorted to a limited number of places where tourists are welcome. 
Last year, 10,375 foreigners visited Tibet, including 1,441 from the United States. 
Tibetan tourism officials say they expect 13,000 visitors this year, including about 1,400 from the United States. 
In general, there seems little risk for Westerners, partly because most Tibetans regard them as allies.
Tibet can be reached from Nepal -- there are two flights a week -- but most tourists arrive on the daily China Southwest Airlines flights from Chengdu, China. 
In my case I went as a journalist rather than as a tourist, but my itinerary was similar to what a tourist might see. 
I spent a week there, and it seems foolish to stay less than that.
Lhasa is 11,830 feet high, and most visitors feel some shortness of breath at first. 
In Andean cities like Cuzco, Peru, foreigners often deal with similar altitudes by drinking coca tea, which contains a raw ingredient that goes into cocaine. 
In Tibet, there is no such exotic remedy, but the Lhasa Holiday Inn -- by far the best hotel in Lhasa, and the place where most foreigners stay -- does offer an oxygen hose in each room to assist those with breathing difficulties. 
Occasionally a new arrival has to fly out by the first available plane to a lower altitude.
Tibet is not a place of luxury, but the hotels and food are adequate. 
Most hotel restaurants serve principally Chinese and Western food, with a certain Tibetan influence: yak burgers, for example, at the Holiday Inn. 
Guides vary enormously, from local Tibetans who are one with the land to Chinese who have only lived in Tibet for a short period.
The pride of Lhasa is the Potala Palace, the former home of the Dalai Lama. 
Since Tibet's spiritual leader fled into exile in 1959, the palace has been turned into a museum and it is one of the most spectacular sights in Asia. 
I find it far more impressive than the Chinese Imperial Palace in the Forbidden City in Beijing. 
While the Forbidden City is sterile, the Potala oozes faith. 
It is the Tibetan version of Versailles: 13 stories tall, 1,300 feet by 1,150 feet, with 16-foot walls protecting a warren of more than 1,000 rooms. 
The Government regards the Potala as a museum, but many Tibetans still regard it as one of the holiest spots in the world. 
They come not so much out of curiosity as out of reverence, which is seen in their eyes as they shuffle from room to room, lighting candles and praying before the jewel-studded tombs of past incarnations of the Dalai Lama.
They wind up narrow stairs, little more than ladders, and emerge on an open roof with views of all of Lhasa.
The rooms in the Potala have names like Chapel of Immortal Happiness and Chapel of the Stages on the Path to Enlightenment. 
The contents are as vivid as the names: altars and carvings are everywhere, all weighed down with gorgeous pieces of cloth of every conceivable color. 
White scarves, left by pilgrims to show their respect, adorn many of the altars. 
The entire Potala is a celebration of color, and clothes and books and carvings and tombs seem to be crammed wherever there is space.
THE Potala was built mostly during the rule of the fifth Dalai Lama, and the regent concealed news of his death in 1682 for a decade because of fear that the mourning would halt construction of the palace. 
Only when it was virtually completed did the regent announce the Dalai Lama's death and launch the search for his reincarnation. 
By the time the successor was found he was already a teen-ager, and he proved to have a strong and rather ungodly interest in the opposite sex. 
The sixth Dalai Lama disappeared in 1706, but he is still fondly remembered for his poetry and sometimes roguish behavior.
Most visitors to Lhasa also tour the Jokhang Temple and the surrounding Barkor Market. 
This area is the political and religious focal point of Tibet, the gathering point of pilgrims who come from hundreds or even thousands of miles -- these days usually by bus, instead of by crawling and prostrating. 
It is also the site of most pro-independence demonstrations in the last few years, but if there is a prospect of a protest then your guides are almost certain to keep you away.
The entrance to the Jokhang is crowded with pilgrims, prostrating themselves, and with vendors who peddle prayer wheels, bugles and other souvenirs. 
The atmosphere is half carnival, half mystical. 
Inside, the oldest part of the temple supposedly dates from the seventh century and houses an ancient Buddha that was carried to Lhasa 1,300 years ago from the Chinese capital of that epoch, Changan, now called Xian. 
This holy of holies is in a cramped, dark room that magnifies the spiritual intensity: pilgrims are shoulder to shoulder, murmuring prayers as they edge their way around the statue.
The Chinese are sometimes reluctant to arrange visits to the monasteries that surround Lhasa, because the monasteries function as an alternative university system and as centers of opposition to the Government. 
If a visit is permitted, it is well worth the trip. 
These used to be the largest monasteries in the world -- Drepung Monastery near Lhasa once had nearly 10,000 monks -- and they are still influential in Tibetan society.
In addition to Drepung, alternatives are Sera Monastery, on the outskirts of Lhasa, and Ganden Monastery, 45 miles by rough road from the city. 
Ganden is one of the most poignant sights in the area: the monastery was devastated in the Maoist period, and most of it today is only rubble. 
It is as if Notre Dame had been bombed. 
The destruction helps explain the bitterness that many Tibetans feel for the Chinese authorities.
In the evening it is well worth taking a bicycle-rickshaw to the area around the Jokhang Temple and perhaps popping into one of the small bars. 
Studying English is the rage in Lhasa, and it is likely that someone will approach to start a conversation. 
I remember a doctor who spoke to me for more than an hour about the political situation. 
He was torn in his emotions: he wanted to get his anger at the Chinese off his chest, but he was also terrified of being arrested for his candor. 
Speaking in Chinese, he repeatedly said he risked being beaten and imprisoned for years for talking to a foreign journalist.
Tourists are allowed to travel to certain other parts of Tibet, and I relished a three-day circuit that encompassed the towns of Shigatse and Gyantse. 
The trip begins with a six- or seven-hour ride along a newly constructed highway that still has a few rough edges: a truck became stuck in a patch of mud, blocking traffic in both directions.
Shigatse was the traditional seat of the Panchen Lama, who ranks second in the religious hierarchy to the Dalai Lama. 
The 10th Panchen Lama died in 1989, and visitors to Tashilhunpo Monastery in Shigatse stroll around the glass case in which his embalmed body is seated. 
A dozen or so monks constantly pray for a rapid incarnation of the Panchen Lama in the form of an infant.
The monastery is built against a hill, and the tombs of past Panchen Lamas are on display, as is the site where the tomb of the 10th is now being prepared. 
The monks consult oracles and study divine lakes for hints about where to find the infant 11th Panchen Lama. 
A few candidates will presumably be selected within the next year or two, and in theory the child who recognizes the personal belongings of the last Panchen Lama will be pronounced the new one. 
There is considerable room for manipulation of the process, and many Tibetans fear that the Chinese authorities will try to select a boy whom they can control and turn into a spokesman for the regime.
AS I wandered through the lanes and corridors of Tashilhunpo, admiring the sculptures and altars, I chatted with Barsan, who came to the monastery in 1947, when he was 7 years old. 
Then there were perhaps 3,000 monks at the monastery, now there are 800, and Barsan says there will never again be as many as there used to be. 
In the Cultural Revolution, he was forced to work for five years as a construction worker and farm laborer, but today he hides what bitterness he may feel.
From Shigatse it is less than two hours by car to Gyantse, a small town whose claim to fame is the Kumbum, part of the Palkhor Monastery on the edge of town. 
The Kumbum, built in 1427, is the largest stupa, a kind of Buddhist tower, in Tibet: built with a dome, it soars heavenward and dominates the arid landscape for miles around. 
A few monks will show you around the dim interior, illuminated by yak- butter candles and crammed with ancient manuscripts.
In the evenings, after the official tourist itinerary is completed, it may be possible to take a four-wheel vehicle and drive independently to a nearby village. 
Traveling without any Chinese official, I found that villagers were extremely friendly and happy to show me around their crude homes.
One of the best reasons to visit Gyantse is simply to enjoy the road connecting it to Lhasa. 
Yes, the dirt road is miserable after rain -- on my trip, many trucks were stuck in the mud, and my four-wheel-drive vehicle frequently had to drive across open fields rather than the road itself -- but the scenery is spectacular. 
The terrain is the classic image of Tibet: a vast emptiness full of mountains and glaciers and occasional herds of yaks. 
The emptiness is broken only by a telephone wire that goes along the road. 
Because of the absence of trees, the telephone poles are not made of wood but of mud bricks.
Â 
SIGNPOSTS FOR A VISIT TO LHASA
Â 
The Border
While the police sometimes tolerate individual tourists who sneak into Tibet by overland routes, the only legal way to enter is as part of an organized tour -- even if it is a tour of one. 
The difference between an illegal individual tourist and an authorized tour group with one person is that the latter has a schedule and an escort and pays hefty fees.
A tour agent will arrange for the Chinese visa and the permission slip to travel to Tibet, both of which are essential. 
Backpackers who cross the border without permission, mostly by bus from Sichuan or Qinghai Provinces, often stay at the budget Yak Hotel in the center of Lhasa. 
On occasion the police have taken to seizing some of these unauthorized visitors, and detaining them rather roughly at the airport until the next flight. 
Budget travelers have made daring midnight escapes from the airport, even swimming a river to avoid soldiers.
The Chinese Government is very concerned about tourist involvement in the independence movement, and so it is illegal for foreigners to give out photos of the Dalai Lama; everywhere you go children will ask for his photo. 
Tibet is generally very safe, but tourists of Asian ancestry, who might be mistaken for local Chinese, should be somewhat cautious about roaming the Tibetan quarter at night. 
A Japanese friend had pebbles tossed in his direction at a monastery; some monks believed he was Chinese.
Â 
Tours
A number of travel agents can arrange the tours, as can Holiday Inn, which manages the best hotel in Tibet. 
Information is available from the Holiday Inn sales office, (800) 331-3831, or from Holiday Inn Lhasa, No. 1 Minzu Lu, Lhasa, Tibet, China (telephone 222-21; telex 68010 HILSA CN). 
The Government tightly regulates tour costs and keeps them high. 
The Holiday Inn's weeklong tour of the Lhasa area, excluding the air fare to Lhasa, costs $1,475 for a single traveler, or $860 each for a couple, meals included. 
Discounts grow as the size of the group grows, with 10 people paying just $590 each.
Some cheaper package tours stay at the nearby Tibet Hotel. 
The Tibetan decor in the rooms is charming, but guests say that service leaves much to be desired. 
There is one tourist hotel each in Shigatse and Gyantse; neither meets international standards.
Â 
Weather
Most tourists visit in the warmer months from April to October. 
In winter, there is some snow and the days are shorter, but Lhasa becomes a more interesting city as the nomads leave the hills and roam the streets of the capital. 
In December, the coldest month, the temperature averages 32 degrees. 
Because the weather is changeable, travelers should take clothing that can be worn in layers -- such as sweaters. 
Sunscreens are also useful, because of the altitude. 
You should not count on being able to buy anything at all other than food in Lhasa, so take film.
Â 
Reading
Partly because of the limitations of the guides, it makes sense to buy a guidebook or two for the journey. 
Perhaps the best is Stephen Batchelor's comprehensive and beautifully illustrated "Tibet Guide" (Wisdom Publications, London); other useful ones include the Lonely Planet guide, "Tibet: A Travel Survival Kit," and Passport Books' "Tibet: A Complete Guide."
The Dalai Lama's autobiography, "Freedom in Exile," is fascinating, although for a more objective version of political events I would strongly recommend an essay by Melvyn C. Goldstein on Tibet in "China Briefing 1990," published by the Asia Society and Westview Press. 
-- N. D. K.

file: The World_Affirmative Action, Chinese Style, Makes Some Progress.txt
text:
ï»¿
SOME years ago, when three Red Guards tried to carry the Cultural Revolution to a village inhabited by the Yao ethnic minority, the Yao peasants dealt with the annoyance in a traditional way: they bound the Red Guards and prepared to slaughter them as a human sacrifice. 
Yao elders eventually managed the release of the young revolutionaries, but the incident left a lasting impression of the delicacy of relations with China's ethnic minorities.
While China is often regarded abroad as a homogeneous nation, some 8 percent of the population is made up of members of 55 minorities. 
Tibetans are the best-known minority -- and an often-cited example of acrimony and repressiveness in the Government's handling of relations with minority groups. 
But the Xishuangbanna District of southwest China is perhaps more representative, and certainly more successful, in the way it has managed ethnic minorities.
The villages around the local capital of Jing hong are full of members of various ethnic groups, wearing distinctive bright clothing and speaking their own languages. 
Fights sometimes erupt when one village believes another is trying to steal its land or its women, but none of the groups is known to have formed a political underground or to have called for independence.
In general, relations with the 25 significant ethnic minorities here in Yunnan Province in Southwestern China appear to be relatively trusting.
"There are a lot of minority problems here, but they're not political as in Tibet," Shen Qirong, a spokesman for the Nationality Affairs Commission Yunnan Province, said in an interview in the provincial capital of Kunming. 
"There've been no calls for independence or separatism, and the problems that arise are in isolated areas, and then they pass. 
They're not systemic."
In Tibet and the far western region of Xinjiang, ethnic tensions have led to clashes with the authorities and to independence movements. 
But many diplomats say that in general, China has managed its other ethnic minorities in an enlightened manner, granting them special privileges to co-opt them into the system. 
Two years ago, at about the same time that students demanding democracy were shot, Chinese Moslems demonstrated to protest a book that they said defamed them. 
The authorities responded not by crushing the demonstrations but by arresting the author and banning the book. 
To be sure, the Moslems were demanding not democracy but suppression of another viewpoint, but the fact that the Chinese listened to the protest at all is an indication of how seriously the ethnic groups are treated.
Outside of Tibet and Xinjiang, where some diplomats expect the separatist movements eventually to triumph, China's policy toward minorities has been quite effective. 
The largest ethnic minority, for example, are the Zhuang, with a population of 15.5 million concentrated in south-central China, but the Zhuang have been partly assimilated and do not cause problems for the Government. 
The 4.8 million Mongols have also been politically quiet, despite concerns that upheavals in the neighboring country of Mongolia would trigger unrest among them.
"China is much more conscious of minorities as groups than most developing countries," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"They have an amazingly well defined minority policy and program. 
You can criticize it, because they don't have real power or because it's often window-dressing. 
But there are efforts to bring minorities into high-profile positions, which has its own value because then they begin to serve as role models."
In Yunnan, one reason for the relative contentment seems to be the preferential treatment given to members of minority groups. 
Typically, ethnic minorities are allowed to marry earlier than members of the Han ethnic majority, and, most important, to have more children. 
Their children can also get into universities with lower examination scores than are required of Han students, and model members of minorities are chosen to fill prominent Government posts. 
The Governor of Yunnan Province, for example, is a member of the Naxi minority.
Because of the affirmative action policy, some families that in the past had tried to assimilate into the Han majority are now applying for declarations that they are members of a minority, and not Han, so that their children will have a better chance of getting into the universities.
In Jinghong, a young man who was registered as Han, and was thus allowed to have only one child, was disappointed when the child was a daughter. 
He checked his geneology, found some Dai minority ancestors, and re-registered himself as a Dai so that he could try to have a son.
Some Han complain that the preferences are unfair, but there is little noticeable resentment against affirmative action policies in China.
A main source of tension in Xishuangbanna in recent years has been the establishment of state-owned rubber plantations in minority areas. 
Nearby villages complain that the plantations take their land, and village children get in fights with the children of the Han Chinese plantation workers. 
The fights escalate, and the police sometimes are beaten when they try to intervene.
"Those tensions have declined dramatically," said Tian Jiaxiang, who is a Dai and deputy governor of Xishuangbanna. 
He said, and some local villagers agreed, that the disputes had been reduced by readjusting land and giving villagers a share of the income from the plantations.
Some members of ethnic minorities grumble that the fundamental problem is that many Han are arrogant and look down on other people. 
The authorities acknowledge that this is a problem, but they also note that there is growing intermarriage between Han and the minorities and suggest that this shows an increasing mutual respect.

file: The World_How Tiananmen Square Helped Rally Support for Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN an odd way, the only people who have done about as much as the Dalai Lama in the last few years to galvanize support for Tibetans are Deng Xiaoping and the other octogenarians who rule China.
Not intentionally, of course. 
But the leadership's crackdown on demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June 4, 1989, and the repressive measures taken since then, while raising the issue of human rights in China generally, have also given a thrust to concern over abuses in Tibet. 
And it has helped to land Tibet, a sparsely populated plateau region north of the Himalayas, firmly on the international agenda.
"Tibet has come out of nowhere," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"There were always a small number of people interested in Tibet. 
But before June 4, they were drowned out by the rest of the people with their love affair for China."
The authorities in Beijing insist that Tibet has been a part of China for many centuries, but Tibetans dispute this and point out that the region was left alone by the Chinese early this century. 
That changed in 1950, when the new Communist Government invaded Tibet, and even more so after the Chinese crushed an abortive rebellion in 1959 and imposed much tighter control.
The United States and other Western governments regard Tibet as a part of China. 
But these days, animosity in the West for the hard-line regime in Beijing has translated into mounting support for the Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled leader and foremost advocate. 
Some believe that irritation at China was a factor in the awarding of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize to the Dalai Lama.
The Dalai Lama's status was further bolstered by his meeting with President Bush earlier this year, intended as a symbol of the Administration's distaste for Chinese repression. 
Likewise, Western ambassadors in Beijing seem much more interested than before in making trips to Tibet, and their No. 1 destination there these days is Drapchi Prison in Lhasa, the capital, where some political offenders are housed.
Potentially the most significant recent move was the launching in the spring of a Tibetan-language service of Voice of America. 
Visitors to Tibet say that the 15-minute daily broadcast has an enormous audience. 
The broadcasts not only provide news and information, but are also apparently taken -- or mistaken -- as a symbol of American support for Tibetan independence.
"The strong feeling in Lhasa is that more and more the U.S. is supporting Tibet," said a foreigner in Tibet.

Within Tibet, the Chinese authorities had a relatively conciliatory policy from the early 1980's through 1987.

The violence appears to have radicalized the population of Lhasa and strengthened the yearning for independence.
Diplomats and scholars often regard as exaggerated propaganda the assertions of Tibetan exiles that China is practicing genocide or a policy of forced sterilization and abortion to curb the number of Tibetans. 
But almost no one doubts the Tibetans' desire for independence. 
And human rights abuses -- torture of monks and nuns, killings of protesters, and long spells of imprisonment for advocates of independence -- are well documented by rights monitors like Asia Watch and Tibet Information Network.
The crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square came three months after clashes in Lhasa between Chinese troops and anti-Government demonstrators in which at least 12 and perhaps more than 100 people died. 
By extension, the scenes from Beijing seemed to crystallize what had been for many people little more than just a notion of the tensions in Tibet.
"People had heard about what had happened in Tibet, but they didn't quite believe it until it became so real on TV and they realized, 'My God, this is also what's happening in Tibet,' " said John L. Ackerly, the legal counsel for the International Campaign for Tibet.

Â

Few people these days seem optimistic about a reconciliation between China and the Tibetan government-in-exile. 
Partly because they now see their movement gaining ground, the Tibetans have little incentive to compromise with Beijing. 
And the Chinese have now so embittered the Tibetans that -- rather like the Shah of Iran in his later years -- they would risk new upheavals and protests if they relaxed their repression.
Moreover, to a degree perhaps unappreciated in the West, suppression of the Tibetan independence movement is one of the few policies of Beijing's hard-liners that appears to draw broad support from Chinese. 
Even young intellectuals in Beijing, who disdain Communism and yearn for human rights for themselves, often say that Tibet is Chinese and should remain so. 
The reasons have much to do with Chinese nationalism, and with a grim resolve that the nation must never again endure the humiliation of a century ago, when China was carved up by more powerful countries and lost territory at its extremities.
"You might have a relatively democratic government" in China in the future, said Guocang Huan, a China scholar at Columbia University, "but such a government probably would not compromise much on Tibetan independence."

RELATIONS between the Chinese and the Mongols have been a bit strained ever since Genghis Khan slaughtered millions of Chinese in the 13th century. 
By one account, the Mongols considered converting all of northern China into a vast pasture; they relented when an adviser pointed out that the Chinese, if spared, could be taxed.
The tradition of mutual distrust is again bubbling to the surface in Chinese-controlled Inner Mongolia, a desert region more than twice the size of California. 
More and more Mongols there are reasserting their ethnic heritage, establishing links with the outside world, and even organizing underground networks to press for democracy and autonomy.
"This is our last chance to achieve democracy, to reassert our culture," Huhehada, a 29-year-old leader of the underground movement, said recently. 
"Mongols need their own culture, their own history -- recorded in their own hands. 
Or else they'll face the fate of American Indians or of Tibetans."
Mr. Huhehada was interviewed in exile in Ulan Bator, the capital of the neighboring independent nation of Mongolia, from which he and other Inner Mongolian dissidents are orchestrating their campaign. 
They say about 2,000 people, half of them living in Inner Mongolia, have joined their newly formed General Coordination Committee of Inner Mongolian Rejuvenation Movements. 
The group is banned within China and the dissidents fear that Beijing will now press Ulan Bator to ban it as well.
Mongolia itself abandoned one-party Communist rule in 1990, and has since seen a tremendous flowering of traditional Mongol religion and culture. 
Mongolian radio can be heard in Inner Mongolia, and the growing contact across the border seems to be a major reason for the surge of nationalism among China's Mongols. 
In addition, Beijing has just announced that it will open the entire border to trade, and that is certain to multiply links with Mongolia and perhaps the demands for change.
Inner Mongolia so far is not nearly as much of a headache for the Chinese leadership as is Tibet, where Buddhist monks and nuns regularly protest for independence and human rights. 
Nor is Inner Mongolia even as much of a concern as oil-rich Xinjiang, the Muslim region of northwest China where there was an abortive armed uprising in 1990. 
But many of the same pressures -- resentment at Chinese arrogance and immigration, yearning for self-rule and prosperity, and outrage at repression -- seem to be at work in Inner Mongolia.
"Our economy is based on colonialism," said Tsenglet, another of the Mongol leaders exiled in Ulan Bator. 
"Our land is rich, but the Chinese take our resources and leave us poor. 
We see that!
And there's been pressure from immigrants. 
We're now a minority in our own land. 
Life for our people is worse than ever."
Â 
Resentments Grow
The statistics do not bear that out: Ethnic Mongols in Inner Mongolia have rising incomes and improving health conditions. 
But living standards are not rising as fast as those of most Chinese, and resentment seems to be growing. 
As in Tibet, Chinese immigration to Mongolia is a particular irritant.
The Han, the main ethnic group in China, began to migrate to Inner Mongolia 200 years ago. 
By the time of the Communist revolution in 1949, the Han reportedly outnumbered Mongols 5 to 1. 
The 1990 census found a total population of 21.5 million, of whom 3.4 million were Mongols -- a ratio of 6.4 to 1. 
It would be even more skewed, except that the Mongols have more children than the Han, and many families of mixed heritage have reclassified themselves as Mongols to win educational benefits and other advantages available to minorities.
There are periodic reports of large anti-Government demonstrations in Inner Mongolia, but many foreign diplomats and Chinese alike are skeptical. 
The situation is murky in part because China normally will not let foreign journalists visit.
The Chinese Government denounces reports of unrest as lies and fabrications. 
But most foreigners who have visited have reported modest signs of discontent, and dissidents are forging links with the West to get out documents and information on human rights. 
"It's been a long-overlooked corner of China," said Robin Munro, a researcher for Asia Watch, a human rights organization that has published two reports about Inner Mongolia in the last 12 months. 
"Until recently, dissident activity there met the fate of being repressed in obscurity and isolation. 
Nobody would know about it. 
But there has been this link forged now with international channels of communication, so that repression in the region is reported on. 
When it's published outside China, it filters back in through international radio stations, the Inner Mongolian dissidents hear about it, and it basically emboldens them to continue."
As everywhere in China, dissidents face considerable risks. 
At least 17 people are known to be in Inner Mongolia's prisons for their political activities; the true number may be much higher.
While many of the dissidents would like to see Inner Mongolia reunite with Mongolia, they acknowledge that this would be difficult to achieve because of the preponderance of Han Chinese. 
Some say they would like to expel the Han, or at least relocate them, while others say they would settle for a solution short of reunification.
"In any case, the first thing we need to get is the freedom to speak out, to express our grievances," said Uringkhai N. Tumen, a 27-year-old in Ulan Bator who heads an underground cultural organization in Inner Mongolia. 
"At the least, we need real autonomy -- real autonomy, not what we have now."

Ever since Chinese troops ''liberated'' Tibet in 1950, the Communist authorities have tried to pressure Tibetans into submission. 
But these days many Tibetans seem more eager than ever to pry themselves from the Chinese embrace, and there are signs that time is running against Beijing.
Government officials acknowledge that they face a long-term struggle against what they describe as ''a tiny number of separatists.''
Yet the very trend of economic and social development seems to be running against the Chinese. 
The worldwide pattern since the early 19th century has been that nationalism increases rather than diminishes as peasants earn more money, drift to cities and become more politically aware. 
In Tibet, as peasants buy televisions and radios to plug into the modern world, they may be swayed by the independence movement and nationalism that already flourish in Lhasa.
Economic factors may provoke even greater discontent. 
Incomes are rising in Tibet, but not as fast as in the rest of China. 
While the region has some natural resources, it is difficult to see how Tibet could catch up with the rest of China - unless it went all-out to attract foreign tourists, a strategy that the Government has judged too risky politically.
''The city dwellers are better off than in the past, but they're not satisfied,'' acknowledged Hu Jinan, the deputy head of the Tibetan Government's Cultural Bureau. 
''They know it's better elsewhere.''
Tibet is officially an ''autonomous region'' of China, but the Government's legitimacy has been in doubt at least since the Dalai Lama, the traditional leader of the region, fled into exile in 1959. 
There is little armed resistance to Chinese rule, partly because Tibetans are Buddhist and generally pacifist, but the Dalai Lama has set up an exile government and many Tibetans would like him to return and lead Tibet as a sovereign state.
Government officials here often seem amazed that Tibetans should resent Chinese rule. 
Indeed, there is little doubt that Beijing has been, by its standards, not only very repressive but also very generous in Tibet. 
Torture is said to be common, and the Government has expelled politically active monks from monasteries and planned new limits on the number of monks. 
But Tibet is materially better off than it used to be, and health and educational standards have risen - although the same would have been expected without Chinese rule.
Each year the central government not only excuses Tibet from its tax obligations but also provides about $275 million in subsidies. 
About one-third goes to salaries, but much of the rest is used for schools, hospitals and infrastructure projects. 
The Chinese seem to feel that they are owed a bit of loyalty and gratitude, but the distrust is so great that they get little credit either in Tibet or outside of it.
Outside of Tibet, the Dalai Lama and those around him have tried to build support by telling of forced sterilization of Tibetans, huge influxes of Chinese and a deliberate policy of either genocide or forced assimilation. 
But many diplomats and other experts regard the anti-Chinese propaganda from the Dalai Lama as little more reliable than the Chinese propaganda about Tibet. 
With access tightly curtailed, the debate about Tibet has been waged more with polemics than with information.
Among the most poignant claims by the Dalai Lama is that Tibetans have become a minority in their own land because of large-scale Chinese immigration. 
But the exile movement's estimate of a Tibetan population of 6 million Tibetans and 7.5 million Chinese is considered misleading because it refers to a vast area of China that extends far beyond present-day Tibet. 
The official Chinese figures for Tibet's population are often viewed as more relevant: 2.12 million ethnic Tibetans and 79,000 permanent Han Chinese inhabitants, not including tens of thousands of Chinese cadres, soldiers and entrepreneurs without permanent residence permits.
Chinese immigration into Tibet has accelerated, but this seems to be a result not of a conspiracy by Beijing but of economic subsidies to the region. 
Chinese traders say they find it more profitable to do business in Tibet than in their home provinces.
Despite rumors about Chinese hospitals killing Tibetan infants, the family planning policy seems to be much more relaxed for Tibetans than it is for Chinese. 
Peasants interviewed said they were allowed to have as many children as they wanted, and most couples seemed to have three to five.
It is also striking how little assimilation has occurred after four decades of Chinese rule. 
Even in Lhasa only a minority of Tibetans speaks any Chinese, and in the countryside it is virtually impossible to find Chinese speakers. 
The Chinese language is not even taught in rural elementary schools, which is as far as most Tibetans pursue their education.
This strategy of trying to buy friends in Tibet with subsidies and various benefits showed some promise of succeeding in the 1980's, but in Lhasa it already seems to have collapsed. 
The last three years of protests, each time brutally crushed, have led to new bitterness on each side.
Despite the repression and mistrust, many Tibetans are optimistic that they will gain independence in the coming decades. 
They are inspired partly by the collapse of Communism in Eastern Europe and partly by signs of a weak and unpopular central Government in Beijing. 
Tibet has turned out to be fairly indigestible, and they hope that Beijing will eventually spit it out.
''We don't like the Chinese,'' a Tibetan in his 20's explained the other day. 
''They've turned to repression and terrorism to keep us down, but most people still want independence and want the Dalai Lama to return. 
Independence is a real possibility.''

text:
ï»¿
Five months after martial law was lifted here, a sullen calm has returned to the narrow lanes of this holy city. 
But Chinese marksmen are still perched on the roofs of buildings overlooking the central square, and many Tibetans suspect that their guns have not been silenced for long.
Here among the snow-swept peaks and glacier-fed rivers to the north of Mount Everest, nationalism is forging a significant challenge to the Communist leaders 1,600 miles away in Beijing. 
This is Deng Xiaoping's Lithuania, and some fear it will become his Beirut - except that Tibet is more vast, amounting to two-thirds the size of Western Europe. 
If China ever crumbles, Tibet is likely to be the first piece to break off, with reverberations across Asia.
A weeklong visit to Tibet - one of the first permitted by a foreign journalist since martial law was lifted May 1 -found no evidence of widespread or serious unrest in the majority rural population, for most peasants and nomads absorb themselves not in politics but in the practical matters of their barley and yaks.
Yet in Lhasa, the discontent and repression seem pervasive in the wake of martial law, which was declared after widespread protests in 1987. 
The mood suggests a dangerous cascade of bitterness that threatens to overwhelm the land that inspired the notion of Shangri-La.
Â 
'We Hate China'
''Everybody wants independence and the return of the Dalai Lama,'' a well-educated Tibetan in his 30's whispered late one evening, after ducking into a building near Jokhang Temple to take refuge from police spies. 
''We hate China and what it has done.''
He spoke in a mixture of terror and fury, and he extended his arms as if handcuffed to suggest what he thought would happen if he were caught. 
A moment later he fled in fright when a jeep pulled up outside and someone shined a flashlight through the window.
While the man was more outspoken than most, he seemed to represent the antagonisms and distrust that are nearly overflowing in Lhasa. 
While the police and troop presence has been reduced since the end of martial law, anti-Chinese protests continue on a small scale and the authorities acknowledge that they face a long-term struggle to subdue what they describe as ''a tiny handful of separatists.''
Â 
Violent Suppression And Rising Distrust
Tibet, now an autonomous region, was ''invaded'' or ''liberated'' by Chinese troops in 1950 - the term depends on the speaker. 
The Dalai Lama was the supreme figure in a theocratic Government, and even though he fled to India in 1959 after an abortive uprising, his influence is everywhere. 
After his flight China consolidated its hold on Tibet, which had been claimed by all Chinese governments since the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, although the western two-thirds of Tibet had been effectively independent since 1912.
In the early and mid-1980's, a conciliatory policy by the Chinese authorities seemed to be winning results, and tensions eased in Tibet. 
But protests beginning in 1987 were violently suppressed, with the police firing on crowds of demonstrators around the Jokhang Temple, and many Tibetans say that since then discontent has risen dangerously.
The Chinese authorities will face a test next Thursday, the third anniversary of the beginning of the recent wave of unrest. 
Posters already have gone up on brick walls around town, calling for demonstrations on that day or on Oct. 
1, China's national day.
Word about the proposed protests is whispered from ear to ear among Tibetans who mingle in the narrow lanes around the Jokhang Temple, but no one knows if people will take the risk and respond.
There have been a few minor incidents in recent months. 
About a dozen monks and nuns were arrested last month during a peaceful protest at the Dalai Lama's old summer residence near Lhasa, and about six more were seized on Sept. 
14 when they marched around the Jokhang Temple and chanted pro-independence slogans.
Â 
Harsher Policies After Martial Law
''Those who try to split the motherland will, if they dare to violate the Constitution and laws, surely be opposed by the broad masses,'' said Mao Rubai, the vice chairman of Tibet's Government. 
He is a member of the Han race, which accounts for 93 percent of all Chinese, while the Tibetan people are of Mongolian stock.
There are some signs of a tougher policy since the end of martial law, including the appointment on May 31 of a new chairman of Tibet's Government, Gyaincain Norbu, a law-and-order man with long experience in the courts and prosecutors' offices.
By official count, there are a few more than 100 people now imprisoned for engaging in illegal separatist activities. 
But most independent estimates are higher.
Officials deny that those imprisoned have been tortured, but most Tibetans say that physical abuse is routine. 
The six people arrested on Sept. 
14 were briefly taken into a police station near the Jokhang Temple, and when they were led out 10 minutes later to be bused away, they were already said to have been beaten.
A comprehensive report earlier this year by Asia Watch, an American human-rights organization, detailed treatment of prisoners that included attacks by trained dogs, assaults with electric cattle prods, suspension by ropes, scalding with boiling water and rapes of nuns.
Â 
Tibetans Express Views on China
Official Chinese publications have occasionally written about Tibetan prisons - describing them as so idyllic that offenders are almost sad to leave - but the authorities refused repeated requests to visit a prison on this trip.
But Gong Liefu, the deputy director of Tibet's Foreign Affairs Office, said that it was illegal for a foreign journalist to ask people whether they favored independence, and that it might be illegal for Tibetans to respond in the affirmative.
Nevertheless, Tibetans made their views known. 
At dusk, as shops closed and most Chinese police withdrew from the streets, they sometimes approached a foreign reporter to speak their mind. 
And even in officially arranged interviews, Tibetans sometimes refused to go along with the official line.
In the heart of the Jokhang Temple, as pilgrims kowtowed in the dust not far away, a senior monk named Tudeng Renqing criticized the expulsion from the temple of eight monks who had taken part in a protest. 
In the presence of about 10 people, including Han Chinese officials, he was then asked for his views about independence, and a silence settled over the room as he paused and thought for several minutes.
''From a religious point of view,'' he finally responded delicately, ''I'd like all believers as well as the general population to act peacefully.''
A reporter suggested that in the circumstances, that sounded like an endorsement of peaceful efforts for independence. 
The lama laughed and beamed.
Â 
Beijing's Backers Offer Reasons
A yearning for independence is common in Lhasa, but it is not universal. 
Some Tibetans insist that independence would be a disaster for the region's development and assert that only a tiny fraction of young people oppose links with the ''motherland.''
Most of the top positions in the Government administration are held by such Tibetans, who point to improved health care and rising prosperity under Chinese rule.
In addition, there seems to be a broad stratum of urban Tibetans who recognize the improvements but are also resentful of Chinese domination. 
They are moderately discontented, but see little alternative to Chinese rule and in any case are afraid of getting in trouble if they oppose the regime.
''We don't thnk about politics,'' said a Tibetan university student over a beer in a privately owned bar. 
''We don't dare. 
We just study.''
Darchi, a 40-year-old peasant interviewed at random as he harvested his barley in a mud-brick village near the city of Shigatse, said: ''We don't want independence. 
Before we had a difficult time and now life is getting better. 
I want to buy a television, and then I can sit back and drink barley beer and watch TV.''
Yet even those, like Mr. Darchi, who are wary of independence adore the Dalai Lama. 
Most homes and temples have photos of the Dalai Lama on the wall, and ordinary people are moved nearly to tears as they touch a Dalai Lama photo to their head when it is given to them.
Â 
Failing Economy Under China's Rule
As China's leaders try to win over the Tibetan population and earn the appreciation of local residents, their challenge is compounded by economic difficulties. 
Despite enormous subsidies from Beijing - some of which go to pay the salaries of Han Chinese officials rather than to benefit local Tibetans - industry in Tibet has grown by only about 6 percent per year over the last decade, compared with about 12 percent annually in the rest of the country.
Officials concede that the economic gap between Tibet and coastal China is growing, not diminishing, and that adds to the perception that the Chinese authorities are mismanaging the local economy.
Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, visited Tibet in July and pledged even greater subsidies over the next decade to build the local economic base. 
But the region's greatest economic resource, tourism, may not be exploited to the full because of fears that large numbers of individual tourists could help provoke further unrest. 
Ngaphu Rinchen, the director of tourism in Tibet, said that while visits by tour groups would be expanded, it would be ''difficult'' to allow individual tourists to return within the next two or three years.
In Tibet all those problems tend to overlay and reinforce the main gulf in the society: that which separates Tibetans and Han Chinese. 
While Chinese complain that Tibetans are lazy and ungrateful, and more likely to show hospitality to a foreigner on the street than to a longtime Chinese colleague, the Tibetans resent what they regard as a superior attitude and colonial policy on the part of the Chinese.
''Life has settled a bit since the lifting of martial law, but it's still tense,'' said a Tibetan in his 20's who has spent the last dozen years in Lhasa. 
''This is a volcano, and someday it will explode.''

text:
ï»¿
AT the end of the world, where the Tibetan plateau suddenly teeters off a cliff in one direction and collides against snowcapped peaks in the other, the Xinsi Monastery looms unexpectedly from the golden wheat fields to preside over the landscape. 
The red-robed monks come bustling out, the dough on their hands an indication that they have been interrupted in their chores rather than their prayers, and they break into welcoming grins as magnificent as the scenery.
It is a scene from Tibet, more Tibetan than Tibet itself. 
Here there are no Chinese troops prowling in the background or Chinese tour leaders curtailing contacts with the monks.
This is Qinghai Province in the west of China, but it used to be the northeast part of Tibet until it fell under Chinese control centuries ago. 
The Tibetans regard Qinghai as part of Tibet, but the Chinese Government's restrictions on travel to Tibet do not apply here. 
Tourists are allowed into Tibet only as part of a costly organized tour -- although this can be a one-person tour -- while foreigners are free to fly to Xining, the provincial capital, from Beijing.
Qinghai -- pronounced ching-hi -- was opened to foreigners only in 1983, and it still is among the least visited parts of China. 
Only about 1,200 Americans go to the province each year, slightly fewer than visit Tibet, and the sight of a foreigner still turns heads even in Xining.
The single greatest splendor in Qinghai is the Kumbum Monastery, better known today by its Chinese name, Taer Si. 
Fifteen miles southwest of Xining, the Kumbum is a stunning collection of temples and compounds set against a hillside, the buildings all painted red and other bright colors, with pilgrims praying and spinning the large prayer wheels and prostrating on the ground. 
The monastery is as noteworthy for the Tibetan pilgrims who come to worship as for the architecture itself. 
When I visited in August, I came across a group of four sturdy young Tibetan men in bedraggled clothing.
We chatted for a bit in Chinese and they said they had come from their homes in Sichuan Province, by way of Lhasa. 
I asked how they had traveled. 
They looked puzzled.
"By foot," said the oldest of them, about 18 years old.
"How long have you been traveling?"
"Two years," the young man said. 
"But we'll be home in another six months."
The monastery was built in the last quarter of the 16th century on the instructions of the third Dalai Lama. 
The site is the birthplace of the founder of the Gelukpa order of Buddhism, Tsongkhapa. 
This was a center of learning -- one of the Tibetan Ivy League, so to speak -- for Tibetan and Mongolian monks, and at the time of the Communist revolution there were still 3,000 Tibetan monks. 
Now the Government has set a limit of 400 monks for the Kumbum, but this is not strictly enforced and there are about 500.
The most unusual sight in the monastery is the 50-foot-long carving made of yak butter. 
The workmanship may not be at the level of the Parthenon frieze, but there are elephants, flowers and religious figures, all in brightly colored deep relief. 
The carving is newly-sculptured each year.
XINING itself is of limited interest: a traditionally Chinese city of cement blocks whose hues are all shades of gray. 
The only important sight within the city is the Dongguan Mosque, which was built in the 14th century and is one of the largest mosques in China. 
The entrance arch is elegant and the plaza-like open space inside is picturesque. 
There is a large Muslim community in Xining -- the province was even ruled by a Muslim warlord immediately prior to the Communist revolution in 1949 -- and the mosque fills to capacity on Fridays for prayers.
Few people in Qinghai speak English, but if you have an evening free you might wander over to the English Corner on Sheng Li Road. 
This is where Chinese men and women gather, particularly on Sundays, to speak English to each other in a caliber ranging from a few words to fluency, and a genuine American is richly prized and quickly surrounded.
The best part about Qinghai is the Tibetan areas, and in general any road south or west will take you to Tibetan villages. 
The current Dalai Lama's native village, Takster, meaning Roaring Tiger, is apparently only about an hour or two by car from Xining, but the authorities told me that the area was closed to foreigners and refused to allow me to visit. 
Other foreigners have gone with impunity, however, and one may well be able to make arrangements with a taxi driver for a day trip. 
Foreign tourists who are caught in closed areas and who act surprised, innocent and apologetic are normally scolded and sent away. 
Occasionally a fine is negotiated, but normally there is no punishment.
One Tibetan area that is often recommended to tourists is Qinghai Lake, an immense body of water that is China's largest salt-water lake. 
Bird Island in the lake is supposed to be particularly beautiful and full of migratory birds in April and May. 
I didn't visit Bird Island, but I found Qinghai Lake itself about as interesting as one would expect a big salt lake to be.
THE highlight of my visit was simply a few days roaming the Tibetan villages around Qiapuqia, a town of about 30,000 in Gonghe County south of Qinghai Lake. 
Most of the townspeople are Han Chinese, but many of the nearby villages are Tibetan and the people are extremely welcoming.
"Uncle, are you a foreigner?" asked an eight-year-old girl who was startled to encounter me on a dirt path near her village. 
I explained in Chinese that I was a genuine foreigner. 
Since I was the first one she had ever seen, she led me to her home. 
Her family was enormously excited at my arrival, and pressed tea and bread on me, but the town was sufficiently remote that all they knew was that I was not Tibetan.
"Are you Han Chinese?" the grandmother asked me, after peering for several minutes at my face, which does not look in the least Chinese. 
I explained that no, I was an American. 
She nodded sagely, to show that she had heard of Americans, but I'm not sure she distinguished in her mind between Americans and Martians.
The best way to make friends in such areas -- in any Chinese village for that matter -- is to take a Polaroid camera. 
Few peasants own a camera, and if you can take some instant photographs and pass them around, the entire village will cluster around and observe in amazement, and peasants will compete to invite you into their homes. 
Of course, none of the villagers speak English, but sign language can be quite eloquent when necessary. 
If a non-Chinese speaker gets somewhere where sign language is insufficient, someone will get the school's English teacher to translate.
About 10 miles from Qiapuqia is the Xinsi, a Tibetan monastery that gets only a few foreign travelers a year. 
The path is not quite wide enough for a car, but it makes a nice all-day hike, or else you may be able to get a lift on a motorcycle.
There are about 100 monks at the monastery, ranging from 7 years old to the late 70's. 
The setting is spectacular: snowy mountains in the background, and an abyss and valley in the foreground. 
It really does seem to be the end of the world. 
The monks speak no English, and not much Chinese, but they were eager to show me around the many temples as well as the kitchens and living quarters. 
There are several courtyards and temples with large carved Buddhas. 
Each of the temples is surrounded by the familiar red prayer wheels.
I hiked back to Qiapuqia from the monastery in about six hours, stopping to talk to Tibetan villagers on the way, and found it an exhilarating walk. 
But one word of caution: the local police were aghast at my activities, because I was a journalist (as I had told everyone I had talked to), and later sent policemen to retrace my steps and interrogate everyone I had chatted with.
This was probably a special case that wouldn't affect an ordinary tourist, but it is a reminder that this is a sensitive region. 
The worst that can realistically happen to you is that you'll be fined and expelled, but it is possible to get local Tibetans in deep trouble if the authorities believe they are engaging in pro-independence activities. 
So avoid meeting in places like your hotel -- where local people may be questioned about why they are talking to a foreigner -- and be discreet in your conversations with Tibetans.
Â 
Â 
Â 
A REMOTE, LITTLE-VISITED AREA
Getting There
Air China has flights every Friday from Beijing to Xining and back, all seats economy class, for $133 each way. 
First class trains are also available, but the journey takes 44 hours from Beijing. 
If flights are full, it is possible to fly to Lanzhou, and take a train, bus or taxi for the half-day ride to Xining.
It is possible to travel from Qinghai to Tibet, by bus or by hitching rides on trucks, but this is technically illegal unless you have a permit to enter Tibet. 
In fact, youthful Westerners do this regularly, and despite occasional crackdowns the authorities seem to tolerate it most of the time. 
The trip, by bus or truck, takes a minimum of three days from Xining to Lhasa.
Even in the summer, Qinghai can be chilly because of the elevation -- Qiapuqia, for example, is more than 9,000 feet above sea level. 
But if you forget warm clothes, yak wool sweaters are available for about $25 in Xining. 
Winters are cold but tolerable, with temperatures below freezing but little snow.
Â 
Accommodations
The best hotel in Xining is the Qinghai Guesthouse, $32 a day for a double, and it is reasonably good, with a working bath in the slightly musty rooms, a television, and fair restaurants. 
Phone (971) 44-888. 
Wang Bingxi of the Qinghai Tourism Bureau, 42-721, can arrange to have you picked up at the airport for a fee.
