file: Tibetan Asks Deng to Lift Martial Law.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Dalai Lama appealed today to Deng Xiaoping, the senior Chinese leader, to use his influence to lift martial law in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.
In a letter delivered to the Chinese Embassy by his office here, the Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhists, also renewed his call to Beijing for talks on Tibet.
Beijing declared martial law in Lhasa on Tuesday, sending in thousands of troops to restore order after three days of anti-Chinese protests described as the worst unrest since an uprising in March 1959. 
By official count, 16 people have been killed in the unrest; Tibetans say the toll is higher, according to Western travelers.
The anniversary of the 1959 uprising was observed today, but the Dalai Lama, who is in his exile headquarters in the Indian hill town of Dharmsala, did not come to New Delhi to take part in protests mounted by Tibetans. 
Beijing crushed the 1959 revolt and ultimately declared Tibet an integral part of China, leading to the Dalai Lama's flight from the country.
Â 
'Chinese Atrocities'
Today, several hundred exiles demonstrated at India Gate, about a mile from Parliament, carrying placards that denounced ''Chinese atrocities'' and called for Tibetan independence.
The demonstrators, many belonging to youth and women's groups impatient with the lower-keyed efforts of the Dalai Lama and his willingness to talk with Beijing, burned a Chinese flag and an effigy of Li Peng, the Chinese Prime Minister.
The Dalai Lama suggested negotiating with China in a speech last September to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. 
He proposed talks in Geneva in January of this year. 
The Chinese did not accept the invitation.
Tashi Wangdi, the Dalai Lama's spokesman and a member of his exile cabinet, said today that there have been several meetings here between the Chinese Embassy and the Tibetans to discuss this and other issues. 
But he added that Beijing has major objections to be overcome before formal talks can open.
Mr. Wangdi said the Chinese objected to the composition of the team the Dalai Lama had proposed sending to formal talks. 
The Chinese also say that the Dalai Lama's suggestion that Tibet become an associated state of China - it is now called an autonomous region - was unacceptable.
In his letter to Mr. Deng today, the Dalai Lama said he hoped ''the Chinese leadership will have the wisdom to realize the true feelings of the Tibetan people and the strength and courage to rectify past mistakes.''
Â 
REPORTS OF NEW ARRESTS
BEIJING, March 10 (AP) - Official Chinese reports said today that Tibetans peacefully celebrated the ''30th anniversary of democratic reforms in Tibet'' - Beijing's characterization of the 1959 uprising. 
But Tibetans reached by telephone spoke of large-scale roundups and pervasive fear in Lhasa.
''There are new arrests,'' a woman said. 
''There are many, but we don't know how many.''
A man came on the line and said: ''Don't talk a long time. 
There are a lot of police. 
We can't talk long.''
China's nightly news said martial law stopped a riot planned for today in the capital. 
State television said more than 30 Tibetan ''rioters'' surrendered to police and admitted to taking part in disturbances this week in Lhasa.

file: Tibetans Fear Loss of a Safe Haven in Nepal.txt
text:
ï»¿
Tibetan exiles in Nepal, fearful that their country of refuge will grow more dependent on China because of an Indian economic blockade, say they are worried about their future in this land, where they are prohibited from taking part in anti-Chinese activities.
Some Tibetans are also concerned that their role in revitalizing Buddhism in Nepal, the world's only Hindu kingdom, may come in for unwelcome scrutiny. 
There are thought to be about 14,000 Tibetan refugees in Nepal, most of them the families of people who fled here from Lhasa in 1959, when the Chinese suppressed a revolt.
A refugee who works with newcomers arriving in Katmandu from Nepal's border with Tibet said immigration officials have been tightening controls as the country begins to feel the effects of India's closing of most of Nepal's southern trade routes.
This aid worker, who asked not to be named, said that Tibetans who reached a Nepali-Chinese border town, Kodari, were given visas for 12 months until about a year ago, when the validity was reduced to three months.
Recently, he said, Tibetans were being told they could stay only 30 days. 
Most Tibetans, who now travel legally on Chinese exit permits and passports, want to visit the Indian town of Dharmsala, where their exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, is based. 
The 30-day limit poses problems for these visitors, who travel a circuitous overland route to India and back.
Radhe Bista, a spokesman for the Nepalese Government, said in an interview that there was no blanket 30-day regulation covering visas for Tibetans, who are regarded as Chinese citizens. 
He said that the immigration officials at Kodari, the only land border crossing, have discretion in granting entry.
Mr. Bista said there was no intention of curbing the activities of Tibetan refugees, who have enjoyed wide freedoms to move about and engage in business. 
Tibetans are credited with starting and building an export trade in woolen and cotton carpets, which is earning much-needed hard currency for Katmandu. 
They also dominate the manufacture and sale of handicrafts to tourists, Nepalese say.
Â 
Indian Embargo
At the Tibetan refugee center of Jawalakhel, south of Katmandu, where many carpets are made for export, exiles said that their business was suffering from the inability to get raw wool and cotton because of the Indian embargo, which began on March 23. 
India says it will allow only essential supplies to enter Nepal.
Nepalese and Tibetans say that most exports are also blocked because of the trade blockade and the Indian decision to stop supplying Nepal with petroleum products needed to transport the goods to Calcutta port by trucks.
The Tibetans' role in advancing the cause of Buddhism in Nepal is just beginning to be noticed, Nepalese and Tibetans say. 
The Tibetan Buddhists do not proselytize. 
But they are devout people who give a large part of their earnings to the building of monasteries and temples, to which Nepalese also come to study and worship.
Nepal has two distinct Buddhist communities. 
The Newaris, original settlers of the Katmandu Valley, are often Buddhist or practice a combination of Hinduism and Buddhism. 
On the Nepal-Tibetan border, there are other Buddhists who follow Tibetan schools of Buddhist teachings.

file: Tibetan_s Tale_ Unrest, Explosion, Crackdown.txt
text:
ï»¿
The first Tibetans to leave Lhasa for Nepal since the Chinese imposed martial law in the city a month ago say several weeks of growing public protests, culminating in attacks on Chinese residents and shops, led to Beijing's action.
In a series of demonstrations in late February and early March, Tibetan nationalist flags were unfurled and emotional crowds chanted ''Independence!
Independence!'' a monk among the 42 Tibetans said in an interview. 
Mobs set Chinese businesses on fire, he said.
The recently arrived Tibetans, including children, traveled overland on Chinese exit permits allowing them to visit relatives in Nepal. 
They left Lhasa two weeks ago and reached Katmandu last week.
Since the early 1980's, China has allowed international travel to and from Lhasa through the Nepalese border town of Kodari. 
Until the recent imposition of martial law, tourists were also able to fly between Katmandu and Lhasa. 
Travel agents here say they have been told that tourist flights may resume as early as Saturday. 
This may indicate that martial law will soon be lifted.
The Tibetan monk, who asked that his name not be used to protect his family and religious colleagues in Tibet, said public disaffection in Tibet, which China formally absorbed after the Communist revolution in 1949, entered a new phase in December.
Â 
A Call to Demonstrate
Other Tibetans in the group have given Tibetan exiles here similar accounts of recent events.
The monk, a follower of the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, said signs began to appear during the night in Lhasa in early December, urging Tibetans to come out on Dec. 
10, International Human Rights Day. 
When protests materialized within a few days, a 31-year-old monk who tried to parade through the streets with a Tibetan flag was intercepted by the Chinese police, who tried to wrench the flag from his hands before finally firing, killing him.
When students came out on Dec. 
18 to demand greater human rights for Tibetans, the monk said, Chinese officials made a major effort to talk with them about their grievances. 
The officials spent more than six hours with the students, lecturing them on loyalty. 
There were no arrests.
On Feb. 
7, the eve of the Tibetan New Year, posters went up overnight in Lhasa asking every family to send one member to a demonstration the next day at the Jokhang Monastery, the focal point of city life. 
The monk said as many as 10,000 people went to hang khatas, white ceremonial scarves that are a sign of honor, on a Tibetan flag that was unfurled there.
After March 1, the monk said, the protests became increasingly regular, and larger. 
In early March, Tibetans marked the anniversary of the unsuccessful 1959 revolt against the Chinese, after which the Dalai Lama went into exile in India.
Â 
Protesters Throw Stones
On March 5, thousands were in the streets, the monk said, and they threw stones at the police, who fired tear gas and then bullets at the crowd.
Tibetans say 104 bodies were found that day by relatives and friends.
The monk said foreign tourists -''especially backpackers,'' he added through an exile interpreter - taught Tibetans how to dip cloths in water and breathe through them to mitigate the effects of tear gas, an act that infuriated the police.
On March 6 and 7, the monk said, enraged mobs, ''their spirit at its peak,'' began to attack Chinese residents of Lhasa and set fire to their shops and other businesses. 
At 4 P.M. on March 7, announcements were read all over Lhasa ordering people to go home. 
Tibetans say the announcements warned that anyone who tried to assemble again would be shot.
At midnight that night, martial law was officially declared.
Since then, the monk said, Tibetans have been required to buy daily permits to go out, even for shopping. 
People on bicycles passing Chinese policemen or troops have to stop and produce these permits or be pulled off the cycles.

file: U.N. Population Plan for China a Test for U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A new United Nations plan to help China control its population growth will provide an early test of the Bush Administration's attitude toward Beijing's forced abortion and sterilization policies, officials and diplomats say.
The United Nations Fund for Population Activities, the world family planning agency, will ask its governing council in early June to approve the $57 million five-year plan under which it will help China promote family planning and develop a modern contraceptive industry. 
This will be the first time the United States, which is a member of the council, has been asked to approve a new plan for China since 1985, when Congress cut off all American contributions to the agency, claiming it was helping China run a population control program that employed compulsory abortion and sterilization.
''There is a new President and a new program so I hope we will also have a new policy and the United States will resume its support for us,'' said Dr. Nafis Sadik, the agency head.
Dr. Sadik said that when she visited Beijing in January, Chinese leaders admitted that ''overzealous'' family planning officials had forced women to have abortions against their wishes.
But they insist that this is against official policy requiring voluntary abortions.
Dr. Sadik, who is from Pakistan and the only woman to head a United Nations agency, said the Chinese told her they are now trying to improve the image of their population policy abroad, cracking down on officials involved in family planning abuses, including coerced abortions.
She said the Chinese leaders also told her that they are anxious for the United States to support the United Nations agency's new population control program.
She said they regard the disagreement over the agency as an ''irritant in their relationship with Washington.''
The Reagan Administration and Congress cut off funding for the agency, which relies on voluntary governmental contributions, in 1985 after American anti-abortion groups accused the agency of helping China implement a population control program that provided for compulsory abortion and sterilization.
The money Congress would have given was allocated instead to voluntary population control programs in other developing countries not run by the United Nations agency.
The withdrawal of American funding has not been a major inconvenience for the agency because other donor countries have stepped up their contributions to fill the gap, officials say. 
This year the fund will have a record budget of just over $190 million to spend on controlling population growth.
Under the 1985 law, the President must determine annually whether China's population control program includes forced abortion.
This task goes to the United States aid agency, which has always said it thinks China compels women to abort unauthorized pregnancies.
China, which has 20 percent of the world's population but only 2 percent of its farmland, is trying to stabilize its population at about 1.2 billion by 2000 by discouraging couples from having more than one child.
As yet Administration officials say they have not decided whether China is ending forced abortions, allowing the United States to give money. 
But a struggle is already under way in the Congress between right-to-life campaigners who want to see the ban continued and those pressing for America to start paying the agency again.
A new bill introduced by Senator Timothy E. Wirth, Democrat of Colorado, would water down provisions of the 1985 law, arguing that the world must do more to limit population growth to protect the environment and make economic development sustainable.
Even with more aid, Dr. Sadik said she thinks China is unlikely to stabilize its population, now growing by 15 million a year, at 1.2 billion. 
An average family still has 2.58 children and only 20 percent of births are first children, she pointed out.
''Maybe they can stabilize at 1.3 or 1.5 billion,'' she said. 
''But that's a lot more people.''

file: Ulan Bator Journal_With Genghis Revived, What Will Mongols Do_.txt
text:
ï»¿
He may have killed people by the millions, but he was also a great nationalist and one of the most brilliant commanders in history. 
So, in one of the most unusual political rehabilitations in any Communist country so far, Genghis Khan is re-emerging as a national hero.
Two of Mongolia's hottest pop songs are about Genghis, the warrior who nearly eight centuries ago founded the Mongol Empire, which eventually stretched from China to Hungary. 
A new vodka and hotel are being named for him, and historians are searching for his grave so that they can build a museum on the site.
This rediscovery of Genghis, after decades in which he was ignored by Mongolia's Communist historians, is just one example of the resurgence of nationalism that is sweeping this longtime Soviet satellite.
The pro-democracy protests that began in December have led the country on a path toward free elections, but, perhaps more worrisome for Mongolia's neighbors, they have kindled a powerful nationalist movement.
Â 
'Good Grounds to Worry'
Some of this nationalism is already rubbing off in small ways on the 500,000 Mongols who live in Soviet Asia - they are studying their history and culture more than ever -but their numbers are small and for now they are far from the top of the list of President Mikhail S. Gorbachev's problems.
China, on the other hand, has about 3.5 million Mongols, mostly next door in Inner Mongolia, and many Western diplomats and Chinese and Mongolian officials see a significant risk that Mongolian nationalism could spread across the border.
''I think the Chinese have good grounds to worry,'' a Mongolian official said in an interview. 
The risk is generally seen as coming from two sources. 
First, the ouster of the Communist leadership here by a democratic opposition may inspire Chinese dissidents. 
Second, the rising tide of nationalism could provoke ethnic unrest in China.
Â 
Old Script Is Returning
For those Chinese who come to Mongolia these days, the signs of the new nationalism are everywhere. 
Even the maps may have to be altered, for Mongolians are talking about changing the names of several cities, including the capital - Ulan Bator means Red Hero - to their pre-revolutionary names.
The traditional script, which resembles Arabic but is written vertically, is also returning to vogue. 
Four decades ago, Mongolia adopted the Cyrillic alphabet, but these days more and more signs are written in the old script.
''I don't know when it will happen, but I'm sure that the old writing will again become the official script,'' said Daavaasambou, director of Mongolia's state museum.
''Mongolia has a world-famous history,'' Mr. Daavaasambou added. 
''But the leaders didn't pay enough attention to history, and they pointed out only the bad side of Genghis Khan, not his good side. 
It is connected to the Stalinist policies implemented here.''
Â 
Critical View of Genghis
Mr. Daavaasambou seemed a trifle embarrassed when a visitor pointed out that the museum itself perpetuated the official line; only one room in the three-story structure is devoted to Genghis Khan, and much of the information is critical. 
Facing a portrait of Genghis is a painting of a dead warrior, with the inscription ''Let there never be war.''
Next to it is a quotation from Karl Marx that refers to Mongols as a warmongering tribe.
''We will take down that quotation from Marx,'' Mr. Daavaasambou said. 
''In its place we will put up a sign with the words of Genghis Khan, 'I do not fear death for myself so long as my nation may live.'
''
In the last few months, even the official press has taken to referring to ''Lord Genghis Khan,'' and a Buddhist revival is under way after a long period of religious suppression. 
Until the 1921 Communist revolution, Mongolia had about 800 monasteries and some 100,000 monks. 
But the authorities suppressed religion, and now there is only one monastery, with 110 monks. 
In the last few weeks, the monks have hatched plans to reopen many monasteries that were closed.
Relations between Mongolia and the Soviet Union may also be touchy in the future because there are growing accusations that the Soviet Union has exploited Mongolia economically. 
One of the mysteries of Mongolia is how a country with 2 million people and 24 million head of livestock can have meat shortages; the answer is that a large amount of meat is exported to the Soviet Union.
Â 
Tougher Bargains Expected
In fact, the Soviets give large amounts of aid to Mongolia, and it is not entirely clear which country is getting the better deal. 
But in any case, Mongolian leaders have been criticized for not standing up to Moscow in negotiating trade agreements, and it is certain that Mongolia's new leaders will drive tougher bargains.
There also seems to be considerable enthusiasm here for the scheduled departure in 1992 of the last Soviet military forces based here. 
But Mongolian officials take pains to point out that theirs is a tiny nation, and that China in particular has only grudgingly given up its claims to sovereignty over their country.

file: We Must Change Our Lives.txt
text:
ï»¿
FREEDOM IN EXILE
The Autobiography of the Dalai Lama.
Illustrated. 288 pp. 
New York:
A Cornelia & Michael Bessie Book/
HarperCollins. $22.95.
Â 
MY TIBET
Text by His Holiness
The Fourteenth Dalai Lama of Tibet.
Photographs by Galen Rowell.
162 pp. 
Berkeley: Mountain Light Press/
University of California Press.
Â Â $35.
Perhaps the time has come when the world will lend a more sympathetic ear to the message of the Dalai Lama. 
His two main concerns for the last four decades have been the same: nonviolence as a way of relating to others - even to nonhuman sentient beings - and an attitude toward life that involves care for the environment. 
These were the messages he brought with him to the West to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989; they are the messages he develops in ''Freedom in Exile,'' his autobiography. 
The world may be ready to listen because more people are convinced today that such messages are needed if the future of this planet is to be assured. 
The timing of the autobiography is perfect. 
What may have seemed too idealistic and naive in the past is now seen by many as the only way to assure peace and preserve life on earth.
The timing of this volume is important also because of the new euphoria over the freedoms acquired by many nations in Eastern Europe in the past year. 
There is a solid hope that this phenomenon of the human spirit reaching toward freedom is but a glimpse of the beginning of even more manifestations of ethnic, racial, national and religious aspirations. 
Could Tibet finally hope for new freedom too?
There is every reason to expect that world pressure will mount in that direction, even though some Western nations fear that China will be offended by such a move. 
The Dalai Lama's book is a political one. 
For three decades he has traveled the globe to keep alive the world's interest in his nation's plight. 
This book is a call for freedom.
Tibet's loss of freedom is the most dramatic event in the life of the 14th Dalai Lama. 
When he was born to a family of small farmers on July 6, 1935, as he explains, there was no way for anyone to know he would become the Dalai Lama. 
However, two years before his birth, the 13th Dalai Lama had died. 
Several years later, according to custom, a search party of high-ranking Buddhist monks, guided by the state oracle and acting on what they saw as special signs, fanned out through Tibet looking for a child whom they could recognize as the previous Lama's reincarnation (as the Dalai Lama says in his book, he is believed by his followers to be the reincarnation of all 13 of his predecessors, the first having been born in 1351).
His explanation of these matters is forthright. 
And the writing is remarkable in that he says at the outset that he wrote directly in English, a difficult task, he adds, since ''my ability to express myself in this language is limited. 
Furthermore, I am aware that some of the subtler implications of what I say may not be precisely what I intended. 
But the same would be true in a translation from Tibetan.''
His story of how he was recognized as the new Dalai Lama and of his installation in the mighty Potala Palace in Lhasa as his nation's leader is well known from the memoirs of several Europeans who were there at the time. 
But he has retained much of the freshness of the child's view of what was happening to him, and his account is moving. 
It is also often amusing, especially when he tells of his famous fascination since childhood with everything scientific and technical - a passion that has led him to become an expert at repairing watches since he was 8 or 9. 
It also led to a hilarious collision with a tree when, as a boy of about 13, he sneaked into the palace garage and took one of only four motor vehicles in all of Tibet out for a private joy ride.
He had not much more time for such carefree fun. 
After the Communists came to power in China in 1949, one of their first moves was to make a claim on Tibet. 
Tibetan officialdom ended the regency that operated the Government on behalf of the youthful Dalai Lama, and, at an age when most Americans are in high school, he became the absolute ruler of Tibet. 
His book tells an impressive story of the education of this young monk-monarch as he tried to negotiate with the Chinese and to save his country. 
Finally, in 1959, with Chinese forces lobbing shells inside the compound of his summer palace, he consulted his oracle, and then he and a group of his closest advisers made their way across the Himalayas into India. 
Through the years they were to be followed by more than 100,000 escaping Tibetans, and today they occupy the Indian town of Dharmsala, where the Dalai Lama has his headquarters, and 50 other refugee centers.
The enormous destruction of Tibetan religion and culture wreaked by the Chinese is well attested to by many refugees, and by visitors to Tibet. 
But there are things no conqueror can obliterate, as is immediately evident in ''My Tibet,'' a volume of photographs taken in recent years by Galen Rowell, with a text drawn from interviews with the Dalai Lama or essays written previously by him. 
Mr. Rowell has caught the natural beauty of that nation as no other photographer has done before. 
Its mystical qualities are a combination of ruggedness and serenity. 
The pictures also testify that the faces of the Tibetan people have not changed from past years. 
They remain fresh and wholesome, shy and inward looking, full of fun and hidden sentiments. 
Mr. Rowell's rich color pictures of the people can be profitably compared with the collection of black-and-white historical photographs to be found in another volume, ''Tibet: The Sacred Realm. 
Photographs 1880-1950,'' first issued seven years ago and recently reprinted by Aperture. 
The conditions of life for Tibetans may have changed, but the great human qualities of these people have not; they glow from the pictures. 
Mr. Rowell's photographs, whether of nomads or the abundant animal life or landscapes and town scenes, reveal changes but they also underscore the idea found in the Dalai Lama's comments on each one - that there are hidden and enduring truths to be found here.
In the three decades since his escape, the Dalai Lama has traveled throughout the world studying, teaching and conferring with members of many religions - and always seeking the world's help in restoring his country to its people. 
But even if more political freedom should come to it, the road to liberation for Tibet will not be an easy one. 
''Freedom in Exile'' shows that the author is aware of the cultural gaps between traditional Tibetan Buddhism and the scientific approaches of the West. 
The long isolationism of Tibet is now over, but the struggle to come to terms with the advances in science and psychology that have occurred in the world is only beginning. 
How much of the old ways can survive not only the Chinese Communist domination, but the scientific and psychological pressures of the whole of Western culture?
It will be more difficult to vindicate rule by oracles, for example, in an age that seeks psychological examination and scientific proof for all such phenomena. 
The rest of the world is unlikely to be convinced that a society and its government should be based on the search for reincarnations of the great leaders of the past. 
Though one admires the foresight of the Tibetans in the past, in raising up and training leaders from childhood, one is struck by the difficulty of combining this method with the democratic ideals that now permeate Western culture and that will continue to dominate the world. 
The Dalai Lama is aware of these problems; to his credit he states that he is not afraid to face them squarely. 
It is evident to him, as to everyone, that even if he is allowed to return to Tibet and lead his people again, there will be no return to the old ways. 
One would hope, however, that the Tibetan experiment of trying to relate the spiritual to the concrete political realities of the world today would come to benefit all nations and all cultures.
There are some trenchant criticisms in this book of the West, for its lack of spiritual roots like those that nourish Tibet, and it is wholesome for us to hear them. 
But there are also some acknowledgments that Buddhists, and especially Buddhist monks and nuns, have something to learn from Western religions about translating the contemplation of goodness into practical action. 
It is the wish of the Dalai Lama, and, one would hope, of all genuine spiritual leaders, that religion can continue to give to all human beings a sense of the value and dignity of life, of the need to treat the world as sacred and of the desire to live in peace and harmony. 
The vision he has brought down from the roof of the world to the world he is exiled to has been broadened, but not lost.
It is good that the Dalai Lama has found currents in the West, including Western monasticism itself, that are points of contact with his own culture. 
Although the anthropology and the concept of the deity that lie under the two kinds of monasticism are different, the concept that the inner workings of the human spirit must be a part of the full equation of what human existence is all about, and that the human person cannot rely totally on materialism and external stimuli for fullness of life, forms a common ground in all monasticism. 
And it is to be hoped that more contacts between these two traditions will take place. 
Those that have already occurred - I presided over the first international meeting of Catholic and Buddhist monks, in Bangkok in 1968 - have enriched members of religious communities on both sides.
On the other hand, the total domination of intellectual life by monasticism that so characterized old Tibet will, I can safely say, never return. 
Studies for all monks must now go beyond the philosophical and mystical to the scientific. 
By the end of his autobiography it is clear that the Dalai Lama recognizes, as many religious leaders in the West do, that the education of people whose lives are dedicated to religion must change greatly. 
The challenge, for him and the Tibetan Buddhists, as for us in the West, is to retain the best from the past and find new freedom for it to evolve.
Â 
'THERE IS TOO MUCH DEVOTION TOWARD ME'
The Dalai Lama wrote ''Freedom In Exile,'' his autobiography, ''to counter Chinese claims and misinformation they spread about Tibet's history, culture and religion,'' he says, ''and to tell the truth about Tibetan independence.''
In an interview this month at Middlebury College in Vermont, where he was attending a conference on religion and environment, the winner of the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize said: ''Tibet has always been a separate, independent country from China. 
Sun Yat-sen, the father of Chinese democracy, considered Tibet a foreign nation, as did the Chinese Communists before their invasion began in 1949.''
Looking forward to a day when the Chinese occupation of Tibet might end, the Dalai Lama, who wants people to see him as ''a simple Buddhist monk,'' said he would step aside as ruler: ''If I return as the leader, it would be an obstacle to developing a genuine democracy in Tibet. 
There is too much devotion toward me. 
It would be better if I remained outside the Government.''
But, he added, the position of himself and other religious leaders, who traditionally governed the country, ''would be up to the Tibetan people.''
Soon after he fled Tibet in 1959, he wrote an autobiography, ''My Land and My People.''
But in the 1980's a British journalist, Alexander Norman, suggested it was time for a more complete account. 
They worked together on the book. 
Mr. Norman taped the Dalai Lama for several hours at a time and prepared a manuscript from the tapes, which they later rewrote together.
The Dalai Lama now has his headquarters in Dharmsala, India, where he tries to keep abreast of events in his country, in part by personally interviewing every refugee who manages to escape about the fate of families and villages under the Chinese occupation. 
He says there has been a massive deforestation as the Chinese have clear-cut millions of acres of Tibetan forests to sell lumber on the export market; and they are grazing dense herds of sheep on the fragile Tibetan grassland, causing rapid erosion. 
But more devastating has been the continuing oppression of the Tibetan people and suppression of religion and culture. 
Refugees say advocates of independence are routinely jailed and tortured, including many Buddhist monks and nuns. 
News of such events rarely shows up in the news media around the world, the Dalai Lama says. 
''We need to raise world awareness about Tibet, to tell the truth about what is really happening under the Chinese. 
An ancient nation with a precious culture is almost dying.''
DANIEL GOLEMAN

file: With Its Population Still on Rise, Beijing Pushes One-Child Family.txt
text:
ï»¿
Throughout China's vast countryside, it is often not so much democracy that stirs emotions as it is the desire to procreate, and few policies cause more heartbreak than the Government's family planning measures.
These days there are signs that the one-child policy will be carried out more rigorously. 
The number of women of child-bearing age is climbing dramatically, leading China to exceed its population targets, and the Government is now calling for tougher enforcement of family planning measures.
Â 
'Many Women Are Scared'
Here in Sichuan Province, as in most of the nation's countryside, population control has caused a mixture of anger, support, frustration, enthusiasm, deviousness and pain. 
Many Chinese intellectuals endorse the policy and believe it has given new hope for their country's long-term development, but it has also ruined marriages, intensified sexist attitudes and led to murder, bribery, abandonment and countless battles between mothers and daughters-in-laws.
"Sometimes the women cry, sometimes they don't," said a woman from Chuan Shi village, here in Guangan County, as she described the pressure on women to have abortions. 
"They dispatch more than a dozen people to your house all at once. 
They don't beat you, but they scold you, and many women are scared and just go to the hospital."
The case of Qi Yongxin, a peasant in Donglou village in Henan, shows how deep passions can run. 
When his wife became pregnant a year ago with his fourth child, a neighbor reported her to the authorities. 
The officials then pressured her to abort it, and Mr. Qi, his father and sister were so enraged that they beat the neighbor to death and crippled his wife and three-year-old child.
Mr. Qi was sentenced to death in March, according to the Peasants Daily, which reported the incident.
There have long been criticisms abroad of China's one-child policy, and the United States has suspended its contribution to the United Nations Family Planning Program because of allegations that the program was bolstering a coercive policy in China.
But the family planning policy has made substantial progress over the last dozen years, with the average number of babies per woman dropping from five or six in 1970 to two or three now. 
Without population control, 240 million more Chinese babies would have been born over the last two decades, official reports say.
Soaring populations and insufficient farmland are a major problem in many developing countries, and supporters of the program say that China has come to grips with the problem better than most -- giving its present and future generations a greater opportunity to rise above the poverty and misery that traditionally was often their lot. 
Most urban Chinese now seem to accept the idea that they can have only one child, and even in the countryside people desire fewer children than their parents had, although they still frequently want more than the Government allows.
Some Chinese describe the policy in terms that Americans might use about the income tax: fundamentally necessary, but they would rather it not apply to them personally. 
Still, others say that in many rural areas, where people are less educated, the policy is simply unpopular.
Â 
2.25 Children Per Woman
The one-child policy is a misnomer in many cases, because there are many exceptions and Chinese women have, on average, 2.25 children. 
Partly because the average is so much higher than one, the Government has had to abandon its original projections.
China is now expected to break the 1.2 billion barrier by 1995, and to approach 1.3 billion by the year 2000, the official newspapers announced in April. 
In contrast, the Government originally planned to keep the population below 1.2 billion by the year 2000.
China's population is now about 1.14 billion, in a territory slightly larger than the United States, but with far less arable land.
Will the missed targets prompt a new crackdown?
So far, the Government has called for tighter controls, and there seems to be a greater attempt to raise fines for evasion and to limit the number of cases where second and third children are allowed.
Official press reports have also called for more spending on family planning, which currently receives less than one percent of the central budget. 
But so far officials deny that a new crackdown is imminent, and there is no sign of another "high tide" of the kind that a decade ago led to many forced abortions in Chinese villages.
Peasants, officials and others interviewed during a weeklong tour of Sichuan Province, and in other parts of China in recent months, said that it was quite rare for the authorities to drag a woman to the hospital to undergo an abortion, but that it still happened.
"Last year there was a forced abortion in my village," said a young woman from Hongjiang Village in Sichuan. 
"More than a dozen cadres went to the woman's house and forced her to go to the hospital for the abortion."
Officials do not disclose national statistics on forced abortion, but Zeng Jian, the director of family planning for Guangan, said that in 1990, the county had "about 100 forced abortions."
This represented about 3 percent of 3,200 abortions that took place in the county in 1990. 
The phrase in Chinese that Mr. Zeng used normally suggests compulsion or physical force, rather than simply pressure tactics.
He added that last year, Guangan, with 1.09 million people, had only 200 unauthorized births, compared to 15,000 within the plan.
Â 
Other Government Tactics
Peasants also described other tactics, such as demolishing houses, confiscating furniture or electrical appliances, or beating the husbands of those who violate the policy.
"They dig a hole in the wall of your house, stick your head through and beat you on the backside," said a peasant from a Shandong Province village wih about 600 families. 
"It happened twice this year in my village."
In recent interviews, Chinese from Sichuan, Anhui, Shandong and Fujian Provinces all reported that demolition of houses was one method that officials sometimes used to deal with peasants who would not or could not pay the heavy fines for breaching the policy.
"It happens every year, but not that much," said a 23-year-old woman from Qingkang village in Guangan County.
Both officials and many peasants, however, say such methods are used infrequently. 
Indeed, visits to villages in many parts of China suggest that unauthorized children are far more common than destroyed houses. 
It is common in some rural areas to see couples with three children, occasionally even four, and local officials are often willing to charge a fine and look the other way.
Â 
Pursuasion, More Than Force
"If they refuse to pay the fine, their radio set and TV may be taken as mortgage -- yes, I've seen this in some places, but it is quite rare," said Shen Guoxiang, the spokesman for the State Family Planning Commission in Beijing. 
"It is quite common to persuade a woman not to have another baby when she wants to have it. 
But it is rare to drag the woman by the hand and force her to have the abortion."
The most common way of persuading couples to have fewer children is simply to offer a series of incentives and fines, and if these fail, to turn to pressure tactics aimed at making people feel guilty if they breach the policy. 
Here in Sichuan, which has a population of 108 million, one-child families get a wide range of benefits. 
These vary but can include monthly subsidies of $1, higher retirement pensions for the parents, greater allocation of land, lower grain taxes and easier access to good schools.
A fine for a child born out of the plan can amount to up to two year's income, but villages tend to set their own fines. 
Some even offer installment plans for families that cannot pay the fine in one lump sum.
Â 
Monitoring System
The incentives are linked to an efficient monitoring system -- which includes about 13 million volunteers -- intended to detect pregnancies as soon as possible. 
In Guangan, villages and townships keep lists of all the women of child-bearing age, and oblige them to undergo gynecological check-ups every three months -- apparently to insure that no one conceals a pregnancy.
One of the most effective methods of preventing unauthorized pregnancies is obligatory sterilization of couples who have already had two or more children. 
But it is common for mothers to flee their villages when they are summoned for sterilization or when they are expecting a baby outside of the plan.
In Guangdong's Wuhua County, last July's census workers discovered that over the years nearly 38,000 children had secretly been born and not registered with the authorities, according to a recent report in the Nanfang Daily.
The most common reason for couples to breach the policy is that they want a son, to continue the family name and ancestry. 
In Chinese tradition, daughters are married out of the family, while sons remain to care for their parents in their old age. 
So parents often keep having children until they have a son.
In some areas, family planning is loosely implemented because the officials themselves do not consider population control a priority or because their family members protest. 
Some peasants say that local officials set an example of evading the family planning controls, so that no one else wants to adhere to the rules either.
In Sichuan's Bai Mao township, Liu Anxiu, the 26-year-old daughter of the village Communist Party leader, acknowledged that she had given birth to two children -- she had to pay a fine of $153 after the second one. 
Ms. Liu's father was in a tough position to urge other villagers to have only one child.
Then, because her children were both daughters, Ms. Liu considered trying again for a son. 
Eventually her relatives dissuaded her, saying it would reflect badly on her father if she had a third child.
"They kept telling me that the children of officials shouldn't have more children," said Ms. Liu. "So I had to listen to them."
NEXT: Millions of baby girls are missing.

file: Yangpu Journal_Months or Millennia After Flood, the Poor Endure.txt
text:
ï»¿
The only solution to her family's problems, Wan Ziyu said glumly, was for her to die.
"Every day I live is a burden for my son," said Ms. Wan, her white hair and wrinkled face betraying her 80 years. 
She looked down at her four-inch long feet, bound and crippled when she was a child, and said, brooding, "It's better for me to die as soon as possible."
The family has always lived on the edge of poverty; what pushed them over was a disastrous flood in eastern China in the summer of 1991. 
The flood, the worst in 100 years in Anhui Province, killed more than 5,100 people, caused $14 billion in economic losses and disrupted the lives of 220 million people.
Â 
Resilience Amid the Debris
The Chinese authorities promptly banned foreign reporters from the area, so the flooding attracted little attention around the world. 
But even now, 15 months later, in what local officials say is the first visit by a Western journalist, it is obvious that the area was devastated and that many peasants will not be able to recover for several more years.
The flooding is also testimony to the legendary resilience of the Chinese peasantry, for some villages are resprouting from the mud and will soon be sturdier than ever. 
International aid experts give the Chinese authorities good marks for organizing relief efforts, and there were no epidemics of disease among the tens of millions of people who lost homes.
Still, that is small consolation for Ms. Wan. She lives with her son and grandson in a mud hut that was supposed to be their temporary quarters to get them through last winter. 
It will have to shelter them this winter as well, and the family has no idea when they will have the $2,000 needed to build a brick home.
Â 
House Is Beyond Reach
"It's far more than we can afford," said her son, Wang Daoyun, who is 44. 
"There's no way we can build a permanent home until my son grows up."
The problem, Mr. Wang said, is that he has less than one-sixth of an acre and he is the only able-bodied person to provide for his mother and his child.
That was bad enough, but then the floods destroyed his home and virtually everything he owned. 
Now even an education for his son, a fourth-grader, is becoming a luxury.
"Already, the boy's school fees are 70 yuan a year," Mr. Wang said, "and next year it'll be 100 yuan. 
I can't pay that much."
(Seventy yuan is equivalent to about $12.75.)
Flooding is an integral part of Chinese history: one of the earliest names in the fog where history emerges from legend is the Great Yu, a heroic emperor who supposedly tamed a great flood in the 23d century B.C. the most capricious river is the Yellow River, which silts up and overflows the dikes to find a new course to the ocean.
When nonstop rains beginning in May 1991 made it clear that flooding in Anhui was inevitable, the Government opened floodgates and cut through dikes so the worst damage would be absorbed by villages like this one rather than by big cities downstream.
This almost certainly minimized the cost in lives, but it also meant that those who suffered most were those who had the least to start with.
"The flood left my rice paddy covered with sand, so that all I can plant is sweet potatoes and rape seed," Hu Changcui, a woman of 56, said as she stood in a crude brick shelter that serves as living quarters until the family can rebuild a home.
"And my son is 23 years old and not yet married!
Of course, we'll have to wait until we can build a house before he can think of getting married."
Â 
The Money Is Running Out
Throughout Anhui Province, 600,000 people are living in temporary housing: straw shacks, mud huts, brick shelters or canvas tents. 
About 700 clinics have yet to be rebuilt, along with 300 schools.
"We still have plenty of needs, but we're about out of funds," said Ye Ruqiang, deputy director of Anhui Province's flood disaster office.
The Government almost certainly could have attracted more foreign aid if it had allowed foreign news coverage. 
But instead the authorities seemed embarrassed, and chose to turn the floods into a huge propaganda effort to improve the image of the army, whose reputation had been sullied when it fired on crowds of pro-democracy protesters around Tiananmen Square in 1989.
The People's Liberation Army played a central role in flood relief and unquestionably saved thousands of lives, and special television programs hailed the soldiers' heroism.
Some families have already bounced back and seem in better shape than ever.
Â 
Now, Let's Find Wives
Miaoqian, a village of 8,000 in in an old lack bed in northern Anhui, has risen anew less than a mile from the old site.
"This is much better than my old house," Li Decao, a 36-year-old peasant, said as he showed off his new two-room house, with a pig and a few hens in the back yard.
Yang Chuanzao, the 30-year-old Mayor, said that soon after the disaster, the number of marriages dropped, because local people could no longer afford to hold a wedding festival and set up a new house. 
But he figures local youths will have more luck finding partners once they are settled in their new homes.
"It's definitely a bit easier for the young men to find a wife now," he said. 
"You're more attractive when you live in a brick house than when you live in a grass shack."

file: Approaches To Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE are three ways of entering Tibet legally, and on each of three trips I have made there as a budget traveler, I have used a different route.
In 1992, on my first trip, I entered from Nepal, joining a tour because of Chinese regulations. 
I chose the Arniko Travel Agency in Katmandu and acquired a week's visa extension in Tibet beyond the departure of the tour. 
We traveled by hired bus from Katmandu to the unpaved climb to Zhangmu across the border in China. 
The next day we ascended the perilous gorge filled with trees, ferns and tumbling water. 
We stopped at mud slides to help local people heave rocks into the road so we could continue on our way. 
Cresting the pass, we left the green, water-drenched gorge and entered the Himalayan rain shadow of brown, beige and taupe.
On this route, which took 10 days from Katmandu to Lhasa, the traveler can visit Sakya Monastery and the former monastery city of Tashilhunpo outside Shigatse, once a pretty Tibetan town but now just another Chinese shambles of stained concrete and cracked blue glass. 
Gyangtse, my favorite Tibetan town, half a day's journey farther southeast on this route, has not yet met that fate. 
A stroll down the main street between Tibetan houses topped by rippling prayer flags takes one to the monastery and the Kumbum, a white wedding-cake structure honeycombed with chapels whose walls are bright with 15th-century murals. 
It is the Ste.-Chapelle of Asia.
I lost count of the passes we crossed bumping along over the potholes, but all were spectacular. 
We also drove along the shores of Lake Yamdrok, 40 miles southeast of Lhasa, a flawless turquoise set among jagged white mountains.
When my tour left Tibet, I moved from the Holiday Inn in Lhasa to the Yak Hotel, one of a handful of hotels run by Tibetans that cater to budget travelers. 
I spent the week learning the ropes -- where to eat (at Tashi's), where to shop (the Barkhor), where else to stay (the Banok Shul, the Snowlands or the Kirey). 
On the flight back to Katmandu on Southwest China Air, I was served a meal consisting of a bag of cashews, digestive biscuits, a boiled duck egg, an apple and cough drops. 
Because there was no regulation of carry-on luggage, baggage obstructed the aisle. 
The Lhasa airport was filthy, crowded and inefficient, but the views of the Himalayas during the flight were superb.
Â 
Chengdu
In 1995, on my second journey to Tibet, I flew from Hong Kong to Chengdu, capital of Sichuan Province, in the northeastern corner of China, where, as part of the needlessly expensive package I bought in Hong Kong, I was picked up by a guide with driver and car.
Chengdu, a heavily polluted town, has a number of interesting, rundown Chinese monasteries, such as the Wenshu and the Quingyang, where people worship by lighting joss sticks and prostrating themselves. 
There is also the "cottage" of the famous eighth-century poet Du Fu, where you can rent a fishing pole and fish in the stocked pond that smells of drains.
I waited four days for the Tibetan permit I'd arranged for in Hong Kong. 
At the end of my two-day package at the $100-a-night Chengdu Hotel, where electric wires snake in and out of holes in the walls and a dingy, feltlike carpeting covered the floors, I transferred to the Traffic Hotel by the bus station, a Spartan, clean place where I shared a triple with two other women for $5.45. 
I shared the bathroom, which was down the hall and also clean, with innumerable people.
Finally my visa and ticket arrived, and at 5:30 A.M. I was picked up at the Traffic by my guide, who funneled me efficiently through all the formalities onto Southwest China Air. 
Food and restrictions concerning carry-on luggage had improved 100 percent since my last flight. 
The new airport outside Lhasa was also an improvement.
I was very careful when I picked up my backpack because I could feel an altitude headache lurking. 
I knew from previous trips that bending over would make the top of my head explode. 
By flying in, I had come up too fast to an altitude of 12,000 feet.
On this trip I had organized, with two other Americans I met in Lhasa, an exhausting, adventurous and fascinating month's journey to Mount Kailas -- the holy mountain, considered the navel of the world by Hindus, Jains and Buddhists -- Lake Manasarowar and the Guge Kingdom. 
We traveled in the back of a baby-blue Chinese truck with a motley group of nine Europeans and Americans. 
Flying in meant that I had time to arrange the Mount Kailas trip before my three-month visa expired. 
Again, I flew out to Katmandu, to see Mount Everest up close.
Â 
Lhasa
In October 1996 I made my third trip, coming in overland from China, starting again in Chengdu. 
One cannot yet go by bus from Chengdu to Lhasa, which would be scenically thrilling, if difficult. 
The roads are bad and the Chinese worry about losing foreigners to accidents. 
One can, however, travel from Chengdu to Lhasa in hops, using different forms of transportation. 
Again I started in Hong Kong, this time booking through Time Travel Agency, which got me a flight and a two-month visa in a record eight hours. 
I would at some point have to get a Tibetan permit as well. 
After my previous experience, I knew that in Chengdu, at the Traffic Hotel's agency, I could get a flight to Xining (pronounced syee-neeng), the capital of Qinghai province, the next stop on the way to Lhasa. 
I spent two days in Chengdu arranging ticket, flight and permit.
During the short flight to Xining on Southwest China air, I munched a spicy potato-chip-like snack while looking down on mountains at first partly forested, then drier mountains terraced top to bottom like layers of phyllo dough.
I shared a taxi into town with Cendi and Hay, a Dutch couple I'd met at the Traffic Hotel. 
Xining has a mixed population of Muslims, Chinese and Tibetans. 
The Muslim men wear white crocheted caps; the women cover their hair with flocked black scarves. 
We thought we'd sighted a mosque on the river but it was our hotel. 
The endless stairs passed a floor housing a roller skating rink. 
On the floor that housed the hotel, we were led to a room for three where orange imitation-taffeta curtains sagged askew on a broken rod but the sheets appeared to be clean. 
With no lock on the door, I didn't mind being three in a room. 
The view across the river was of bluffs striated in yellow and red reminiscent of the landscape of Utah.
CENDI, pronounced "Sandy," asked the reception clerk for the name of a good Muslim restaurant. 
We piled into a taxi and for $1.35 were taken to a largely empty restaurant, clean and swagged with red velvet hangings. 
With the help of my Chinese conversation book, we ordered "sheep meat," eggplant, mixed vegetables, steamed bread and rice. 
The "sheep meat," flakes of lamb on toothpicks, was superb.
The next morning Hay, pronounced "Hi," toted my backpack to the train station for me. 
For $22.50 I had a bottom bunk with two blankets in a hard sleeper, Chinese second class. 
Because it was a local, it was relatively empty. 
At first we passed villages of small, flat-roofed brick houses with carved wooden arches and protruding wooden rafters. 
There was piped-in music, nasal American rock and saccharine Chinese pop.
The land became parched, fields disappeared into sloping sand dunes as we passed Quinghai Lake (Koko Nor), the largest lake in China, which contains an island breeding ground for birds. 
Other passengers bought food at the stations through the windows or from a cart that came down the aisle selling snacks. 
Not trusting Chinese dining cars, I had gone to a supermarket in Hong Kong and bought Laughing Cow cheese, Danish camembert, canned tuna, tea bags and a tin of duck with orange rind.
After probably three hours, we entered an area of grasslands where yak grazed. 
Two men sat on the bunk opposite me playing a game akin to checkers, but they had really come to stare at the only Westerner on board. 
The dining car chef came by to have a phrase-book conversation with me. 
Everyone smoked. 
I forbade it in my area, how ever, by pointing at the appropriate phrase in my book. 
My companions were mildly surprised, but willing to go along for the pleasure of staring at me.
We arrived in Golmud, formerly Tibetan, now a Chinese town, a small oasis in a barren area, at about 7 A.M. The Golmud Hotel dorm ($5) housed only a young Japanese man who had worked as a cook's assistant in Milan. 
He was going home to Tokyo to open an Italian restaurant. 
I went over to the office of CITS, the Chinese equivalent of the old Russian Intourist, and booked the last leg of my trip, from Golmud to Lhasa by bus, for $160, including a three-day tour, a low-end hotel and the necessary Tibetan permit. 
One could not just buy a bus ticket. 
My total was an outrageous price, since locals pay $9.50 for the bus.
When I returned to the dormitory, my Japanese friend had been replaced by a young American, Brian, from Oakland on his first foreign trip. 
We went out to the market, where we inspected plastic pails and garish-colored yarns and had an excellent dinner of shredded pork, cloud ears and red tofu at a place around the corner from the hotel.
At 10:30 the next morning we took a van to the bus station, where we were issued bits of paper by female bureaucrats. 
Our fellow passengers were a mixed lot -- four Japanese, Brian, myself, two Tibetan nomad men with long swords in silver scabbards and gold caps on their teeth, and a number of bearded Muslims wearing straw hats over white caps, which made them look Amish. 
One Tibetan, unsheathing his sword, peeled an apple in one long corkscrew.
There were flimsy curtains on the windows and the seats were covered in electric-blue plush. 
The bus started out clean but accumulated cookie wrappers, orange and apple peels, cigarette butts and other garbage. 
Rest stops were rare, so it was advisable to get out for every one of them, and we did, with women going to one side and men to the other (there were no toilets). 
Everybody chain-smoked except the Muslims.
We drove through sand dunes and jagged rock for two hours. 
At 4 P.M. we came to a row of restaurants on one side of the road and a row of white-topped mountains on the other. 
Brian and I watched a man blast a heap of goats' heads with a blow torch, then smash them open for their brains. 
In one restaurant, where the owner's wife fed her baby spoonfuls of soup, we motioned to have our bowls of dried noodles, bought in the Golmud market, filled with boiling water. 
Brian opened the can of stewed duck with orange peel and we feasted.
After dinner, climbing through barren rock, we came round a bend almost hitting a herd of horses. 
By nightfall the road was unpaved and terrible. 
Chinese Army convoys streamed by all the way to Lhasa. 
I slept a little but the road was like corduroy. 
Awakened by a bump, I gazed into a snowstorm thickly covering road and countryside. 
I was cold despite long underwear, sweaters and a down jacket because I had to keep the window open to thin out the smoke.
In the morning it was snowing lightly. 
I took two of Brian's aspirins for my altitude headache, which I wouldn't have had if I'd drunk enough water, but I was worried by the infrequency of the rest stops.
We were surrounded by big hills of velvety green. 
Large black birds with rufous bibs on their chests roosted on electric poles beside the road. 
A herd of antelope burst from a hill, racing us. 
The antelope were replaced by sheep and goats with twisted horns, yaks with babies trotting beside them, and black-and-gray nomad tents.
PASSING a battalion of snowy mountains we saw men and women making prostrations along the road. 
It would be weeks before they prostrated themselves all the way to the Jokhang in Lhasa, whereas we arrived late that afternoon, 28 hours after starting from Golmud, coming in along the ugly new strip of Chinese office buildings. 
I spent a month trekking around Lhasa, visiting temples and monasteries there and in the Yarlung Valley, a day's trip southeast, before flying to Katmandu.
This last is the most rewarding route I've taken into Tibet, since I was able to see countryside while avoiding a tour. 
If it were possible to take a bus from Katmandu to Lhasa without being in a group, I might find that the best way. 
But the next time I go, I will go via Golmud.
Â 
Places to bunk down
The best time for a trip to Tibet is late August through November.
Â 
Where to Stay
CHENGDU, CHINA: The Traffic Hotel: an inexpensive travelers' hotel, charges about $4 for an immaculately clean bed in a triple with bath.
XINING: The Young Fu Hotel: $3.40 will get you a bed in a triple with bath and hot water.
GOLMUD: The Golmud Hotel: There are two hotels next to each other but under one name -- the only place you can stay in Golmud. 
One is cheap, about $2.75 for a bed in the dorm with slept-in sheets and a nasty bathroom down the hall. 
The other is about $8 with cleaner sheets and private bath.
LHASA, TIBET: The Chinese-owned Holiday Inn is about $100 a day. 
The Yak, the Kirey, the Banok Shul and the Snowlands are all around $4.75 for a dorm room. 
Private rooms, single or double with bath are about $22. 
These are Tibetan-run ventures.
Â 
Travel Agents
HONG KONG: Time Travel, 16th floor, Block A, Chungking Mansions, 40 Nathan Road, Kowloon; (852) 2723-9993. 
They can get you a flight to Chengdu within eight hours.
KATMANDU, NEPAL: Arniko Travel, Nag Pokhari, Naxal, Post Office Box 4695, Katmandu; (977-1) 414-594; fax (977-1) 411-878. 
A two-week tour, all inclusive, by bus to Lhasa is around $1,000.

file: As Dalai Lama Woos Beijing, Tibetans Pray for His Return.txt
text:
ï»¿
On an old stone stairway beside the Potala Palace, the empty fortress where the Dalai Lama once presided over Tibet, an elderly woman navigated her way down a long procession of steps after coming here to pray.
"I always come carrying the hope that I will live long enough to see the Dalai Lama here again," said the woman, Chanchup Lhamo. 
"But I am getting old, and now I am afraid I may never get the chance."
Tears spilled down her cheeks.
"People tell me that good things will come in the future," said Mrs. Lhamo, 76, wiping her eyes with the sleeve of her sheepskin-lined robe. 
"But I wait and wait and never see it. 
It never comes."
An intensely religious people who revere the Dalai Lama as a god and a king, Tibetans nurture a fervent desire to see their leader return to the Potala Palace, vacant since the day he fled to India in 1959. 
Many do not hesitate to say they would happily sacrifice all of their material possessions to see the Dalai Lama in Tibet for a single day.
With each passing year, fear grows that any return or visit by the Dalai Lama is less likely. 
Beijing exercises tight control over Tibet and has little incentive to negotiate with the exiled religious leader.
Yet international pressure on China to relax its grip on Tibet has mounted in recent years, and the Dalai Lama himself is proposing a new initiative that he hopes will lead to talks with Chinese leaders. 
Ultimately, he would like to see an agreement allowing more self-rule for Tibet under Chinese sovereignty and, of course, to visit his homeland.
Courting support for his proposal, the Dalai Lama is expected to meet with Vice President Al Gore at the White House during his current visit to Washington. 
During his last visit, President Clinton dropped by, and he may well do so again this time.
Tibetan exiles have said the Dalai Lama would like to meet the Chinese President, Jiang Zemin, at a holy Buddhist mountain in northern China. 
A secluded location where the Tibetan leader can technically travel as a monk, not as a political figure, may be conducive to quiet talks.
On the surface the political atmosphere in China seems more open to negotiations on Tibet than at any time in a decade. 
Within the conclave of Beijing's secretive politics, President Jiang has been steadily gaining power, giving him potential leeway to shift ground on China's most sensitive foreign policy problems, Tibet and Taiwan.
Hopes among Tibetan exiles lifted when Mr. Jiang seemed to respond with mild favor to a suggestion by President Clinton during his visit to Beijing last June that Mr. Jiang someday meet the Dalai Lama, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his nonviolent work to gain greater freedom for Tibet.
But China's position on Tibet has yet to soften. 
Chinese officials have reacted negatively to news reports about the Dalai Lama's new proposal, voicing irritation that it has been discussed publicly rather than sent to Beijing quietly through the informal back channels that Chinese leaders ordinarily prefer.
Essentially, Beijing's position is that it will not recognize the Dalai Lama as a religious leader of Tibetan Buddhists until he declares total allegience to Beijing, affirming that Tibet has always been an inseparable part of China.
For the last 40 years, China's main concern has been to keep a firm political and military grip. 
Even a one-time visit here by the Dalai Lama could set off utter pandemonium among worshipers, who uncontrollably mobbed delegations that included siblings of the Dalai Lama in the 1980's.
Chinese officials have often said they regard the Dalai Lama as an agent of anti-China forces who relies on political and financial backing from large foreign powers, namely India and the United States.
The Dalai Lama's calls for greater autonomy, Beijing insists, are a way to gain international support for his longer-term goal, making Tibet an independent nation, which is Beijing's greatest fear.
So Beijing insists on verbal declarations of allegiance to the Chinese nation by the Dalai Lama and insists on the same from other prominent Tibetan Buddhist lamas, who are considered "living Buddhas," or reincarnations of deceased lamas.
"All living Buddhas have to be patriotic," said Ma Chongying, deputy director of the Minority and Religious Affairs Bureau in Tibet. 
"If you're not patriotic, there's no such thing as being a living Buddha. 
This is an unchangeable principle."
Equally unchangeable, it seems, is the common reverence here for the Dalai Lama, despite relentless denigration by the Chinese authorities. 
A visitor to Tibet who mentions the Dalai Lama's name to a local resident is rountinely greeted with a toothy smile and a big thumbs-up.
No open worship of the Dalai Lama is permitted. 
A favorite practice, displaying his picture, is banned except in private homes. 
Monks and other worshipers sometimes ask visitors for a likeness of the Dalai Lama, but only out of earshot from the men and women in plainclothes who loiter around religious sites in large numbers.
In the long run, Chinese officials evidently hope that the Dalai Lama issue will disappear. 
Looming behind all the current efforts at negotiation is the critical question of succession, traditionally decided through a highly mystical procedure of locating the Dalai Lama's reincarnation in a young boy somewhere on the Tibetan plateau.
Chinese leaders are likely to prevent Tibetan religious leaders from choosing a new reincarnation of the Dalai Lama or to control the process so tightly that Beijing in fact determines the choice. 
The current Dalai Lama is 63.
"When the Dalai Lama dies, he dies," said Mr. Ma, the religious affairs official. 
"There will be no replacement."
Yet at the Potala Palace, a 1,000-room mansion that majestically crowns the entire valley surrounding Lhasa, Tibet's holy capital, pilgrims come each day to worship the Dalai Lama, even if they do not mention his name too loudly while doing so.
Inside one room of the Dalai Lama's former living quarters, a small throne draped with green and white silk embroidery, offset by a long row of gold-encased cabinets filled with Buddhist statues and jewelry, is covered by thousands of white scarves brought by devoted pilgrims.
On a recent morning, an elderly couple dressed in the long black and maroon robes of herdsmen from the countryside stepped forward to prostrate themselves on the worn stone floor. 
Their two children followed suit on the floor behind, as did a granddaughter in a bright yellow parka.
A Lhasa policeman, with a mild paunch and dark sunglasses, watched silently from the back of the room. 
After the family moved on to the next room, he stepped forward and put a 10-yuan note, the equivalent of about a dollar, on a silver chalice.
Â 
Tibet at a Glance
Â 
GEOGRAPHY -- Bordered by the Himalayas, Tibet is often called the Roof of the World. 
It is more than twice the size of France, and has large deposits of gold, copper and radioactive ores.
Â 
POPULATION -- 2.4 million in the Tibetan Autonomous Region, which does not cover the whole of the Tibetan plateau. 
All told, there are 7 million Tibetans in China.
Â 
HISTORY -- A powerful kingdom for centuries, Tibet was ruled by a Dalai Lama from the 17th century, but fell partly under Chinese sway from 1720 until 1911, when Tibetans reasserted their independence. 
After the Communists took power in China in 1949, Tibet became a "national autonomous region" of China in 1951. 
The Chinese suppressed a revolt in 1959, during which the current Dalai Lama escaped to India. 
In 1965, the Tibetan Autonomous Region was formally established. 
During the Cultural Revolution, thousands of Tibetan monasteries were destroyed. 
The ban on the Tibetans' religion was lifted in 1978, but they continue to chafe at Chinese rule.
