file: Asia-Pacific Issue_Journey to a Sacred Mount.txt
text:
ï»¿
ALTHOUGH Mount Kailas, at 22,028 feet, is not one of the highest Himalayan peaks, it is among the world's most beautiful mountains. 
A delicately curved pyramid with a rounded top, its most striking feature is concentric bands of dark rock on which snow accumulates, forming stripes of black and white.
But it is something beyond physical beauty that, for more than a thousand years, has drawn pilgrims, who perform a kora -- a 32-mile walk around the mountain, ascending almost 5,000 feet along the way -- to pay homage to the gods. 
Kailas, the most sacred mountain in mainland Asia, is considered the home of gods of three faiths: Hinduism, Buddhism and Bon, the ancient religion predating Buddhism in Tibet.
Last May, my husband, Philip, and I drove across western Tibet to Mount Kailas (also known as Kailash) and nearby Lake Manasarovar, and to the splendid murals in the monasteries of Tholing and Tsaparang, capitals of the medieval kingdoms of Guge. 
Accompanied by three Sherpas provided by a trekking agency in Nepal, we rode from Katmandu to Zhangmu on the Tibetan border, a trip of seven hours. 
There we met our Tibetan crew and transferred our gear onto a large truck that also carried 10 55-gallon drums of gasoline, since there are no service stations in western Tibet. 
From there, we rode in a Land Cruiser (the terrain makes it essential to travel in vehicles with high ground clearance) with our Tibetan guide and driver.
Upon arriving in Tibet one is catapulted within a few hours to high altitudes. 
Our route lay across the Changtang, the wild, desolate plateau of northwestern Tibet, where on average we traveled and slept at altitudes equal to the more than 14,000-foot height of the Matterhorn.
As we drove across the Changtang I suddenly remembered a line of Pascal from my college French class, about the terrifying immensity of enormous spaces. 
Scoured by fierce winds, under a sky glowing from one horizon to the other with golden light, and set between snowy mountains that seem to float in the blue, the Changtang is an immense space made for the deities with which the Tibetans have populated it through religious beliefs. 
Nearly empty, inhabited mainly by nomads (and, these days, by clusters of Chinese soldiers and officials), the Changtang is alive with spirits.
In May its color was golden, but our guide said that during the summer rains its thin, sparse grass would turn green. 
Wildlife was abundant: kiang (wild asses) ranged in the distance, small, slender gazelles darted across our track and woolly hares bounded away from our vehicle. 
An eagle stood on the ground -- no trees to perch on here. 
Although the land is barren, we saw numerous lakes, each a slash of vivid turquoise, the color so bright it seemed to burn against the golden land.
Across the huge, empty space and in the clear, dry air even a solitary creature, however distant or small -- yak, horse or person -- is startlingly visible, a black shape against the yellow plain, arousing anticipation and excitement. 
At long intervals we would see a nomad in Tibetan dress -- sheepskin cloak, felt boots, fur cap (one man wore a wolfskin cap), perhaps alone on horseback, more often herding yak or sheep. 
We saw one man herding his yaks on a bicycle. 
A herd of the massive, shaggy creatures on the move was an impressive sight.
Occasionally we saw a single nomad's tent or a cluster of two or three, and stopped several times to follow our guide into one, where he would sit cross-legged on a rug on the ground, smoking, offering cigarettes and accepting cups of Tibetan tea (a brew made in a churn with salt and butter). 
The tents, some woven of coarse black yak wool, were held up by wooden poles, with a slit overhead to let out smoke from the open hearth.
In one tent we found only a child and his gaunt, bent grandmother, tending a metal pot steaming on the fire. 
A little portable shelf served as an altar, on which were laid the yak-butter lamps Tibetans use for worship, and an object covered with a white cloth. 
Glancing at her for permission, I raised a corner of the cloth and saw photographs of monks: I then clasped my hands and made the worship gesture of touching head, mouth and heart, evoking a smile from the old woman. 
At another encampment we saw women in spectacular jewelry: silver amulets, necklaces of turquoise and coral and long earrings. 
One had silver coins worked into her braided hair.
We averaged about 18 miles an hour and 156 miles a day, following traces of tire marks considered to be roads. 
We jounced, bounced, pitched and churned in the Land Cruiser; I sat on my down jacket to cushion the shocks, and sometimes posted as if riding a horse. 
Our Sherpas took turns in the extra car seat, otherwise riding in the open back of the truck. 
At day's end their bones hurt, and they were covered with dust.
The austere beauty and silence of the landscape are interrupted at intervals by clusters of square, squat concrete buildings sprouting antennas and satellite dishes -- Chinese Army and Government posts that our guide called "administrative centers."
Sometimes we camped, sometimes we stopped in an administrative center at a guesthouse, a kind of rough Tibetan motel. 
Rooms held a few cots, a little iron stove and a bucket of sheep-dung pellets for fuel; some had an outdoor latrine, some not even that.
The only town along our entire route was Gar (called Ali by the Chinese), with grandiose buildings lining a wide main street. 
We stopped at a large hotel with an imposing facade and a huge, cavernous lobby, where we had some difficulty finding a light bulb for our room. 
None of the toilets were functioning and guests had to use the latrine. 
Guests (who were mainly traveling government functionaries) often use a blowtorch to cook in their rooms, as did our Tibetan guide's cook.
A LONG, tough ride to the western edge of Tibet brought us to the monasteries of Tholing and Tsaparang, where despite severe damage during the Cultural Revolution, there are important murals from the 15th through 17th centuries in relatively good condition; the statues had fared worse. 
The murals depict deities and high lamas and scenes of court life, showing foreign emissaries in Islamic and central Asian dress paying respect to Tibetan royalty.
From there we turned southeast to reach Darchen, the small settlement at the base of Mount Kailas and the starting point for the kora. 
Here for the first time we met other groups of Westerners at the guesthouse, which offered camp beds in narrow concrete rooms and an unroofed latrine outside the gate. 
Strolling through Darchen, carrying a rock or two to ward off the fierce Tibetan mastiffs guarding the houses, we watched a group of nomads separating a large flock; the women, heads and mouths wrapped in huge shawls against the relentless wind and dust, swung ropes to drive the sheep.
Our guide hired a few Tibetan pilgrims to carry our gear for the kora and we started the next morning. 
On the first day we walked about six and a half hours through a long, deep valley between walls of sheer red rock. 
Along the kora route are numerous sites associated with spiritual masters and supernatural beings, where pilgrims perform devotions. 
The east face of Kailas loomed above: a forbidding, serious place, desolate, silent, swept by the wind -- a fit home for the gods.
We followed the orthodox Buddhists, who circumambulate in a clockwise direction, but occasionally we saw Bon pilgrims, who walk counterclockwise. 
In late afternoon we stopped at a little six-room guesthouse belonging to a small monastery, with walls and floors of dried mud and rough wooden planks for a bed, upon which some men in sheepskin cloaks and turquoise earrings, their hair in wild, tangled braids, laid out dirty cotton mattresses and covers for our crew. 
With intense cold and a wind that did not stop buffeting us until early in the morning, my husband and I slept in our tent.
The next morning we rose before 5 to make an early start for the pass one must cross to circle the mountain. 
In late May the pass was still covered with snow and icy patches. 
As we climbed, we passed a woman who was prostrating her way around the mountain, an act of the highest devotion, which can take 13 days or more. 
Making the prayerful gesture of touching clasped hands to head, mouth and heart, and then raising her arms high, she flung herself upon the frozen, rocky ground, then rose, walked the few steps to the place her fingertips last touched, and prostrated herself again. 
She wore a thick apron and canvas shoes on her hands to keep them from being scraped raw.
AFTER nearly four hours, reaching the pass at 18,600 feet, where prayer flags placed by pilgrims and monks fluttered atop a cairn, we shouted "Lha Gyalo!"
(Victory to the Gods!) like all pilgrims. 
The snow and pile of rocks were strewn with colorful scraps of clothing left by the faithful as marks of devotion.
From the pass we descended to another long valley and after nine exhausting hours stopped to camp outside a shelter of mud rooms; we completed the kora at noon the next day. 
We took the standard two and a half days to walk the 32 miles, with an ascent of 4,920 feet, but some Tibetans can do the kora in one.
The weather cleared as we drove southward for 90 minutes to Lake Manasarovar, where we first visited Chiu Gomba, a little monastery (recently rebuilt) perched on a craggy knoll above the plain. 
A group of nomads about to start a circumambulation of the sacred lake were worshiping here, eyes bright with reverence. 
The women wore brightly colored cloaks on which were sewn applique in bold geometric patterns and contrasting colors, such as red and gold on a green background, and many necklaces, amulets and earrings.
From a ridge behind the gomba, we had a splendid view of the lake and of Kailas, rising high above the nearby mountains, an image of utter purity -- inviolate, unclimbed because it is sacred. 
There are no buildings, no hotels or guesthouses, no promenade walk along the lake shore to spoil the prospect, the integrity of this holy place. 
We had spent 16 days in Tibet, driving 1,380 miles. 
We continued on foot with our Sherpas for five and a half days, over 65 miles on some of the roughest trails in Nepal, to the airstrip at Simikot and a flight to Katmandu.
Three colors -- blue, gold and white -- linger in my image of Tibet: the blue of the sky and the unearthly azure of the lakes, the golden plain and golden light, the snowy mountains. 
Silent, often empty. 
Cleaned to the bone by the winds. 
A beautiful, wild place, where the human spirit feels it can stretch without limit. 
And where the Tibetans still believe in their beloved gods and in spirits that cling to the mountains and ride on the wind.
Â 
Arranging for the trek and getting equipped
Â 
Planning a Journey
Our trip for two was organized by Himalayan Explorers, Post Office Box 1737, Sanu Gaucharan, Katmandu, Nepal; telephone (977 1) 422-656, fax (977 1) 471-529, a trekking agency in Nepal that obtained our visas for Tibet and made all arrangements. 
The agency provided our food and sent three Sherpas who cooked, managed our camping and led our return trek through northwestern Nepal. 
We brought our own camping gear, but the agency will supply it if necessary for about $50 a person.
Above the Clouds Trekking, Post Office Box 398, Worcester, Mass. 
01602-0398, (800) 233-4499, is also reported to be another good organizer of similar trekking tours.
Our trip took 25 days (16 spent in Tibet) and cost $4,980 a person, including visas. 
The Simikot-Nepalgang-Katmandu flight at the end cost $180 a person extra. 
We spent about $400 on incidentals, including tips (about $50 for each Sherpa, more for the lead guide). 
Travelers should bring United States currency because traveler's checks are not accepted in Chinese banks in western Tibet.
Â 
Weather and Altitude
In May, the Tibetan plateau was mainly sunny and cool during the day, ranging from the upper 40's to the 60's. 
Temperatures at night were in the 20's or 30's.
Because of high altitude, sunglasses and sunblock for skin and lips are essential; ski goggles or industrial safety goggles and bandannas are helpful against wind and dust, as are eyedrops for irritation. 
The Mount Kailas region can be severely cold and windy. 
Travelers should take warm sleeping bags. 
To walk around the mountain, take warm, windproof clothing and good boots.
Medical care is not available, so a medical kit, including antibiotics, is necessary.
From Kailas you can return to Zhangmu by a four-wheel-drive vehicle. 
If you plan to trek out through Nepal, altitudes will decrease and temperatures will be warmer. 
The exceedingly rough and occasionally dangerous trails of the Humla district make a pair of collapsible trekking poles useful. 
M. R. L.

file: Birthday Party for Dalai Lama Draws Chinese Protest to India.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Government has expressed disapproval over a three-day 60th birthday party for the Dalai Lama here last week at which the exiled Tibetan religious and political leader spoke out against the Chinese occupation of his homeland.
"The birthday celebrations were more than a religious function or birthday reception," a Chinese Embassy spokesman said on Monday. 
"We regard it as political, and we will take up this matter accordingly with the Government of India."
Last week, hundreds of people from Asia, the United States and Europe traveled here Delhi to express support for the Dalai Lama, who won the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize.
Thousands of followers as well as diplomats and officials thronged a reception in the state-run Ashok Hotel to greet him.
"In recent times, unspeakable misfortune has overtaken my country," the Dalai Lama told his supporters, praising India for enabling his refugee community to keep its traditions alive.
"The continued Chinese occupation of Tibet poses an increasing threat to the very existence of a distinct Tibetan national and cultural identity," he added.
He described his campaign as one to "save my people and their unique heritage from total annihilation."
The Chinese Ambassador to India, Pei Yuanying, said, "What we are opposed to is political activity held under the cover of birthday celebrations."
India and China fought a border war in 1962 and began renewing trade and political relations in 1976.
India's position is that Tibet is part of China. 
But it gives support to the Dalai Lama, regarded as the world's most beloved Buddhist monk, to preach Buddhism and speak about his traditions.
The Dalai Lama fled his homeland with tens of thousands of supporters in 1959 when an armed uprising against the Chinese failed, and has since lived in exile in India.

file: BUDDHA VS. BEIJING_ A special report._Booming China Threatens Spirit of Tibet.txt
text:
ï»¿
At daybreak, thousands of Tibetan worshipers march a path that circles this holy city, twirling prayer wheels and murmuring tributes of faith. 
Clad in dark Tibetan robes or silk tunics, they wind their way around a gold-roofed temple where the scent of smoldering juniper branches, a traditional offering, rises from a blackened shrine.
Past a dilapidated Chinese factory, down an ill-paved city street, their daily parade then takes the faithful right by a row of gambling houses and massage parlors that represent the gaudiest element of a growing Chinese presence here. 
Yet few Tibetans even glance into these places of imported debauchery as they walk by, keeping their focus on the sacred trail.
Tibet, a mountainous desert whose people have preserved a remarkably intense form of religious devotion despite decades of persecution by the Chinese, is now in the next stage of a grindingly long battle between Tibetan tradition and Chinese modernity. 
Today it is the onslaught of China's free-wheeling economic boom that most threatens Tibet's resilient Buddhist culture.
"They try to beat us, to silence us, to overwhelm us," said an elderly, dough-faced monk, whispering in a dark corner at Sera Monastery, a sprawling complex at the edge of town. 
"You can see they are not succeeding; just look at all the people who come to worship every day."
Tibet's exiled leader, the Dalai Lama, is in Washington seeking support for his efforts to persuade Chinese leaders to allow more self-rule for Tibet, even under Chinese sovereignty. 
Apart from international pressure, however, Beijing has little incentive to negotiate.
China exercises firm military and political control over Tibet, as it has since 1959, when the Dalai Lama fled to India. 
In the last four years the authorities have sharply tightened restraints on Buddhist monasteries, seen as centers of dissent, and limited the number of monks allowed to worship.
No sign of protest or potential violence is evident in Lhasa today, and for a city that is ethnically divided -- there is a distinctly Tibetan half and a Chinese half -- there is little palpable tension. 
In open-air markets selling fruit, clothing and distinctive Tibetan jewelry, crowds of both groups mix easily.
The authorities still limit access to Tibet, but are cautiously allowing more Western journalists to enter, including the first reporter from The New York Times since 1990.
Yet after decades of trying, Beijing's political and now economic efforts to fully transform Tibet into another province of China still founder on Tibetans' extraordinary religious fervor. 
Religion and culture create such a deep gulf between Chinese and Tibetan ways of life that it is hard to foresee any easy resolution.
The most striking aspect of daily life in Lhasa today is the passionate worship by Tibetans of every station. 
One must rise at dawn to see the daily, two-hour march around central Lhasa that draws thousands of worshipers each day, but thousands more pilgrims who come from elsewhere in Tibet to pray at the region's holiest sites are evident everywhere in town.
All day long at the gate of the Jokhang Temple, the most revered structure in Tibet, dozens of worshipers carry out an act of prostration by lying face down on cold stone, only to stand up again, hands together, and repeat the motion hundreds of times. 
Dirt-poor pilgrims, filthy from weeks or even months of travel, pray next to well-dressed businessmen and women from Lhasa.
"The Chinese don't understand our religion," said Chuni, 25, a health administrator who came to the Jokhang to pray one recent evening, and who like many Tibetans uses only one name. 
"They think we are uneducated and inferior. 
They will never understand."
Â 
The Resentment Wears a Mask
A layer of good-natured Tibetan fatalism, Ms. Chuni said, often shields the animosity that ordinary Tibetans feel toward Chinese. 
Underneath, she said, most Tibetans deeply resent the Chinese presence here.
Tibetans are unlikely to forget the relentless efforts to destroy their culture that came in the years after Chinese forces consolidated control in 1959. 
Calling it liberation, the Communist authorities banned religious worship, demolished monasteries and killed untold thousands of Tibetans who resisted.
Times change, as do methods. 
But China's aim in Tibet remains the same, to integrate it more closely with the rest of "the motherland."
In the 1960's that meant tearing down almost anything old and parroting fanatical political slogans; today it means building almost anything new in the name of economic development.
Officials in the Chinese Government point to the undeniable benefits built with Beijing money in recent years: roads and telephones that allow communication in previously impassable areas, hospitals and schools that offer care and general education in a land that had almost none during the centuries it was run by a theocracy.
Chinese authorities make much of the stubbornly medieval nature of Tibet's old society, where slaves of various grades were taught that they suffered for misdeeds in a past life.
But material gains have come on Chinese terms. 
All Tibetans are required to be literate in Chinese for the best jobs, in government or state industry; few Chinese ever learn Tibetan, even officials who have lived here for decades. 
Schools are theoretically bilingual, but in practice Chinese dominates.
Â 
The Economy: For Whose Benefit?
Many Tibetans, accepting the fact of Chinese dominance, push their children to study Chinese, because it broadens their chances for decent employment. 
Some send their children to study at schools in China proper. 
"I am sad that so many children cannot read or speak Tibetan well," said a 35-year-old employee at a state-run department store, and mother of a 9-year-old girl. 
"But I want what is best for my daughter."
Like many other Tibetans, this woman complained that economic gains in Tibet have overwhelmingly benefited Chinese here, not Tibetans. 
It is hard to measure, since economic status is not measured by ethnic group, but Tibetans uniformly say that unemployment among Tibetans is many times that of unemployment among Chinese.
A senior Chinese leader, Hu Yaobang, deplored the colonial attitude that prevailed among Chinese officials here when he visited in 1980. 
Much has changed in Tibet since then, but perhaps not the mindset of the average Chinese official. 
In a small but telling example, Chinese officials still insist that Beijing time be observed throughout Tibet -- as it is elsewhere throughout Chinese-controlled territory -- even though this means sunrise in November here comes after 8, and sunset after 7.
Although Beijing clearly hopes a rising economic tide will draw Tibetans closer to the Chinese way, local officials assigned here often seem more interested in taking advantage of loose restrictions to make money in any way possible. 
As in most of China, a local official has wide latitude in economic matters, as long as his or her political patron is secure.
An attractive park called Sun Island, where the path of holy worship takes thousands of Tibetans each morning, was converted two years ago into a resort area of gambling halls that operate openly, even though they are technically illegal. 
Across the street is a long row of massage parlors with come-hither names, equally open and, because they are clearly fronts for prostitution, equally illegal.
"Gambling?
How could we allow gambling?" asked Nima Tsering, a Deputy Governor of Tibet, in an interview. 
"No gambling is allowed in China."
Asked if he was truly unaware of what happened on Sun Island, Mr. Tsering quickly backtracked.
"Maybe our supervision is not perfect," said Mr. Tsering, one of many ethnic Tibetans in the Chinese Government here. 
"Maybe this phenomenon does exist in some cases. 
We know about it. 
We're keeping an eye on it, and we'll decide what to do when the time comes."
Many Tibetans are as disgusted by the crass presence of the Chinese here as they are by the fact that Chinese businessmen and workers keep arriving each day. 
Exactly how many Chinese live in Lhasa has become a matter of constant interest.
Official Lhasa statistics record that out of 198,000 current residents, including Chinese workers who have obtained a temporary residence permit, 55 percent are Tibetan and 45 percent are Han, China's dominant ethnic group. 
Yet Mr. Tsering conceded that this figure does not include the innumerable Chinese itinerants who fail to register.
Many Chinese and Tibetan businessmen estimate that at least 60 percent of the people in Lhasa at any given time are Chinese. 
Yet it is hard to know with accuracy because Chinese workers typically stay anywhere from five days to five years.
In addition, Chinese statistics do not include Chinese military personnel. 
International military experts say there are probably about 50,000 Chinese military personnel stationed in Tibet, as well as an unknown number of paramilitary police officers. 
After protests erupted here in 1987 and 1989, however, Chinese soldiers have been ordered to keep out of view as much as possible.
Although outside critics of China's Tibet policy denounce what they see as a monolithic Chinese plan to overwhelm Tibet, the day-to-day reality of Chinese expansion here appears to be relatively limited and haphazard.
Tibet's economy, though growing by 10 percent, reached only $927 million last year, a tiny amount considering that more than half of it came in the form of direct grants from Beijing. 
Yet Chinese businessmen here say there is a larger, unrecorded economy of trading in consumer goods and commodities that draws thousands of businessmen and workers from neighboring Sichuan Province, overflowing with 110 million people, compared with Tibet's 2.4 million.
In fact, several Chinese businessmen here complained that their biggest obstacles here lie not in Tibetan culture, but in the corruption among local officials, who often make money in the form of "fees" that are unlikely ever to appear in provincial balance sheets.
For all the attention and problems that the Chinese presence in Lhasa produces, it represents a small part of the larger picture in what is still a desperately poor region. 
More than 80 percent of the population in China's Tibetan Autonomous Region lives outside cities and towns as herdsmen and farmers with an average income of $10 a month.
The official population of the Tibetan Autonomous Region is only 2.4 million. 
Yet the larger Tibetan plateau, each corner carved into another Chinese province, includes a total population of roughly 7 million Tibetans.
One of the traditions that ordinary Tibetans very much keep alive is to save their meager earnings for years in order to make a pilgrimage to Lhasa. 
Virtually every Tibetan who can comes here to worship.
Â 
Herdsman's Family Who Came to Pray
One recent morning, Thondrup, 57, a herdsman from northern Tibet, described how he had prepared for years to bring his family to Lhasa.
For a total of 11 people, including his wife, 2 daughters and sons-in-law and 5 grandchildren, Mr. Thondrup rented a truck to make the journey. 
It took eight days and nights of terrible roads and volatile weather to reach the capital.
"We came to pray," said Mr. Thondrup as he sat outside the Potala Palace, the former residence of the Dalai Lama. 
"It is the most important thing we do in our lives."
Offering a simple interpretation of the Tibetan belief that an act of worship brings good will that will pay off in a future life, Mr. Thondrup said his family members could improve their karma by visiting each of the main religious sites in Lhasa.
The only other time Mr. Thondrup came to Lhasa, 15 years ago, he came on a combination of horseback, truck and bus. 
It took three weeks each way.
New roads, Mr. Thondrup said, have greatly improved livestock trading in his area and fattened his wallet. 
Yet it has hardly made him more partial to Chinese officials, whom he regards as patronizing and bribe-hungry.
"All they think about is money," he said.
For all the material improvement in Mr. Thondrup's life, like most Tibetans he seems to care far more about prayer and devotion to the Dalai Lama.
"All Tibetans want the Dalai Lama to come home, more than anything else," he said.
In the end, here lies the unsolvable dilemma for the Chinese authorities in Tibet. 
Regardless of the physical improvements that have been made, the health care and the education, and the fast-growing economy, most Tibetans do not hesitate to talk about their religious attachment to the Dalai Lama.
Almost without exception, ordinary Tibetans here eagerly say that they would happily sacrifice all their own material goods, as well as all the modern advances in Tibet, if only the Dalai Lama would come home for a single day.
Asked to consider this quandary, Mr. Tsering, Tibet's Deputy Governor, took a deep breath and exhaled.
"Some people do have this ideal," he said. 
"But Tibet needs to be more modern. 
We need science and technology. 
That was the old society. 
We need a new society."

file: Dalai Lama Finds China_s Threats A Subject for Humor and Anxiety.txt
text:
ï»¿
Among the pilgrims who flock to the Dalai Lama's home-in-exile in these Himalayan hills, many regard him as a living god -- some of them Buddhist monks like the Dalai Lama himself, others refugees from faiths and places far removed from his native Tibet.
Since he fled to India in 1959, the Tibetan leader has grown accustomed to the cult of reverence in which Tibetans and non-Tibetans have enveloped him, especially since his teachings on nonviolence earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989. 
But when the veneration gets a bit too much, the 60-year-old Tibetan has a way of puncturing the balloon.
"In the 1960's, the Chinese Communists described me as a wolf in a monk's robe, as a murderer and a rapist," he said in an interview in an old bungalow here that is part of the compound given to the Tibetans by the Indian Government. 
"Then there are people who call me a Living Buddha."
"But these are two extremes," he said, breaking into a throaty chuckle. 
"In reality, I am just an ordinary human being."
If this were true, the Dalai Lama could contemplate a quiet retirement here, after a life that was never his own from the moment in 1940 when he was installed, as a 5-year-old peasant's son, on the Dalai Lama's throne.
But recent years have underlined his importance as the spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhists, and Beijing's apparent determination to whittle away his influence among the six million Tibetans in China.
The Dalai Lama has rarely been more alienated from the Chinese leadership than he is now. 
In January 1995, 15 years of sporadic and ultimately unproductive contacts with Chinese intermediaries on Tibet's future were broken off by China. 
Since then, China has reverted to a bitter hostility, to the Dalai Lama and to Buddhist institutions in Tibet.
Amnesty International says China began a new wave of arrests among Tibetans monks, nuns and independence activists about the time it broke off talks with the Dalai Lama. 
The rights group has published detailed reports of beatings of those arrested, and Chinese officials warned recently that they would close monasteries and nunneries if resistance continued.
The crackdown is a return to patterns that China has followed for decades. 
Although the repression eased after 1979, when Deng Xiaoping began the dialogue with the Dalai Lama by saying everything was negotiable except Tibet's remaining part of China, the cumulative damage has been enormous.
According to pamphlets issued by the Dalai Lama's office, the Chinese have closed or destroyed more than 6,000 monasteries and killed 1.2 million Tibetans since Communist troops overran Tibet in 1950.
Along with the current crackdown, the old vituperation against the Dalai Lama has crept back. 
Official Chinese diatribes have described him as a "splitist" and a "traitor" for not accepting China's demands that he acknowledge Tibet as "an inseparable part of China."
China also demands that he dismantle the Tibetan government-in-exile in Dharmsala, and "stop engaging in activities to split the motherland," including his frequent overseas trips to promote Tibet's cause.
In November, the confrontation took a turn for the worse when China engineered the installation of its own candidate for the position of Panchen Lama, Tibet's second most important religious official.
The move, seven months after the Dalai Lama announced his own nomineee, left Tibetans with two 6-year-old boys, each identified as the reincarnation of the former Panchen Lama, who died in Beijing in 1989 at age 50. 
The Dalai Lama's choice, Gendun Choekyi Nyima, has disappeared, apparently into house arrest in Beijing, along with his parents and 50 monks and Tibetan laypeople associated with his nomination.
Some Tibetan officials suggest there may even have been moves in the last year by China's security agencies to mount an attempt on the Dalai Lama's life in Dharmsala, or perhaps against senior members of his entourage.
In December, the Indian authorities arrested three young Tibetans who crossed into India from Tibet earlier in the year in the guise of refugees. 
According to Tibetan officials here, two men and a woman, all in their 20's, are being held in an Indian jail after telling investigators they were recruited by Chinese security agencies, trained in techniques of infiltration, intelligence-gathering and weapons-handling and sent here to keep watch on the Dalai Lama.
Tempa Tsering, information chief in the exile government, said diaries taken from the three showed they watched the Tibetan leader closely. 
"They told us that they had been ordered to settle in Dharmsala and wait for further instructions," he said. 
The Indian authorities have tightened the Dalai Lama's security, assigning additional policemen to keep a round-the-clock watch inside his compound in the village of McLeod Ganj, 6,000 feet up in the hills above Dharmsala.
In the presence of a man who bears the titles of Holy Lord, Gentle Glory and Ocean of Wisdom, there is an absence of the portentousness that often accompanies a meeting with a president or prime minister. 
But behind the jocularity with which he greeted a visitor, the Dalai Lama seemed like a man with his patience wearing thin. 
At one moment he was joshing about his chances of living another 20 or 30 years. 
The next he was discussing the possibility that China may have entertained the idea of having him killed.
From what he had been told, he said, the three young intruders had said they had instructions to keep a watch on him. 
But whether this meant they might have planned to kill him was something else.
"I don't consider that someone will want to threaten my life," he said. 
"Personally, I have no enemies."
By discussing the possibility of an assassination attempt, he offered a measure of the distance he and his onetime interlocutors in China have traveled since the 1980's, when they held more than a decade of secret discussions on Tibet.
The talks culminated in 1988 in a speech by the Dalai Lama in Strasbourg, France, in which he offered publicly for the first time a formula he has called "the middle way" -- a future in which Tibet would remain part of China but with wide autonomy in all matters except foreign policy and defense.
China denounced the formula, calling it "a disguised form of independence," but even making the offer came at a cost for the Dalai Lama. 
Tibetan exiles, especially the younger ones, saw it as a betrayal of Tibet's claim to independence.
China's return to a hard-line policy has found its clearest expression in the machinations over the new Panchen Lama. 
Behind arguments about the obscure procedures involved in divining which Tibetan child is the reincarnation of the spirit of the dead lama, the two Panchen Lamas -- China's, and the Dalai Lama's -- seem like an embodiment of the two Tibets, one favored by the Dalai Lama that would be semi-free, the other wholly a captive of China.
To Tibetans, China's willingness to hijack procedures that are at the heart of the mystique of Tibetan faith is almost the ultimate affront, the more so since Chinese statements in recent months have heaped contempt on the boy chosen by the Dalai Lama. 
The Chinese have asserted that he once drowned a dog, "a heinous crime in the eyes of Buddha," and that his parents were "notorious for speculation, deceit and scrambling for fame and profit."
China's nominee, Gyaltsen Norbu, has been presented as a paragon of Buddhist virtues.
"My main concern is for the Panchen Lama himself," the Dalai Lama said, referring to Gendun Choekyi Nyima, his own nominee, of whose whereabouts Chinese officials have professed ignorance. 
The Tibetan leader said he feared that the boy could be subjected to brainwashing.
"It's a clear example of bullying and shortsightedness," he said of China's actions.
Under pressure to find ways of responding to China's assertiveness, the Dalai Lama has been confronted by Tibetan youths who have urged a return to the kind of armed insurgency that was mounted against Chinese rule in the 1950's. 
But these youths, he said, should think things through.
"It's very easy to see these mujahedeen in Afghanistan and the Middle East, but if we really put it in practice -- first of all, sufficient weapons, from where?
And how to send them to Tibet?
Through India?
Impossible. Through Nepal?
Impossible. One or two guns, maybe; nothing more."
In any event, he said, if Tibetans stuck to nonviolence, they would find that things in China would change in ways that would make possible political concessions that are currently unimaginable. 
Behind the stern mask of the current Chinese leadership, he said, there are strong democratic stirrings in China.
"I always believed that the Tienanmen Square massacre was a temporary setback for the democratic movement," he said.
A visitor here does not have to go far to find people, some close to the Dalai Lama, and not all of them young, whose respect for him as a spiritual leader is accompanied by a sense that he is a dreamer. 
Among these people, it was a matter for black humor when the Dalai Lama was quoted recently as saying he expected to be back in the 1,000-room Potala Palace in Lhasa by the end of the decade.
While conceding that this may have been an exaggeration, the Tibetan leader said he still believed that a breakthrough would come within five years, and that he would live to sit once more on the Lion's Throne that is the Dalai Lama's traditional seat of power in Lhasa. 
If people think he is dreaming, he said, they should look at recent history, for example in the former Soviet Union and in South Africa.
"And so it will be in our case," he said. 
"We have had our own dark period for 40 years, but for us too, things will surely change."

file: Echoes of a Fallen Kingdom.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the remote badlands of far western Tibet lie the two remaining sites of the ancient Kingdom of Guge: Tholing, the 11th-century Buddhist monastery that was, in its time, the region's most influential lamasery; and Tsaparang, the old capital of Guge. 
At both sites, now largely in ruins, statuary and dozens of well-preserved murals in the brilliant West Tibetan style offer glimpses of a vanished age.
You are not likely to be jostled by fellow tourists as you move about these amazing remnants of a lost kingdom, since very few people get to this rugged area of Tibet. 
Tholing, near the isolated military town of Zanda, is on an escarpment above the Sutlej River. 
Tsaparang, about 15 miles away, is perched on a lonely crest of towering rock. 
Depending on road conditions, it takes about six days to drive here from Lhasa, the capital of Tibet.
It was in Lhasa last July that my friend Judy and I hired Dorje, a Tibetan guide, and Sonam, a driver, to take us by Land Cruiser to western Tibet. 
It was to be my second trip through the region. 
Along the way, we circumambulated the holy mountain of Kailash, and made a side trip to the monasteries of Tirthapuri and Gurugam. 
Near the village of Nabru we turned left onto a jolting dirt road and headed for Zanda, more than 100 miles away.
We drove through barren mountains in a fantasy of colors. 
On one side of our Land Cruiser was a pale lemon mountain spotted with dark green scrub. 
On the other, a formation of barren rock in mineral hues of green, fawn, red and ash. 
Among nomad tents, yaks browsed on a yellow-green scrim of vegetation. 
Often, we sent goats and sheep scrambling across the road. 
Dogs from the tents chased our wheels, but Sonam, a good Buddhist, was very careful.
We had lunch at a restaurant, which was a box without windows surrounded by black yak-hair tents. 
A man sold us delicious yogurt from the female yak, the dri, and tea to drink or mix with tsampa (ground roasted barley). 
Judy and I pulled out the dried salami I'd transported from Fairway in New York and lunched on yogurt, salami and tea, while Sonam and Dorje kneaded yogurt and butter tea into their tsampa.
After lunch, we descended into the badlands that surround Tholing and Tsaparang. 
From above, the terrain's colors were a tender green and ash. 
Down among the fantastic shapes -- castles, pinnacles, spires, citadels -- cut by tiny streams, they became rose-blush and beige.
Zanda, across a bridge over the Sutlej River, is the usual base for visiting Tholing and Tsaparang. 
As we approached, we could hear the sound of drilling Chinese soldiers from the nearby military garrison.
Once a Tibetan town full of nomads selling supplies from their tents and tables, Zanda is now a small Chinese military town with few ethnic Tibetans in evidence. 
There is one dusty main street lined with concrete-block shops whose goods tumble into the street. 
Shopkeepers sit at their doors playing mah-jongg with their neighbors.
We settled into a clean, inevitably dusty room in the new wing of the Chinese hotel on the main street, the only hotel in town. 
The toilet is an outhouse beside the building, next to the water spigot at which one does laundry. 
Such are the priorities that there was a TV in our room, as well as a pail of water for bathing and a thermos of hot water for tea. 
You are charged what the manager thinks you can pay. 
Bargaining is, therefore, in order. 
We settled on $10. 
The fee for foreigners for seeing Tsaparang -- about $40 at 8.28 yuan to $1 -- is steep. 
In the permit office, on Zanda's only street, the secretary, wearing a pantsuit and garden party hat and without a desk or chair of her own, answered the telephone. 
You receive 10 free postcards with your permit, but that lagniappe doesn't keep you from feeling taken.
The next morning we drove less than an hour on washboard roads to Tsaparang. 
Dorje and Sonam, excited at the opportunity to see Tsaparang for the first time, went off to find the guide who lives near the ruins while Judy and I gazed at the citadel towering above us. 
Except for a small structure at the top painted with traditional Tibetan designs and the gate at its base, the citadel was indistinguishable from the other rocky pinnacles in the badlands. 
It is a mountain among fellow mountains.
Our guide, an elderly man, was impatient at our desire to linger, so we headed up the stone path that led through the ruins.
Most of the buildings, which are either cut from rock or built of mud brick, are in ruins, destroyed during the Cultural Revolution. 
But the three primary chapels, which contain the treasures of Tsaparang, are intact. 
They lie along the path that climbs the mountain like gems strung on a necklace.
The Kingdom of Guge was founded in the ninth century after the assassination of King Langdarma, a persecutor of Buddhists. 
In the 11th century, King Yeshe O, working with the famous Sanskrit translator, Rinchen Zangpo, and the Indian master Atisha, reintroduced Buddhism to western Tibet. 
Soon Tsaparang, and Tholing, also made of mud brick, were built, along with other temples and monasteries. 
The influence of the Guge Kingdom, particularly the monastic center of Tholing, was felt from Kashmir to Assam.
In 1624 Father Antonio del Andrade, a Portuguese Jesuit, found his way to western Tibet. 
Within a few years, he had made so many Catholic converts that local Buddhists became alarmed and called in the neighboring kingdom of Ladakh to drive the new Christians from Tsaparang and the surrounding area. 
The Ladakhis were delighted to have an excuse to invade, and the end result was that the Guge Kingdom, which had tolerated the Christians, was essentially wiped out.
In 1948 a German Buddhist monk, Lama Govinda, came to Tsaparang and Tholing with his wife, Li Gotama, and photographed everything. 
That is the only reason we know what the temples looked like before the arrival of the Red Guards in 1967. 
They destroyed many of the statues and, in Tholing, a number of buildings, before closing down the sites and leaving them to the mercy of wind and weather throughout the years of the Cultural Revolution.
That morning we had Tsaparang's citadel to ourselves, with only the occasional hawk flying above us for company. 
At 14,000 feet, climbing was arduous, but the first site -- the White Temple, Lhakhang Karpo -- was not that far. 
The building is peaceful with slender, red wooden pillars ending in carved capitals, its ceiling composed of intricately painted geometric designs.
With our flashlights (a necessity, since the only illumination in the buildings is from skylights), we could make out the delicate features, fine noses and rounded chins of the Buddha statues on lotus pedestals. 
Two snarling guardians at the entrance, Tandrin in red and Dorje in blue -- their hard lacquered exteriors damaged so that the innards of straw are exposed -- are still vital in their aggressive poses. 
The brilliantly colored murals of gods and goddesses are rendered with great delicacy. 
All spaces are filled with rich painted ornamentation -- animals, flowers, trees, temples, imaginary beasts.
The Red Temple, Lhakhang Marpo, a short distance up the path, is entered through its original wooden doors. 
In the upper left panel a carved Buddha meditates between what appear to be two angels. 
To the left of the entrance, below deities in billowing scarves and elaborate jewelry, are panels depicting horses carrying timber for the construction of the temple, goats with panniers of dirt and the king and queen with visiting dignitaries, assembled for the consecration of the temple. 
Water damage and vandalism in this chapel have been repaired with stunning ineptitude. 
But at least there is no confusion as to what is original and what is attempted renovation.
The Dorje Jigje Lhakhang, a small temple farther along the path, is filled with painting of wrathful Tantric deities, but in small panels to the right of the entrance, is a scene depicting, in minute detail, people going off to market with woven baskets on their backs. 
Finally, at the top of the citadel, a lung-straining climb up stairs and through low-roofed tunnels, is the tiny, red Mandala Lha khang. 
It has no skylight. 
A platform in the middle of the room once was the setting for a three-dimensional mandala. 
Wrathful deities take up the large spaces on the wall, but beneath them are gory and macabre paintings of the eight great cemeteries of India.
We ate that night at a small Chinese restaurant near our hotel. 
We had looked into other restaurants along the main street, but found that most were really brothels for the Chinese military.
The Chinese couple who run this no-name restaurant were willing to let me go into the kitchen and assemble the raw materials for dinner or lunch -- noodles or rice, squash, any unknown vegetable I saw, onions, garlic, lamb or eggs or chicken. 
Sometimes this combination appeared as soup, sometimes as stir-fry. 
Sometimes Judy got all the lamb and I got the egg. 
Sometimes meat and egg were mixed up together. 
One day the wife showed us a potato and made slicing motions. 
We had potato chips with lunch that day. 
The plain meals were never more than $2.
The next morning we walked over to Tholing, which we could see from the second-story corridor of our hotel. 
The monastery, positioned above the Sutlej River, broad and swift-flowing at this time of year, is a complex of rectangular buildings, the most interesting of which is the Yeshe O Temple, with its open mud-brick work and red mud-brick towers. 
The complex is in the process of reconstruction, since the Red Guards tore down much of it, brick by brick.
THE admission fee for Tholing is $8.50, which you pay when you acquire your permit for both Tholing and Tsaparang. 
There is an additional $3.50 to be paid to the tiny, unsmiling caretaker, who is quite willing to let you wander at your own pace. 
Once again, we were the only people going through the buildings.
Rinchen Zangpo was responsible for building Tholing. 
The 15th- and 16th-century murals are like those in the Red and White temples in Tsaparang and represent a synthesis of Himalayan styles from Tibet, Kashmir and Nepal.
The Yeshe O Temple, with its handsome towers, is in the midst of renovation. 
New doors, with locks and brighter red paint, have replaced the rickety old ones through which I had seen, on a journey to Tholing in 1995, the row of holes from machine-gun bullets that had shattered the old images. 
In the shape of a mandala, the building used to contain several chapels. 
Other, reconstructed buildings in the complex were, like the Yeshe O, not yet open.
The Lhakhang Karpo and the Dukhang, however, were open. 
Once again, a powerful flashlight is essential. 
These temples are similar to Tsaparang's -- high ceilings, slender red wooden pillars and geometric decorations on the ceiling. 
The Lha khang Karpo is distinguished by two crudely carved deodar pillars on either side of its front door. 
The portraits inside of Tsong Khappa, Sakya Panchen and other Buddhist prelates, were painted in the 15th and 16th centuries, but still look fresh.
In the Dukhang, a single-story assembly hall, there is a series of portraits of important figures, including Yeshe O, the founder of the monastery, meticulously painted in the clothing of their time. 
Deities on the other walls sit serenely, garbed in magnificent textiles and jewelry.
Slowly our last flashlight batteries failed as we moved from picture to picture. 
Regretfully we left Tholing and wandered back to the hotel, past the watermelon seller and the dusty shops to our hotel and dinner.
After a terrible dust storm, so acute that our little restaurant had to close its door and light candles, a gentle rain fell during the night. 
The following morning we had a last glance at Tholing as we took our backpacks down to the Land Cruiser. 
We drove out through the badlands and into the mineral-colored mountains, washed in brilliant light.
Â 
If you go
The best time to travel in Tibet is from June to October. 
Trips to Tholing and Tsaparang can be arranged through travel agencies in Lhasa; we used the Shigatze agency, in the Yak and the Snowlands Hotels.
If you hire a Land Cruiser, you will also hire a truck. 
The latter is an emergency vehicle to haul you out of rivers and to carry extra fuel and baggage. 
The package includes the guide and the two drivers.
All of this plus the permits for each of the areas you will travel through will cost about $4,000 to $5,000. 
If you pack more people into the Land Cruiser it will cost less per person but you will be crowded under difficult conditions.
The pilgrimage to Mount Kailash is usually included in this trip. 
Returning by the shorter, smoother southern route might bring the price down a little. 
The cheapest way to go is hitchhiking (as a woman, I never felt threatened), preferably on China Mail trucks; you can bargain with the drivers, but the typical fee for a long trip is $20. 
You will also need a permit for Mount Kailash (travel agencies usually sell them). 
Other permits ($5 to $10) can be acquired in transit.
The government hotel in Tsaparang should cost around $10 a night. 
Like the restaurant, it is nameless. 
Meals cost about $2. 
Your guide will find a hotel and restaurant for you.

text:
ï»¿
WHAT makes the subject of Tibet such a tricky one for filmmakers is that the moral lines of right and wrong in the China-Tibet confrontation have become so tightly drawn in the popular imagination that there is little room left for ambiguity or subtlety.
This is not to say that China's savage treatment of Tibet has left great ambiguity, but simply that such a good-guys-versus-bad-guys relationship makes it hard for anyone to break free from the powerful field of presumptive gravity that surrounds the subject. 
No matter how authentic the sets and costumes or how "big" the director or stars, films about Tibet find themselves inescapably bounded by a determinism that grows out of what we Westerners unconsciously think about when we imagine Tibet.
We tend to see Tibet through one of the most powerful utopian mythologies of this century -- of a fabled, Shangri-La-like refuge from the outside world. 
When the Chinese People's Liberation Army marched into Tibet's capital, Lhasa, in the 1950's, it occupied not only a geographic place but this beloved Western fantasy as well. 
It violated not only Tibet but our yearning to believe that there was still a place on this shrinking planet where spiritual purity, physical isolation and natural beauty endured and where legions of Buddhist monks spent their lives meditating rather than making Buicks.
Then suddenly the specter of China, land of revolutionary violence, godless (and Buddhaless) Communism and crypto-colonial occupation, intruded on Tibet and our Western reverie. 
Where we saw a benign spiritualism, they saw an oppressive feudal theocracy and a backward serf class in desperate need of Communist "liberation."
So deeply rooted in the Western psyche is our version of Tibet that it has become virtually part of our mental DNA. 
One way or another every article, book or film on Tibet must contend with the political and cultural determinism of this myth. 
But, alas, when a film's conclusion is more or less foregone, it loses the kind of literary tension and mystery that gets us involved. 
Of course, we may feel outraged, an understandable feeling when contemplating Tibet's sad modern history. 
But outrage is rarely enough to hold our attention.
Because conclusions are incipiently imbedded in the very subject matter, Tibet presents a difficult artistic challenge for filmmakers, a headwind against which the spate of recent Tibet films -- Martin Scorsese's "Kundun," Jean-Jacques Annaud's "Seven Years in Tibet" and numerous documentaries -- have had to sail. 
And the fact that Mr. Scorsese and Mr. Annaud could not go to Tibet to shoot only made their efforts more detached from the real place and more dependent on the "imagined Tibet."
Now comes "Windhorse," a low-budget feature film (it cost a mere $300,000, while "Kundun" cost $30 million and "Seven Years in Tibet" $65 million), written, directed and produced by the documentarian Paul Wagner, who won Academy and Emmy Awards for his 1985 film "The Stone Carvers," a portrait of the Italian-American craftsmen who work on the Washington Cathedral. 
With "Windhorse," which opened April 30, Mr. Wagner wanted to pick up where these other films left off.
"No one had covered what had happened since then," he writes of the 1950's in his production notes. 
"To date, over a million Tibetans have been killed by the Chinese. 
There is no freedom of speech and no free press in Tibet, and I've heard of teen-agers being tortured with cattle prods just for wanting to practice their religion. 
That's the situation as it is, not 40 years ago."
Mr. Wagner was determined to shoot at least some of "Windhorse" in Tibet itself. 
But realizing that the Chinese would never grant him permission, he set off in the grand tradition of other Western interlopers who have stolen into Lhasa. 
Posing as a tourist, he and a crew of nonprofessionals managed to film covertly with a Sony mini-DV (digital video) Handycam. 
He says he wanted "to push the envelope in terms of the authorities," to get a sense of what it was like to live and work under China's domination.
Recognizing that certain production values would be lost by using a guerrilla mode of feature filmmaking, Mr. Wagner tried to turn this liability into an asset. 
Indeed, being forced to operate in the same politically supercharged and fearful atmosphere that permeates Tibetan life under occupation does give "Windhorse" an edgy cinema verite authenticity missing in the other, bigger-budget Tibet films. 
And the fact that actors speak Tibetan and Chinese gives the film a further feel of verisimilitude.
THE story centers on a Tibetan family that becomes ensnared in the struggle for freedom from China after a cousin, Pema, who is a Buddhist nun, is arrested and tortured to death. 
The sister, Dolkar, leaves her Chinese boyfriend and quits singing syrupy propaganda songs about "the motherland" in a Lhasa disco, while her ne'er-do-well brother gives up his dissolute life to join the resistance and help smuggle a tape of Pema's story out of Tibet.
Mr. Wagner got interested in Tibet after his own niece, Julia Elliott, who had been living in Katmandu, Nepal, was detained, stripped of her film and camera, interrogated and forced to sign a confession by Chinese police officers while on a trip to Lhasa. 
As Mr. Wagner learned more about Tibet's plight, he became increasingly incensed.
"Tibet has a kind of urgency about it," he told me. 
"It's classic David and Goliath stuff. 
And in my professional work, I love to deal with underdogs."
With Ms. Elliott as his co-writer, Mr. Wagner set off in 1996 on an exploratory trip to Lhasa and quickly fell under the sway of Tibet's unique allure. 
"It is easy to become enamored of the incredible costumes, the intensity of religious faith, the elaborate culture and above all the mountains," he told me as he was editing his film. 
"Tibet has been a temptingly unreachable place. 
For us, it is wanting what we can't have."
Mr. Wagner has captured an elusive piece of this intriguing place's history. 
Yet, as in other Tibet films, we know before we begin that Tibetans will be abused by Chinese subjugators and that there will be no cathartic moment for the victims. 
In this sense, Tibet films are something like Greek tragedies, except it is not a tragic flaw in an individual that brings about inevitable downfall, but the hopeless situation in which Tibetans find themselves.
Although old Tibet has all but vanished and Lhasa is turning into a charmless Chinese city, we Westerners still love to retreat into virtual versions reconstructed on film sets. 
As one of the characters in Frank Capra's 1937 film version of James Hilton's novel "Lost Horizon" presciently says when asked by a colleague if he believes that Shangri-La actually does exist, "I believe it because I want to believe it."
But films like "Windhorse" present such a somber vision of Tibet that it is ever more difficult to conjure up our old fantasies of this fabled land. 
China's reckless occupation has turned this dream, and Tibet's reality, into something of a nightmare. 
That nightmare binds every Tibet film into a strange, subliminal confinement, which makes it not only harder to believe in Shangri-La but also harder to make a film that surprises us with its originality.

file: FILM_What China Would Bury in Moroccan Sand.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Moroccans who were working on "Kundun," Martin Scorsese's movie about the Dalai Lama's boyhood, seemed unimpressed by the transformation of their hometown into the capital of Tibet, complete with Buddhas painted on the hillsides and golden rooftops topping houses in the casbah below. 
Then again, Jerusalem was just down the road, where Turner Network Television had recently shot "David," its latest work in the "Bible" series. 
Perhaps the locals are just inured to strange sights.
Into this town, where tempests are usually strictly of a meteorological variety, came the news that the Chinese Government had denounced "Kundun."
The Chinese have been anything but blase about the goings-on in this town, a gateway to the Sahara nestled in the foothills of the snowcapped Atlas Mountains.
On Nov. 
22, the news broke that the Chinese Government was complaining about the Walt Disney Company's involvement in producing "Kundun."
The movie chronicles the life of the Dalai Lama, who has called for Tibetan independence from China.
"We are resolutely opposed to the making of this movie," a Chinese official said last month. 
"It is intended to glorify the Dalai Lama, so it is an interference in China's internal affairs."
Those on the set when China's denunciation of "Kundun" broke preferred not to discuss their reactions, though the movie's screenwriter, Melissa Mathison, said: "I'm glad it's all out in the open. 
I'm sort of surprised at the dimensions, but I'm not surprised the Chinese would try to stop the movie."
The story has raged on in newspapers around the world, with Disney saying that it will go ahead with the domestic distribution of "Kundun" next year. 
For those involved in the project, which will finish shooting by the end of the month, this is yet another chapter in what has been the long, incident-filled story of the movie's development.
That story begins with the Dalai Lama. 
In 1937, a 2-year-old boy was identified as the 14th reincarnation of the Dalai Lama, the spiritual and political leader of Tibet. 
The boy, Tenzin Gyatso, and his family were taken to Lhasa, the country's capital, where he grew up in the Potala Palace. 
He spent his childhood in study, cared for by other lamas and abbots from the country's greatest Buddhist monasteries.
In 1950, China, led by Mao Zedong, invaded Tibet, its neighbor and former trading partner. 
In response, the Dalai Lama was officially enthroned, at the age of 15. 
At first, the Tibetans thought the Chinese would be supportive, but in 1954, when the Dalai Lama made an official visit to Beijing, it was clear that this was not the case.
"Religion is poison," said Chairman Mao, making his intentions clear.
Despite Chinese occupation, the Dalai Lama and his Tibetan Government refused to make concessions. 
When he turned to the West for help, it did not come. 
When the Dalai Lama's summer residence was shelled, the cabinet decided that he had to leave the country.
In 1959, he crossed into Dharmsala, India, where he still lives, heading a Government in exile.
Ms. Mathison, a screenwriter best known for "E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial," first heard of the Dalai Lama when she was a student at the University of California at Berkeley. 
"Even before I wrote 'E.T.'
I had thought that this would be a great movie," she said.
"I am sort of famous for little-boy stories, and this was a fantastic little-boy story, a story of destiny and nurturing and tragedy, the idea of finding a 2-year-old child and then investing in him everything that is good about human beings, your people and about your beliefs, and then asking that he try to save your country."
In 1990, she wrote a proposal and asked the actor Richard Gere, a well-known supporter of the Tibetan cause, for help in getting it to the Dalai Lama. 
The Dalai Lama himself wrote back to say he would be interested in discussing the project. 
A meeting was set up for April 1990, when he was to be in California to receive an award.
Ms. Mathison recalled that she and her husband, Harrison Ford, went to meet the Dalai Lama at the Red Lion Inn in Santa Barbara. 
"I did a pitch, basically," she said. 
"He said: 'Yes, you may do the movie. 
I'm going to Santa Cruz to rest for two days. 
Why don't you come up and we'll talk?'
"
They accepted that invitation, as well as the next one: to come to India.
A year after first meeting the Dalai Lama, with a draft of a screenplay completed, Ms. Mathison and Mr. Ford went to Dharmsala. 
For six days they talked, and Mr. Ford read the script aloud to him.
"His Holiness would make corrections, or his memory would be jogged and he'd say, 'This reminds me of something' and tell us a story," Ms. Mathison said. 
"And when Harrison got to the end of the script, his Holiness said: 'Good. 
Very good. 
Very strong. 
Very beautiful.'
"
Back home, she began the process of trying to interest a director in the project. 
The one she wanted was Mr. Scorsese, largely because she thought the issues would appeal to him.
"First of all," she said, "it's the story of the male society. 
Secondly, the story of a loyalty to an idea and this man who had the strength, with all of the universe working against him, to stand up to that idea. 
The religious overtones I knew would appeal to Marty. 
I saw it as a story of a kind of wise guy, and I knew he would get what it was about."
She was right.
"There was no doubt," said Mr. Scorsese. "Whether I like it or not, a lot of my movies have religious elements or themes. 
But the key for me in this story is the concept of how you live a life of compassion. 
And I think that goes all the way back to the first lines of 'Mean Streets': 'You don't make up for your sins in a church. 
You do it in the streets. 
You do it at home.'
"These are things that have always fascinated me. 
I've always been torn between what is preached in church and what is acted upon, how people really live. 
And how does one answer such incredible violence and upheaval with nonviolence?
Why is the man who is nonviolent actually stronger?"
After he agreed to take on the project, Mr. Scorsese worked with Ms. Mathison on the script, which he describes as a "story about a little boy who loses a lot in life and gains in other ways."
In March, Mr. Scorsese, Ms. Mathison and others went to India to begin preparation for the film they assumed would be shot there. 
The complex task of casting fell to Ellen Lewis, who has cast all of Mr. Scorsese's movies since "New York Stories," in 1989.
"To do it with people from Tibet is the only way you can do this kind of film," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"You go right back to the lesson of De Sica and Rossellini at the end of World War II. 
You just do it with the people in the street."
He added: "I've worked with a great many nonactors in the past 25 years, although I've never worked with nonactors from a different culture. 
Almost half the speaking cast in 'Casino' was nonactors. 
Many of the people in 'Goodfellas' were nonactors, including my mother."
MS. LEWIS EMBARKED on an elaborate tour of rural India -- "video camera in hand, cows mooing in the background," she said -- to gather people to play the 34 speaking parts, including four to play the Dalai Lama at various ages. 
From New Delhi, she went on to Dharmsala, where the largest population of exiled Tibetans now live.
She was accompanied by Namlha Taklha, the movie's chief technical adviser, who is the widow of Lobsang Samden Taklha, the Dalai Lama's brother. 
They traveled through India, visiting Tibetan enclaves. 
Since they needed Tibetans who spoke English, Ms. Lewis also visited a variety of American and Canadian cities. 
In the end, she cast 15 people from India and the rest from North America.
Although she found the Tibetans receptive to working on "Kundun," which in Tibetan means "the presence of a great incarnation," many were eliminated from consideration because they could not speak English. 
She also found casting difficult because "Tibetans are not an emotive society, they don't show emotion, and that doesn't work for acting."
Some of the cast were chosen solely on the basis of videotape auditions. 
Others had ties to the Dalai Lama's family. 
Mrs. Taklha's nephew, for example, plays the Dalai Lama as an adult. 
The Dalai Lama's niece plays his mother.
Ms. Mathison had already begun trying to get permission to shoot the film in India. 
"I did my stint in the ministers' office, sitting for hours, drinking cups of tea, hoping to talk to somebody," she recalled. 
When Mr. Scorsese became involved, he also tried. 
"We spent a year meeting with the Indian Government to try to get permits to shoot there," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"We met with practically everyone and tried everything. 
But when I went back this past April, we became aware that it was difficult for the Indian Government to give us permission for political reasons. 
China is on their border. 
Ultimately we were told that they 'could not make a decision at this time.'
"
Morocco was suggested as an alternative, partly because its high desert and mountains are extraordinarily similar to those of Tibet, and it is here that many members of the production staff have been working since May.
The production designer Dante Ferretti's journey, like Ms. Lewis's, began in India, where he met four times with the Dalai Lama, who made drawings of the layout of the interior of the Potala, which is controlled by the Chinese.
Mr. Ferretti also met with Mrs. Taklha, and benefited from her finds, including a tiny booklet about the enthronement and snapshots of the actual event. 
Fabrics for the sets and costumes were bought in India.
"I was overwhelmed to see the Tibetan civilization that no longer exists be re-created in Morocco," Ms. Mathison said.
Many of the Tibetans in the cast had seen Tibet only in photographs. 
Ms. Mathison said one young woman had said, on seeing the costumes, "Was Tibet as rich as this?"
Then she hid herself in a corner and wept for what was lost.
Mr. Scorsese witnessed similar displays of emotion. 
"The first day, when many of them had just arrived, I showed them the set of the Potala. 
A number of them prayed, and a few of them were crying."
About a 15-minute drive on the route to Marrakesh from Ouarzazate's hotel zone, the parking lot outside L'Hotel Oscar is filled with beat-up movie trailers. 
The hotel was built for a James Bond film and later appeared on an Egyptian street in "The Jewel of the Nile."
Lhasa rooftops have been affixed to existing structures. 
A sound stage has been built here, as has a replica of the facade of the Dalai Lama's summer palace in Norbulingka, near Lhasa.
Several tents are set up to house 1,600 costumes, including monks' robes and Chinese military uniforms, as well as elaborate Tibetan and Chinese headdresses, all made by hand. 
The budget for the film is $30 million.
On this brilliantly sunny November day, 550 extras were roaming around before the filming of the enthronement scene began on the sound stage. 
Draped in maroon robes, the 129 real Tibetan monks, some from the Dalai Lama's own monastery, were impossible to distinguish from 73 other Tibetans and about 350 Moroccans, who, with their shaved heads, had achieved a similar look.
Inside, the Palace's throne room was thick with the smoke of hundreds of yak butter candles (actually, honey-colored wax), which glinted off the ornate gilt Buddhas.
As the monks took their places, Mr. Scorsese headed for the set from his rickety trailer nearby. 
Despite his surgical mask and a hat to keep out dust from a sandstorm, he looked dapper. 
Tossing a maroon scarf around his neck, he announced wryly, "We love these windstorms."
Because of the intensity of the Chinese reaction to the project, a few of those connected with the film worry that there will be repercussions for some of the Tibetans involved. 
There has already been some discussion of altering their names in the credits, to conceal their participation. 
Even more troubling for the film makers is the fact that the parents of the man playing a main character still live in China.
Asked if there is a possibility that China would ban future Harrison Ford movies because she wrote the script for "Kundun," Ms. Mathison said she was not at all concerned, and pointed out that they had not banned any movies starring Mr. Gere, perhaps the most vociferous advocate of the Tibetan cause in Hollywood.
"It's a wonderful movie, and it's going to be released no matter who releases it," she said in her apartment on Central Park West in Manhattan the day the story about China's reaction to the project was emerging in The New York Times. 
"Disney has said they're very high on it."
Another movie being filmed in Argentina, "Seven Years in Tibet," has apparently escaped censure by the Chinese. 
Based on a book by the mountain climber Heinrich Harrer, "Seven Years in Tibet" is being directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud for Columbia Tri-Star and stars Brad Pitt as Mr. Harrer.
"It's interesting that suddenly, in 1996, a number of these movies are being made," Mr. Scorsese said. 
"It's very good for the cause of Tibet. 
And hopefully, one doesn't take away from the other."

THE MOROCCAN TOWN of Ouarzazate, 125 miles southeast of Marrakesh, bears a name that in Berber means "city of silence."
But this outpost, which was developed by the French as a garrison in 1928, is now anything but. 
First the tourists came, and then the movies. 
Ouarzazate (pronounced WAR-za-zat) has gone Hollywood.
dd French, Arabic and Berber are native tongues, and many film crews speak Italian or English. 
When Martin Scorsese scouted the location 10 years ago for "The Last Temptation of Christ," Ouarzazate had two streets and no electricity. 
There were no cars. 
Today, many still live without electricity or plumbing.
The only movie theater in town, population 20,000, closed six months ago, so it is doubtful whether "Kundun" will be seen here until it is released on video. 
But it has already become a custom to declare an official holiday here when TNT's Biblical productions are shown via satellite, since televisions are plentiful. 
The local residents, many of whom work as extras, are eager to see themselves and their hometown on the screen.
Since 1951, more than 50 movies have been made here. 
The draw is a ready-made Biblical setting that looks more than 2,000 years old and cheap labor. 
A scene from Bernardo Bertolucci's "Sheltering Sky" was shot here, as were Elaine May's "Ishtar," Franco Zefferelli's "Jesus of Nazareth" and David Lean's "Lawrence of Arabia," as well as "The Jewel of the Nile."
An airplane from that film still sits in back of the soundstage where part of "Kundun" is being shot.
Over the past four years, TNT has made six films here; the fifth, "Samson and Delilah," was shown this month. 
And filming for the network's "David," with Jonathan Pryce and Leonard Nimoy, has just been completed.
While on location, actors and crew can stay at the 225-room Berbere Palace hotel, built in 1991.
